activities.differentiation: Provide a visual word bank with symbols for colors, textures, and smells.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally state at least two descriptive words for a given object.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for introduction, 30 minutes for guided group observation of three objects, 15 minutes for summarizing and recording vocabulary.
activities.safety: Ensure objects have smooth edges to prevent splinters or cuts.
activities.task: Introduce the concept of qualitative properties by showing a wooden block, a plastic cup, and a metal spoon. Guide students to describe how each looks, feels, and smells. Write their descriptive words on the board and explain that these are called properties.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw their observations or use pre-printed checklists if writing is challenging.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students record at least three accurate qualitative properties for each of the five objects.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 70 minutes for rotating through five stations (14 mins each), 10 minutes cleanup.
activities.safety: Ensure rocks are clean and large enough not to be swallowed. Remind students to waft smells gently.
activities.task: Set up five observation stations with different everyday materials. Students rotate through the stations, observing the objects and recording three qualitative properties (color, texture, smell) for each in their notebooks.

activities.differentiation: Provide a scribe for students with severe dysgraphia, allowing them to dictate their three words.
activities.mastery_criterion: The student lists three appropriate qualitative descriptors, such as brown, hard, and woody smell.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup and instructions, 40 minutes for independent observation and writing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.safety: Ensure wooden blocks are sanded smooth.
activities.task: Provide each student with a wooden block. Ask them to independently write down three words that describe how it looks, feels, and smells on their assessment sheet.

activities.differentiation: Use rulers with high-contrast markings and highlight the zero line with a permanent marker.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can correctly align the zero mark of a ruler with the edge of an object during guided practice.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes demonstration, 30 minutes guided practice measuring two objects, 10 minutes review.
activities.safety: Remind students not to bend plastic rulers to prevent snapping.
activities.task: Demonstrate how to use a ruler to measure length in centimeters. Show how to align the zero mark with the edge of the object. Measure a pencil and a book as a class, writing the results with the cm unit.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn alignment lines on the images for students who struggle with positioning the ruler.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately measure and record the lengths of at least 8 images within 0.5 cm accuracy.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes measuring 10 different images, 15 minutes sharing results.
activities.safety: Ensure paper edges are smooth to avoid paper cuts.
activities.task: Students work in pairs to measure the length of various printed images of local crops (maize leaves, sugarcane sticks) using a ruler. They record the measurements in centimeters in a structured table.

activities.differentiation: Enlarge the printed lines and provide a magnified ruler for students with visual impairments.
activities.mastery_criterion: The student writes the correct measurement within 0.5 cm of the actual length and includes cm for all five lines.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent measurement, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Give students a worksheet with five printed lines of varying lengths and a ruler. Ask them to measure each line and write the length in centimeters next to it.

activities.differentiation: Pair students to double-check each other's alignment before writing the final number.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students independently align the ruler and read the correct centimeter value.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 25 minutes measuring and charting, 10 minutes review of the chart.
activities.task: Students retrieve their rulers and measure the length of their own pencils and erasers, recording the values on a sticky note to place on a class chart.

activities.differentiation: Tape one end of the string to the desk to help students measure without the string moving.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly measure and sequence the strings based on their centimeter length.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes distribution, 25 minutes measuring and sorting, 10 minutes verification.
activities.safety: Ensure strings are not wrapped around fingers or necks.
activities.task: Provide students with pieces of string of different lengths. They must measure the string in centimeters and order them from shortest to longest on their desks.

activities.differentiation: Use objects with drastically different masses for clear visual cues.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which side of the balance scale holds the object with more mass.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes introduction, 30 minutes guided demonstrations with various objects, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure the balance scale is stable on the table to prevent it from falling.
activities.task: Introduce the balance scale. Demonstrate how placing objects in the cups causes the scale to tip. Show that the side that goes down has more mass. Compare an apple and a grape as a class.

activities.differentiation: Provide a recording sheet with pictures of the objects where students just circle the heavier one.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and record the heavier object for at least 5 pairs using the balance scale.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes group work testing 6 pairs of objects, 15 minutes cleanup and review.
activities.safety: Instruct students to place objects gently into the balance cups to avoid breaking the scale.
activities.task: Students work in small groups with a balance scale. They are given pairs of classroom items (e.g., marker vs crayon, scissors vs glue stick). They predict which has more mass, test it, and record the results.

activities.differentiation: Provide a worksheet with pictures of the objects where students circle the heavier one.
activities.mastery_criterion: The student correctly identifies the object in the cup that goes down as having more mass.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 10 minutes teacher demonstration of 3 pairs, 10 minutes independent recording.
activities.task: Conduct a whole-class demonstration using a balance scale. Place an eraser and a sharpener in the cups. Ask students to independently record on their worksheet which object has more mass based on which cup goes down.

activities.differentiation: Use a magnifying glass icon for qualitative and a ruler icon for quantitative on the T-chart.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that quantitative properties use numbers and qualitative properties use descriptive words.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 30 minutes interactive sorting on the board, 10 minutes summary.
activities.task: Explain the difference between qualitative (words/senses) and quantitative (numbers/measurements) properties. Create a T-chart on the board and sort examples like red, 10 cm, heavy, and 5 grams as a class.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the numbers on the quantitative cards in red to provide a visual scaffold.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 15 out of 20 property cards and can justify one of each type.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes sorting and peer discussion, 15 minutes class review.
activities.task: Students receive a deck of cards with various properties written and illustrated on them. In pairs, they must sort the cards into Qualitative and Quantitative piles, justifying their choices to each other.

activities.differentiation: Read the properties aloud for students who struggle with reading comprehension.
activities.mastery_criterion: All four properties are sorted into the correct categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Provide a worksheet with a list of properties: red, 15 cm, heavy, 30 degrees. Ask the student to write them into Qualitative and Quantitative columns.

activities.differentiation: Use physical gestures consistently when saying the words to reinforce memory.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can match the term malleability to flat objects and ductility to wires.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes introduction, 30 minutes passing around safe examples, 10 minutes vocabulary review.
activities.safety: Ensure the ends of the copper wire are taped or blunted to prevent poking.
activities.task: Introduce malleability by flattening a piece of clay or foil, and ductility by showing a copper wire. Explain the definitions and have students repeat the terms while doing hand motions (pressing flat, pulling long).

activities.differentiation: Provide a chart with pictures of the materials and simple check boxes for flat or wire.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify which materials demonstrate malleability and which demonstrate ductility.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes station exploration, 15 minutes cleanup and sharing.
activities.safety: Monitor that students do not wrap pipe cleaners tightly around fingers.
activities.task: Students explore stations with safe materials (foil, clay, pipe cleaners). They test if they can flatten them (malleability) or stretch them into wire shapes (ductility) and record their findings on a chart.

activities.differentiation: Include a small icon of a hammer next to malleability and a pulling hand next to ductility on the worksheet.
activities.mastery_criterion: Both terms are correctly matched to the corresponding material form.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Show a picture of aluminum foil and a copper wire on a worksheet. Ask the student to draw a line connecting the correct term (malleability or ductility) to the corresponding picture.

activities.differentiation: Use a highly visual before-and-after poster of a rusting bicycle.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state that a color change like rust indicates a chemical property.
materials: rusty nail in a sealed clear jar
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes observation, 30 minutes discussion on environmental exposure, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Keep the rusty nail in a sealed clear plastic jar so students can observe it without touching rust.
activities.task: Show a shiny iron nail and a rusty iron nail. Explain that the color change is evidence of a chemical property reacting to the environment (air/water). Discuss how this is different from just painting the nail.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters: 'I know it is a chemical property because I see...'
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the apple and the bubbles as chemical changes and justify it using evidence of color change or gas production.
materials: pictures of brown apples and melting ice
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes demonstration, 50 minutes group analysis of pictures, 20 minutes class discussion.
activities.safety: Teacher conducts the vinegar/baking soda demonstration. Students wear safety goggles if close. No tasting.
activities.task: Students observe a teacher demonstration of baking soda and vinegar creating bubbles. They then look at pictures of cut apples turning brown and melting ice. They discuss in groups and write down which show chemical properties (bubbles, color change) and justify why.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral justification for students who struggle with writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: The student selects chemical property and cites the color change or environmental exposure as evidence.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent writing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Show two images on a worksheet: a shiny metal gate and a rusty metal gate. Ask the student to circle if the material changed due to a physical or chemical property, and write one sentence justifying their choice based on the color change.

activities.differentiation: Use clear, unambiguous pictures (avoid tricky items like dormant seeds for the introduction).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally explain one reason why a cat is living and a rock is not.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 30 minutes interactive chart building, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Introduce the concepts of living and non-living things. Discuss observable traits like needing food, growing, and moving on their own. Create a class chart sorting pictures of a cat, a rock, a tree, and a car.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so they can discuss their choices before writing them down.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify at least 10 out of 12 hidden items into the correct categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes for the simulated nature walk and sorting, 15 minutes review.
activities.safety: Ensure the classroom is clear of tripping hazards during the walkaround.
activities.task: Simulate a nature walk using large posters of national protected areas around the room. Students walk around with a clipboard, finding hidden picture cards of entities (animals, plants, rocks, water) and sorting them into a living/non-living T-chart.

activities.differentiation: Ensure pictures accompany all words for pre-readers.
activities.mastery_criterion: All four items are placed in the correct categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Provide a worksheet with a list of words and pictures: dog, rock, tree, bicycle. Ask the student to draw a line to sort them into Living and Non-living boxes.

activities.differentiation: Pre-cut a selection of images for students with fine motor difficulties to choose from and glue.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students independently select and correctly categorize four images.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 25 minutes cutting and gluing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Give students old magazines. They must cut out two pictures of living things and two pictures of non-living things, and glue them onto a divided paper.

activities.differentiation: Provide L and N cards for students to hold up instead of writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the category for 8 out of 10 called items.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes distribution, 25 minutes relay game, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Conduct a whiteboard relay. Call out an item (e.g., cloud, bird, volcano, grass). Students write L for living or N for non-living on their personal whiteboards and hold them up.

activities.differentiation: Use hand gestures for each quality (e.g., hand moving up for grow, eating motion for feed).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can repeat the four essential qualities (grow, reproduce, move, feed) when prompted.
materials: storyboard pictures of a dog's life cycle
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes storytelling, 30 minutes discussing the qualities, 10 minutes vocabulary repetition.
activities.task: Explicitly teach the essential qualities of living things: they grow, reproduce, move, and feed. Use a simple story of a puppy growing into a dog, eating food, moving around, and having puppies to illustrate these points.

activities.differentiation: Include clear visual cues on the scenario cards.
activities.mastery_criterion: Groups correctly match all scenario cards to the corresponding biological quality.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes group matching activity, 15 minutes class review.
activities.task: Students work in groups with a set of scenario cards (e.g., a caterpillar eating a leaf, a plant getting taller, a cat with kittens, a dog running). They must match each scenario to the correct quality (feed, grow, reproduce, move).

activities.differentiation: Read the words aloud for the class while they circle.
activities.mastery_criterion: The student circles exactly grow, reproduce, move, and feed.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Provide a worksheet with a list of actions: grow, read, reproduce, feed, move, fly. Ask the student to circle the four actions that all living things do.

activities.differentiation: Provide a physical 3D model of a germinating seed for tactile exploration.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can describe the first thing that comes out of a seed (the root).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explaining the stages, 30 minutes setting up the class demonstration, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure students wash hands after handling seeds. Do not use chemically treated seeds.
activities.task: Explain the process of seed germination. Show a time-lapse video (if possible) or a series of large posters showing a seed sprouting roots, then a stem, then leaves. Set up a class demonstration of a bean in a clear cup with wet paper towels.

activities.differentiation: Number the backs of the cards so students can self-check their sequence.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sequence the 4 stages of germination.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes sequencing and gluing, 15 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Students are given a set of mixed-up picture cards showing the stages of maize germination. They must sequence them in the correct order from dry seed to small plant, and glue them into their notebooks.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank (seed, root, leaf) for students to label their drawings if they wish.
activities.mastery_criterion: Drawings show progression: a plain seed, a seed with a small root, and a seed with a larger sprout/leaves.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes drawing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Provide a worksheet with three blank boxes labeled Day 1, Day 3, and Day 5. Ask the student to draw the changes in a germinating bean seed based on what they learned.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to point to the matching diagram and explain orally.
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the correct stimulus-response match and one for identifying the before/after evidence; both are required.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes image observation, 15 minutes pair matching, 15 minutes evidence discussion, 10 minutes individual check, 10 minutes accessible oral feedback.
activities.safety: No experiment on student eyes, skin or pulse; use supplied records only.
activities.task: Use only teacher-supplied picture pairs and fictional before/after records. Match a supplied change in lighting or movement with the response shown in two fictional records. Cite one visible change.

activities.differentiation: Provide a matching worksheet where students draw a line from the stimulus picture to the response picture.
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the correct stimulus-response match and one for identifying the before/after evidence; both are required.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes instruction and safety rules, 50 minutes testing and recording, 20 minutes class discussion.
activities.safety: No experiment on student eyes, skin or pulse; use supplied records only.
activities.task: Use only teacher-supplied picture pairs and fictional before/after records. Match a supplied change in lighting or movement with the response shown in two fictional records. Cite one visible change.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames: 'When I run, my body _____. This is a response to _____.'
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the correct stimulus-response match and one for identifying the before/after evidence; both are required.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent writing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.safety: No experiment on student eyes, skin or pulse; use supplied records only.
activities.task: Use only teacher-supplied picture pairs and fictional before/after records. Match a supplied change in lighting or movement with the response shown in two fictional records. Cite one visible change.

activities.differentiation: Provide physical objects instead of pictures for students who need tactile input.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which objects require batteries or a plug to function.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for the toy demonstration, 15 minutes for group sorting, 5 minutes for wrap-up.
activities.safety: Ensure battery compartments are screwed shut. Do not use devices that plug into the wall for this demonstration.
activities.task: Introduce electrical and non-electrical devices by showing a battery-operated toy car and a wooden push car. Discuss what makes each move. Show pictures of household items and sort them on the board into 'needs electricity' and 'does not need electricity'.

activities.differentiation: Provide a checklist with images for students who struggle with drawing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 18 of the 20 objects and accurately record their findings.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for exploration, 40 minutes for sorting and discussion, 30 minutes for journaling.
activities.safety: All electrical items must be battery-operated or completely unplugged with cords secured. No exposed wires.
activities.task: Students work in small groups to explore a 'mystery box' containing 20 different safe, unplugged everyday objects (e.g., hairbrush, remote control, book, flashlight, spoon, calculator). They must test or examine each object, discuss with their group, and sort them into two physical hoops labeled 'Electrical' and 'Non-Electrical'. They then draw their sorted groups in their science journals.

activities.differentiation: Read the names of the objects aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies at least 4 out of 5 electrical devices from a mixed set of images.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Students complete a worksheet with 10 images of household items (television, broom, mobile phone, book, fan, etc.). They must circle the ones that need electrical energy to work.

activities.differentiation: Use a brightly colored ball and dark sand instead of flour for better visual contrast.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state that the ball dropped from higher up made a bigger hole because it had more energy.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for demonstration, 15 minutes for discussion, 10 minutes for recording observations.
activities.safety: Ensure students stand back so flour does not get in their eyes. Sweep up any spills immediately to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Discuss amusement park rides like a slide (tobogán). Ask why sliding from a higher point makes you go faster. Demonstrate dropping a heavy plastic ball into a deep tray of flour from 10 cm and then from 50 cm. Discuss how the higher drop gave the ball more energy, creating a larger crater, just like starting higher on a slide gives more energy.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the conclusion (e.g., 'When the block was higher, the splash was...').
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately record that higher drops cause higher splashes and write a logical conclusion.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes setup, 40 minutes experimenting and marking, 30 minutes writing conclusions and cleaning up.
activities.safety: Wipe up spilled water immediately to prevent slipping. Do not use glass objects.
activities.task: Students work in pairs with a basin of water and a plastic block. They drop the block from 20 cm, 40 cm, and 60 cm, observing the splash. They use a large piece of chart paper behind the basin to mark how high the water splashed each time. They write a sentence concluding how height affects the splash.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-labeled graph axes for students who need support with data organization.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully measure the craters and create a bar graph showing a positive correlation between height and crater size.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes experimenting, 45 minutes graphing, 15 minutes sharing results.
activities.safety: Ensure sand is kept in the trays. Do not throw stones; only drop them straight down.
activities.task: Students model volcanic rocks falling from different heights. Using a sand tray, they drop pumice stones from various measured heights and measure the width of the impact craters. They create a simple bar graph showing crater width versus drop height.

activities.differentiation: Allow verbal explanations instead of written ones.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students draw a larger crater for the 50 cm drop and mention height or energy in their explanation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes drawing, 10 minutes writing, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Flashback activity: Show students a picture of the flour tray experiment from the teach activity. Ask them to draw what the tray looked like after a 10 cm drop versus a 50 cm drop, and write one sentence explaining why they look different.

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual diagram of the two trees.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students select the tall tree coconut and justify it by referencing height and energy.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading, 15 minutes writing, 5 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Read a short scenario: 'A coconut falls from a very tall tree, and another falls from a short tree. Which one will hit the sand with more energy?' Students must write their answer and justify it using evidence from past experiments.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to dictate their explanation to the teacher.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately predicts that a higher drop results in more displaced water and justifies it using the concept of mechanical energy.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes analyzing the diagram, 30 minutes writing the prediction and explanation.
activities.task: Look at a diagram of two identical spheres, one held 20 cm above a cup of water and one held 60 cm above. Predict which sphere will cause more water to spill and explain why using evidence from class experiments.

activities.differentiation: Use a buzzer instead of an LED for visually impaired students.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can define conductor as allowing electricity to pass and insulator as blocking it.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for demonstration, 15 minutes for vocabulary introduction and discussion.
activities.safety: Strictly use only 1.5V AA batteries. Never use wall outlets. Ensure wires do not short-circuit for long periods to prevent overheating.
activities.task: Build a simple circuit using a 1.5V AA battery, two wires, and a small LED bulb. Leave a gap in the wires. Test a metal paperclip to close the gap (light turns on) and a plastic spoon (light stays off). Introduce the terms conductor and insulator.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn T-charts with pictures of the objects to be tested.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly test and classify at least 8 out of 10 objects.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes testing at stations, 15 minutes reviewing results.
activities.safety: Only use 1.5V batteries. Monitor groups to ensure they do not short the battery directly.
activities.task: Station rotation: Students use safe 1.5V battery circuits to test 10 different classroom objects (eraser, foil, copper wire, wooden block, etc.). They record their predictions and actual results in a T-chart labeled 'Conductors' and 'Insulators'.

activities.differentiation: Limit the material choices to two distinct options (one metal, one rubber) for students who need simplified decision-making.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully test materials and correctly categorize them as conductors or insulators based on the LED lighting up.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes planning, 40 minutes testing, 30 minutes recording and presenting.
activities.safety: Only use 1.5V batteries. Ensure students understand this is a model and real wall outlets or wires should never be touched.
activities.task: Students test various materials (rubber bands, cloth, foil, paper, paperclips) by placing them in a gap in a simple 1.5V battery circuit to see if the LED lights up. They categorize the materials as conductors or insulators based on whether they block or allow electricity to flow.

activities.differentiation: Provide physical samples of the materials for students to hold while taking the assessment.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 given materials into conductors and insulators.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent sorting.
activities.task: Sort a list of materials (copper wire, plastic spoon, human body, rubber eraser, iron nail) into two columns: 'Conducts Electricity' and 'Blocks Electricity'.

activities.differentiation: Use sound-making toys (electrical to sound) as an additional example for auditory learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally describe that the battery makes the fan blades move.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for demonstrations, 15 minutes for building the anchor chart together.
activities.safety: Ensure fan blades are soft or enclosed so fingers cannot be injured.
activities.task: Show a battery-operated fan turning on (electrical to mechanical) and a wind-up toy moving (potential to kinetic). Discuss how energy doesn't disappear but changes its job. Create a simple anchor chart with arrows showing the changes.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference sheet with the anchor chart for students to check their matches.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully match all pairs and articulate the transformation happening.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes explaining rules, 60 minutes playing the game, 15 minutes group review.
activities.task: Students play a matching card game in pairs. They must match a 'Before' card (e.g., a battery, a wound-up spring) with an 'After' card (e.g., a moving toy car, a spinning fan) and state the energy transformation out loud to their partner.

activities.differentiation: Pair students up so one can draw while the other writes.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students identify at least 3 objects and correctly state their energy transformations.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instructions, 50 minutes scavenger hunt, 25 minutes sharing findings.
activities.safety: Instruct students not to touch wall outlets or switches without permission.
activities.task: Classroom scavenger hunt. Students walk around the room with a clipboard to find 5 objects that transform energy (e.g., pencil sharpener, clock, light switch). They draw the object and write what energy it uses and what it turns into.

activities.differentiation: Read the scenarios aloud for students.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches at least 3 out of 4 scenarios to their energy transformation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Draw lines to connect the object (e.g., a fan plugged into a wall, a child sliding down a slide) to the correct energy change (e.g., electrical to mechanical, potential to kinetic).

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual diagram of solid -> liquid -> gas with heat arrows.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that the sun's heat caused the ice to melt into liquid water.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes initial setup and prediction, 15 minutes later for observation and discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure bags are sealed tightly so water does not leak and cause slipping hazards.
activities.task: Place an ice cube in a sealed plastic bag in a sunny window and another in a dark, cool closet. Ask students to predict what will happen. Check back later to see the melted ice. Discuss how adding heat changes solid to liquid, and conceptually discuss boiling water to make gas.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn panels where students only need to add the heat source and write the sentence.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately depict the three states and correctly identify that adding heat causes the changes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes planning, 60 minutes drawing and writing, 15 minutes sharing comics.
activities.task: Students create a 3-panel comic strip showing the journey of an ice cube. Panel 1: Solid ice. Panel 2: Heat is added (sun or stove), turning it to liquid. Panel 3: More heat is added, turning it to gas. They must write a sentence under each panel explaining the role of heat.

activities.differentiation: Use colored water to make the water level easier to see.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students reason that the heat from the lamp caused the liquid water to turn into a gas.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes setup, 50 minutes observation and recording, 20 minutes concluding discussion.
activities.safety: Use teacher-supplied time-sequence images of shallow water dishes under different warming conditions. Students do not handle hot lamps or heated water.
activities.task: Compare teacher-supplied time-sequence images and water-level records for two shallow dishes under different warming conditions. Describe the observed change and use the supplied heat-transfer model to explain it. No lamps or heated water are handled.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw their prediction instead of writing it.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly predicts the state change and justifies it by referencing the addition or removal of heat.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading, 20 minutes writing.
activities.task: Read a short scenario: 'Maria leaves a bowl of ice cubes in the hot sun. What will happen to the ice, and what must she do if she wants to turn that water into a gas?' Write your prediction.

activities.differentiation: Use highly contrasting objects (very clear vs very dark) for clear visual distinction.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify which object makes a dark shadow and which lets light through.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes demonstration, 10 minutes vocabulary discussion.
activities.safety: Do not shine the flashlight directly into anyone's eyes.
activities.task: Use a strong flashlight in a darkened room. Shine it through a clear glass cup, a piece of wax paper, and a thick book. Ask students to observe what happens to the light and the shadow on the wall behind each object. Introduce transparent, translucent, and opaque.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-cut cardboard shapes for students with fine motor challenges.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully combine opaque and translucent materials to create a functional shadow puppet.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 50 minutes building puppets, 25 minutes testing and performing.
activities.safety: Monitor scissor use. Ensure flashlights are not shined in eyes.
activities.task: Students create a shadow puppet theater. They are given black cardboard (opaque) and colored tissue paper (translucent). They must design a puppet that has both a solid shadow body and glowing colored eyes/features. They test their puppets behind a sheet with a flashlight.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of items to 3 for students who need a quicker task.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort all 5 items based on memory of material properties.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes sorting, 20 minutes discussing why they sorted them that way.
activities.task: Flashback activity: Provide a quick sorting tray with 5 small items (coin, clear plastic cup, wooden block, tissue paper, glass marble). Students must quickly sort them into 'Shadow Makers' and 'Light Passers' based on previous lessons.

activities.differentiation: Provide a picture of a greenhouse to help visualize the scenario.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students select clear plastic and justify it by stating it lets light pass through.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading and thinking, 20 minutes writing.
activities.task: Read a scenario: 'We need to build a greenhouse to help plants grow. Should we use wood or clear plastic for the roof? Why?' Students write their answer recalling that plants need light to pass through.

activities.differentiation: Provide physical objects for the students to look at while taking the test.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 materials as light-blocking (opaque) or light-passing (transparent/translucent).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent sorting.
activities.task: Given a list of items (a thick book, a clear glass window, a wooden door, a piece of clear cellophane, a metal spoon), sort them into a table with two columns: 'Forms a dark shadow' and 'Lets light pass through'.

activities.differentiation: Use a larger prism or a water prism if the spectrum is hard to see.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state that white light is made of many colors.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes discussion and drawing the observation.
activities.safety: Do not shine the flashlight in eyes. Handle the glass prism carefully to avoid dropping and breaking it.
activities.task: In a dark room, shine a flashlight through a glass prism onto a white wall to create a rainbow. Discuss how the white light from the flashlight is actually made of many colors, and the prism breaks them apart.

activities.differentiation: Tape the CD to the desk so students only have to manipulate the flashlight.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully project a spectrum and record the multiple colors that came from the white light.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 50 minutes experimenting and tracing, 25 minutes sharing.
activities.safety: Ensure CDs do not have sharp cracked edges. No shining lights in eyes.
activities.task: Students use old CDs and flashlights to explore light decomposition. They shine the light at the back of the CD at different angles to project rainbows onto paper. They trace the colors they see with crayons to document that white light breaks into multiple colors.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-colored discs for students to just assemble and spin.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students observe and state that spinning the colors makes them look white, showing white light is made of colors.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes coloring, 30 minutes assembling, 30 minutes spinning and discussing.
activities.safety: Ensure students have enough space to spin their discs without hitting others.
activities.task: Students create a 'rainbow spinner' (Newton's disc). They color a paper circle with the colors of the rainbow, attach it to a string, and spin it fast. They observe how the colors blend back together to look almost white, reinforcing that white light is a mix of colors.

activities.differentiation: Read the options aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies that white light can be broken down into multiple colors using a prism.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Look at a diagram showing a flashlight shining white light into a glass triangle (prism) and a rainbow coming out the other side. Circle the sentence that best describes what is happening: A) The glass paints the light. B) The light is broken into many colors. C) The light is blocked.

activities.differentiation: Use large, clear visuals of the color mixing process.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state that mixing base colors creates new colors.
materials: Cyan, magenta, and yellow liquid watercolors or food coloring
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes demonstration, 10 minutes discussion about printers.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not drink the colored water.
activities.task: Demonstrate mixing primary paint colors (cyan, magenta, yellow) in clear cups of water. Show how mixing two colors creates a new color (e.g., yellow and cyan make green). Explain that this is how printers make all the colors in a picture.

activities.differentiation: Tape the cellophane to cardboard frames to make them easier to hold.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately record the new colors created by overlapping the subtractive primary colors.
materials: Cyan, magenta, and yellow cellophane squares
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 50 minutes experimenting, 25 minutes recording.
activities.task: Students are given squares of cyan, magenta, and yellow cellophane. They hold them up to the light in pairs to see what new colors they can make by overlapping them. They record their findings by coloring in overlapping circles on a worksheet.

context_tasks.local-crops: Paint a coffee plant with green leaves, red berries and a brown stem using cyan, magenta and yellow paint. Record which mixtures produce each target color.

activities.differentiation: Provide a color mixing guide chart for students who struggle to remember combinations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully mix the primary colors to create green, red, and brown for their painting.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes planning and mixing practice, 50 minutes painting, 20 minutes cleanup and gallery walk.
activities.task: Paint a pattern containing green circles, red triangles and brown rectangles using only cyan, magenta and yellow paint. Record each mixture and adjust one unsuccessful mixture using the observed result.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw a diagram of ink mixing instead of writing a sentence.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly describes that mixing a few base colors allows printers to create many different colors.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading the prompt, 20 minutes writing.
activities.task: Answer the following question in one sentence: How do inkjet printers make pictures with many different colors if they only use a few ink colors?

activities.differentiation: Provide physical signs for students to hold.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify red as danger/stop and green as safe/go.
materials: Large printed images of safety signs
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes showing signs, 15 minutes discussion on importance.
activities.task: Show large images of local traffic signs (red stop sign) and school emergency exit signs (green). Discuss what the colors mean (red = stop/danger, green = safe/go). Ask students why it is important that everyone agrees on what these colors mean.

activities.differentiation: Provide templates of blank signs (circles, triangles, rectangles) to help start the drawing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students use the correct color for their sign's purpose and state its meaning during their presentation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes brainstorming, 45 minutes drawing, 30 minutes presentations.
activities.task: Students design a safety sign for a local public space (like a park or crosswalk). They must recall and use the correct color: red for a warning/danger sign or green for a safe area/route. They draw the sign and present it, stating the meaning of the color they used.

context_tasks.seismic-risk: Use a teacher-approved school evacuation plan. Apply the supplied color code to its existing routes and obstacles; do not invent or change an emergency route.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-drawn outline of the classroom map.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly apply green for safe routes and red for hazards on their map.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes school walk, 45 minutes mapping, 15 minutes sharing maps.
activities.safety: Ensure students walk calmly during the school tour.
activities.task: Apply a supplied red/green sign code to a fictional floor-plan drawing with marked obstacles and a marked clear route. Compare the coding with a partner and justify one choice using the key.

activities.differentiation: Read the options aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches safety colors to their general meanings in a school or community context.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent matching.
activities.task: Match the color of the sign to its meaning: 1. Red sign with white letters. 2. Green sign with white letters. A) Emergency/Safe route. B) Stop/Danger.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-built sequence for students to observe and label if they struggle with building.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully build a sequence and correctly label at least two energy transformations.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes building, 30 minutes drawing and labeling, 30 minutes sharing with the class.
activities.safety: Ensure objects used are safe and do not pose a projectile hazard.
activities.task: Students build a simple sequence using safe classroom objects (e.g., a toy car rolling down a ramp to hit a bell). They draw their sequence and label the energy transformations happening at each step (e.g., potential to kinetic, kinetic to sound).

activities.differentiation: For students needing visual support, draw a bold line around the 'equator' of the foam ball so the spinning motion is more obvious.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the skewer and identify it as the model's axis, and describe that Earth spins on a similar imaginary line.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for introduction, 15 minutes for the teacher demonstration, and 15 minutes for guided student observation and Q&A.
activities.safety: Teacher prepares the model; no skewers, points or cutting tools are used by students.
activities.task: Use a teacher-preassembled globe or foam-ball model with a blunt paper-tube axis. Demonstrate rotation and point to the imaginary axis. Students do not pierce or assemble the model.

activities.differentiation: Offer a printed rotation diagram or a partner-operated model for students who cannot comfortably rotate the model.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble the model and spin it in place rather than moving it in a circle.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes model inspection, 10 minutes teacher demonstration, 15 minutes paired explanation, 10 minutes individual diagram check.
activities.safety: Only the teacher prepares the models. Use no pointed skewers or sharp tools in the student activity.
activities.task: Use preassembled models made by the teacher with a foam ball and a blunt paper tube. In pairs, demonstrate spinning in place and point to the rotation axis. Students do not pierce or assemble the models.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use a physical stick to temporarily mark the axis before placing stickers if they struggle with the abstract concept.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify opposite ends of the spheres as the poles where the imaginary axis would pass through.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes to explain the task, 15 minutes for hands-on identification with different objects, 5 minutes to share results.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety. Ensure clay is not ingested.
activities.task: Students are given various spherical objects (a plastic ball, a crumpled paper ball, a clay sphere) and must identify where the imaginary axis would be by drawing a line or placing a sticker on the 'poles'.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with outlines of a top and Earth for students to draw the axis line on.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students draw a vertical or slightly tilted line through the center of both the top and the Earth model in their diagrams.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for spinning tops, 20 minutes for drawing diagrams, 10 minutes for class discussion comparing the two.
activities.safety: Ensure tops are spun on flat surfaces and not thrown.
activities.task: Students compare a spinning top to their Earth model. They spin the top on their desks and draw a diagram showing the imaginary axis of the top compared to the Earth model.

activities.differentiation: Allow verbal explanation in place of physical assembly if a student has motor skill limitations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly inserts the axis and spins the model in place, stating the skewer is the imaginary axis.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for individual assessments (rotating through students), 5 minutes for wrap-up.
activities.safety: Teacher prepares the model; no skewers, points or cutting tools are used by students.
activities.task: Use a teacher-preassembled globe or foam-ball model with a blunt paper-tube axis. Demonstrate rotation and point to the imaginary axis. Students do not pierce or assemble the model.

activities.differentiation: Place a bright sticker on El Salvador on the globe so students can easily track when their country moves from day to night.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which side of the globe is experiencing day and which is experiencing night during the demonstration.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for room setup and introduction, 20 minutes for the demonstration and explanation, 15 minutes for student questions and guided observation.
activities.safety: Ensure the room is not completely pitch black to prevent tripping. Do not shine the flashlight directly into students' eyes.
activities.task: Darken the room and use a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth. Shine the light on one side of the globe, explaining that the lit side is day and the dark side is night. Slowly rotate the globe to show the cycle.

activities.differentiation: Provide a stand for the flashlight if a student has difficulty holding it steady.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly rotate the ball in place while keeping the light source stationary, identifying day and night areas.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions and grouping, 20 minutes for hands-on practice, 10 minutes for role-swapping and cleanup.
activities.safety: Instruct students not to shine flashlights in eyes.
activities.task: In pairs, students use a small ball on a stick and a small flashlight. One student holds the 'Sun' steady while the other rotates the 'Earth', observing how the light hits the surface.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-shaded gradient on the Earth for students who need help understanding where the light stops.
activities.mastery_criterion: The half of the Earth facing the light source is colored brightly, and the opposite half is colored darkly.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instruction, 20 minutes for coloring and labeling, 10 minutes for peer review.
activities.task: Students are given a worksheet with a drawing of the Sun and the Earth. They must color the side of the Earth facing the Sun yellow (day) and the side facing away black or dark blue (night).

activities.differentiation: Allow students to point to the areas while the teacher rotates the globe if they cannot manage both objects.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the lit area as day and the shadowed area as night while rotating the globe, keeping the flashlight still.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for setup, 25 minutes for individual assessments, 5 minutes for wrap-up.
activities.safety: Do not shine flashlight in eyes.
activities.task: Using a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth, show why it is daytime in one country and nighttime in another by rotating the globe.

activities.differentiation: Use tactile markers (smooth vs rough) on the ball for visually impaired students.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students immediately and correctly identify the white side as day and the black side as night.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for introduction, 10 minutes for rapid-fire questioning, 5 minutes for summary.
activities.task: Teacher holds up a ball half-painted white and half-painted black. Teacher asks the class to point to the side experiencing 'day' and the side experiencing 'night'.

activities.differentiation: Use larger cards with high-contrast images.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort all activity cards to the corresponding day or night globe image.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes to distribute cards, 10 minutes for the sorting activity, 5 minutes to check answers.
activities.task: Students complete a quick matching card game where they match images of daytime activities with a picture of a sunlit globe, and nighttime activities with a shadowed globe.

activities.differentiation: Place a small figure on the globe so students can visualize the perspective of a person standing on Earth.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state that the Sun appears in the East in the morning because of the direction Earth spins.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explanation, 15 minutes for demonstration, 10 minutes for guided questions.
activities.safety: Do not shine light in eyes.
activities.task: Explain that Earth rotates from West to East. Use a globe and a stationary light source to show how a specific point on the globe enters the light from the East first, making the Sun appear to rise in the East.

activities.differentiation: Guide the flashlight for students who struggle to create the arc motion smoothly.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students draw long shadows on opposite sides of the block for morning and evening.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for setup and safety reminder, 20 minutes for shadow tracing, 10 minutes for discussion.
activities.safety: Strictly enforce that students must not look at the real Sun. This activity uses flashlights only.
activities.task: Students use a small block (representing a building) on a piece of paper. Using a flashlight moving in an arc (to simulate the apparent motion caused by rotation), they trace the shadow of the block in the 'morning' and 'evening'.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the reasoning portion.
activities.mastery_criterion: The Sun is drawn on the East side, and the sentence mentions Earth spinning West to East.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instruction, 15 minutes for drawing and writing, 5 minutes for review.
activities.task: Students are given a simple map with East and West labeled. They must draw a Sun on the side where it would appear in the morning and write a one-sentence reason based on Earth's rotation.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to sit in swivel chairs if standing and rotating is difficult.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that their left side (representing East) enters the light before their face.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for the physical simulation, 10 minutes for debriefing.
activities.safety: Ensure the lamp cord is taped down to prevent tripping. Lamp bulb should not be too hot.
activities.task: Students stand in a circle around a central lamp (Sun). They slowly rotate their bodies to the left (West to East) and note which shoulder (East) sees the light first.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use the block and shadow model to explain if they prefer it over the globe.
activities.mastery_criterion: Prediction is East, justified by demonstrating that the eastern side of a location rotates into the light first on the globe.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for individual assessments, 5 minutes for wrap-up.
activities.task: Based on the fact that Earth rotates from West to East, predict where you will see the Sun in the morning and explain why using your globe model.

activities.differentiation: Use highly contrasting stickers (e.g., neon colors) for visibility.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state that different places have different times because the Sun hits them at different moments.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for introduction, 20 minutes for the globe demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.
activities.task: Place two labelled locations A and B at different longitudes on a globe model. Rotate the model toward a fixed lamp and compare when each location enters the lit side. Discuss the model limit: clock time is set by conventions as well as longitude.

activities.differentiation: Pre-mark the two countries on the globes for students who struggle with geography.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that the country to the East experiences morning (and breakfast) first.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for pair work, 10 minutes for class discussion.
activities.task: Use two labelled locations at different longitudes on a supplied globe diagram. Apply the given rotation direction and compare which enters the lit side first.

activities.differentiation: Use maps with only 3 or 4 distinct zones to reduce visual clutter.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly deduce that zones to the East are later in the day.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes to explain the map, 20 minutes for worksheet completion, 10 minutes for review.
activities.task: Students look at a simplified, color-coded time zone map. They answer questions like: 'If it is noon in the red zone, is it morning or afternoon in the blue zone to the East?'

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual timeline showing El Salvador time vs Europe time side-by-side.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students choose morning, reasoning that Europe is ahead in time and evening there would be too late.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for scenario reading, 20 minutes for writing the decision and justification, 10 minutes for sharing.
activities.task: Students are given a scenario where they must call a relative in Europe. They must decide if they should call during their own morning or evening to ensure the relative is awake, justifying their choice based on rotation.

activities.differentiation: Read the assessment prompt aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student states it is later in Spain because it is to the East and rotated into the sunlight before El Salvador.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for independent assessment, 10 minutes for collection and transition.
activities.task: Use a supplied simplified time-zone map with locations A and B and an explicit offset. Determine which location has the later clock reading using that offset.

activities.differentiation: Have students count out loud or clap to represent the passing of days as the globe moves to emphasize the length of time.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can define revolution as Earth's path around the Sun and state it takes one year or 365 days.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explanation, 15 minutes for the physical demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.
activities.safety: Ensure the walking path is clear of tripping hazards.
activities.task: Explain Earth's revolution around the Sun. Place a large yellow ball (Sun) in the center of the room. Walk a smaller globe around the Sun in a large circle, explaining this path is the orbit and takes 365 days (1 year).

activities.differentiation: If doing both motions is too complex, have the student just focus on walking the orbital path first.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully demonstrate both rotation and revolution simultaneously without confusing the two.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for group practice, 10 minutes for debriefing.
activities.safety: Ensure students walk slowly to avoid dizziness or collisions.
activities.task: Students create a floor model of the orbit. One student stands in the center as the Sun. Another student holds a globe and walks the orbital path, ensuring they also spin the globe (rotation) while walking (revolution).

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn orbital paths for students who need spatial guidance.
activities.mastery_criterion: The model shows the Earth on a drawn circular/elliptical path around the central Sun, correctly labeled.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for material distribution, 15 minutes for modeling and drawing, 5 minutes for cleanup.
activities.task: Students use clay to make a small Sun and a small Earth. They place them on a piece of paper and draw the orbital path with a marker, labeling it '365 days'.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to verbally state the time if they struggle with writing numbers.
activities.mastery_criterion: Drawing shows Earth circling the Sun, with an arrow indicating the path, labeled '365 days' or '1 year'.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for drawing, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Draw a diagram showing the Earth and the Sun. Draw an arrow to show the movement of revolution and label how long one complete movement takes.

activities.differentiation: Provide whiteboards with a dot in the center to help anchor the drawing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students draw a circle or ellipse around a central point representing the Sun.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for distribution, 10 minutes for drawing and holding up, 5 minutes for feedback.
activities.task: Quick whiteboard activity: Teacher says 'Show me the path of revolution'. Students quickly draw the Sun, Earth, and the orbital path on their mini whiteboards and hold them up.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use thumbs up/thumbs down instead of standing/sitting.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify true statements about revolution and its 365-day duration.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for rules, 10 minutes for the game, 5 minutes for summary.
activities.safety: Ensure chairs are pushed in to avoid tripping when standing up and sitting down.
activities.task: True or False game. Teacher reads statements like 'Earth's orbit takes 1 day' or 'Revolution is when Earth goes around the Sun'. Students stand up for True and sit down for False.

activities.differentiation: Use a clock face to visually add the 6 hours (quarter of a day) four times to make a full circle.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state that the extra 6 hours each year add up to a full 24-hour day every four years.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explanation, 15 minutes for the block demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.
activities.task: Explain that Earth's orbit actually takes 365 days and about 6 hours. Use 4 blocks, each representing 6 hours. Show that over 4 years, these blocks add up to 24 hours, creating one extra day (leap year).

activities.differentiation: Pre-count the cubes for students to save time and focus on the concept.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully group the four 6-hour cubes to demonstrate the creation of the extra day.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for group modeling, 10 minutes for discussion.
activities.task: Students work in groups with linking cubes. They build four towers of 365 cubes (represented by a large block) and add one small cube (6 hours) to each. They then combine the 4 small cubes to make a 'new day' block.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the 28th and 29th days on the calendars to draw attention to the change.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students identify the year with 29 days and write that it happens because the extra hours from the orbit added up.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for calendar observation, 15 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for review.
activities.task: Students look at calendars for February over a 5-year period. They must identify the leap year and write a sentence explaining why that specific year has 29 days based on Earth's orbit.

activities.differentiation: Discuss the scenario verbally in a small group before asking students to write.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students deduce that without the extra 6 hours, we would never need to add an extra day to February.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for scenario introduction, 20 minutes for writing/drawing, 10 minutes for sharing.
activities.task: Students are given a hypothetical scenario: 'What if Earth's orbit took exactly 365 days with no extra hours?' They must write or draw what would happen to our calendar (no leap years).

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw the 4 blocks of 6 hours to support their written explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Explanation connects the extra 6 hours of the orbit to the accumulation of a new 24-hour day over four years.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for writing the explanation, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Explain why we add an extra day to February every four years, using the exact time it takes Earth to orbit the Sun.

context_tasks.water-sanitation: Explain that while some places have four seasons, El Salvador mainly experiences two: the dry season (época seca) and the rainy season (época lluviosa). Show pictures of the local landscape during both seasons.

activities.differentiation: Use highly contrasting photos (very dry vs very wet) to make the distinction clear.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can name the dry and rainy seasons and identify one visual difference (e.g., green vs brown vegetation).
materials: Photographs of El Salvador landscapes in dry and rainy seasons
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for explanation, 10 minutes for photo observation, 10 minutes for discussion.
activities.task: Compare a twelve-month rainfall chart with two landscape image sequences. Identify sustained drier and wetter periods using repeated observations rather than a single day.

activities.differentiation: Include text labels on the image cards for early readers.
activities.mastery_criterion: All cards are correctly sorted into the two local seasons.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 15 minutes for sorting, 10 minutes to review answers.
activities.task: Students sort a series of image cards (umbrellas, dry cracked earth, green lush trees, dusty roads) into two columns: Dry Season and Rainy Season.

context_tasks.local-crops: Using the local crops context, students analyze when farmers might plant maize versus when they harvest coffee, linking these activities to the need for water (rainy season) or dry conditions.

activities.differentiation: Read the crop information aloud to the class.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students link planting activities that need water to the rainy season.
materials: Information sheets on maize and coffee
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for reading, 15 minutes for analysis and matching, 5 minutes for sharing.
activities.task: Given a fictional plant requirement card and monthly rainfall data, choose a period that meets the supplied water requirement and justify it. Do not prescribe real crop planting dates from a simplified chart.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with the school building already drawn so students only need to add environmental details.
activities.mastery_criterion: Drawings accurately reflect the environmental conditions and appropriate clothing for both local seasons.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for drawing, 10 minutes for sharing with a partner.
activities.task: Students create a two-panel drawing. On one side, they draw their school during the dry season; on the other, during the rainy season, including appropriate clothing for themselves in the drawing.

context_tasks.water-sanitation: Name the two main seasons that are most noticeable in El Salvador and write one characteristic of each.

activities.differentiation: Allow verbal responses for students who struggle with writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies the lower- and higher-rainfall periods and cites relative values from the supplied chart.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 10 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Use a supplied rainfall chart to name a sustained drier period and a sustained wetter period. Cite one difference in the data.

activities.differentiation: Use a sponge to show how the ground absorbs water until it is full, making the concept more concrete.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that too much water makes the soil loose, leading to landslides during the rainy season.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for discussion, 15 minutes for the physical demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.
activities.safety: Ensure water and soil are kept in the tray to prevent slipping hazards on the floor.
activities.task: Discuss how intense rain during the rainy season can cause natural hazards like floods and landslides. Show a simple physical model: pour water over a mound of loose soil in a tray to demonstrate a landslide.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames: 'I think the [landscape] is vulnerable because...'
activities.mastery_criterion: Students select the steep hill and justify it by stating the rain will wash the loose soil down the slope.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for picture observation, 20 minutes for reasoning and writing, 10 minutes for class discussion.
activities.task: Students are given pictures of different landscapes (a steep hill with no trees, a flat paved area, a riverbank). They must decide which area is most vulnerable to a landslide during the rainy season and justify why.

context_tasks.water-sanitation: Using the water and sanitation context, students read a short scenario about a town's drinking water pipes breaking due to a river overflowing. They must infer which season this occurred in and explain their reasoning.

activities.differentiation: Read the scenario aloud and discuss as a group before asking for written answers.
activities.mastery_criterion: Uses the rainfall and river evidence, then states that a season label alone cannot establish that a flood occurred.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for reading, 20 minutes for writing the inference and justification, 10 minutes for review.
activities.task: Compare a fictional rainfall record and a diagram of a river near a water pipe. Identify when the supplied record supports concern about flooding, and explain why a season label alone cannot establish that a flood occurred.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw their justification if they cannot write it clearly.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student selects the rainy season and justifies it by explaining that intense rain softens the earth, causing the hillside to collapse.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for independent work, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Read a short description of a landslide blocking a road. Decide during which season (dry or rainy) this is most likely to happen and justify your answer.

activities.differentiation: Provide tactile plant models for students with visual impairments.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the roots and stem on a diagram and state their functions in water transport.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for introduction, 15 minutes for observing the celery, 15 minutes for explaining the diagram.
activities.safety: Ensure food coloring is non-toxic and students do not ingest the celery.
activities.task: Introduce plant roots and stems using a pre-prepared celery stalk in colored water to demonstrate water transport.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn outlines for students who struggle with fine motor skills.
activities.mastery_criterion: Diagrams correctly label roots for absorption and stems for transport.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes drawing and labeling, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety with drawing materials.
activities.task: Draw and label diagrams of local crops, specifically identifying roots and stems.

activities.differentiation: Pair students to assist each other with taping and assembling.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students explain how their model represents water moving from yarn (roots) up the straw (stem).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 25 minutes building, 10 minutes explaining models.
activities.safety: Ensure scissors used for cutting yarn are blunt-tipped.
activities.task: Build a physical model of a plant using straws for stems and yarn for roots to simulate water transport.

activities.differentiation: Use cards with high-contrast images and larger text.
activities.mastery_criterion: All root cards are matched to absorption and stem cards to transport.
materials: Sorting cards with images and text
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes explaining the activity, 25 minutes sorting, 10 minutes reviewing answers.
activities.safety: Ensure cards have rounded edges to prevent paper cuts.
activities.task: Sort cards showing different plant parts and match them to their functions (absorption vs transport).

activities.differentiation: Allow students with mobility issues to use a pointer instead of walking.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly walk the path and verbally state the function of the part they are standing on.
materials: Large floor mat with plant diagram
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes taking turns on the mat, 10 minutes wrap-up.
activities.safety: Ensure the floor mat is non-slip to prevent falls.
activities.task: Trace the path of water on a large floor mat depicting a plant, walking from the roots up the stem.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses for students who struggle with writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the root as the part that absorbs water and the stem as the part that transports it.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes completing the diagram, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Label a provided diagram of a plant with the parts responsible for absorbing and transporting water.

activities.differentiation: Provide individual smaller felt boards for tactile learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify food and oxygen as the outputs of the process shown on the board.
materials: Felt cutouts of sun, plant, food, oxygen clouds
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes introduction, 20 minutes interactive felt board demonstration, 15 minutes guided questioning.
activities.safety: Ensure felt pieces are large enough to not be choking hazards.
activities.task: Explain photosynthesis outputs using a felt board model showing sunlight entering and food/oxygen being produced.

activities.differentiation: Assign specific, simple roles for students who need clear, structured tasks.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly state they are making food and releasing oxygen during the role-play.
materials: Props for sun, food, and oxygen
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes assigning roles, 25 minutes role-playing, 10 minutes debriefing.
activities.safety: Ensure clear space in the classroom to prevent tripping during role-play.
activities.task: Role-play the process of photosynthesis where students act as plants producing food and releasing oxygen.

activities.differentiation: Provide templates with pre-drawn panels for students to color and label.
activities.mastery_criterion: Comic strip clearly depicts the plant producing food and oxygen.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes drawing, 10 minutes sharing comics.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety with drawing materials.
activities.task: Create a comic strip showing a plant making its own food and releasing oxygen into the air.

activities.differentiation: Provide puzzles with fewer, larger pieces for students needing simplified tasks.
activities.mastery_criterion: Puzzle is assembled correctly with food and oxygen placed as outputs.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes assembling puzzles, 10 minutes review.
activities.safety: Ensure puzzle pieces are made of non-toxic materials.
activities.task: Assemble a puzzle that shows the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis, focusing on the outputs.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to dictate their explanation to the teacher if writing is a barrier.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student states that plants make their own food and release oxygen.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 25 minutes writing, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Write a short explanation of what a plant produces when it makes its own food using sunlight.

activities.differentiation: Provide clear visual icons alongside text labels for each category.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the category for each of the three examples provided.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes introduction, 20 minutes examining samples, 15 minutes categorizing together.
activities.safety: Ensure no students have allergies to the plant samples used. Do not ingest.
activities.task: Introduce categories of plant utility (food, medicine, raw materials) using real examples like cotton, mint, and corn.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-selected lists of plants for students who need help choosing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize their selected local plants into the three utility groups.
