activities.task: Show pictures of beaks, tongues, and tentacles, explaining how each is used for feeding.

activities.differentiation: Provide larger seeds and wider straws for easier manipulation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully matches the tool used to the corresponding animal feeding structure.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes setup, 30 minutes activity, 15 minutes cleanup and review.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not ingest the seeds or share straws.
activities.task: Use tools like tweezers and straws to pick up different items, matching the tool to an animal structure.

activities.differentiation: Provide fewer options per matching round to reduce cognitive load.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly places all picture cards next to the appropriate diet description.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 35 minutes matching, 10 minutes review.
activities.safety: Ensure tape dispensers are used safely.
activities.task: Match animal pictures to their feeding structures and diet descriptions on a large poster.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank for the feeding functions.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student matches 4 different structures to their correct feeding function.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Match the animal structure (strong beak, long tongue, tentacles) to its feeding function.

activities.differentiation: Use a sponge and water to visually demonstrate extraction of dissolved substances.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can state that gills extract oxygen from water and lungs from air, and use this to infer habitat.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 25 minutes explanation, 15 minutes visual demonstration, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.safety: Ensure students remain seated during the presentation.
activities.task: Discuss the differences between gills and lungs, focusing on oxygen extraction in water versus air, and model how to deduce an animal's habitat based on its respiratory organs.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-written labels for students to paste into the diagram.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly deduces the habitat for all three animals and provides a valid anatomical reason.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 30 minutes diagramming, 15 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Analyze profiles of three unknown animals with different respiratory structures (gills, lungs, skin) and deduce their habitats, justifying the choice.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters such as 'The animal must live in water because...'
activities.mastery_criterion: Student includes the fact that gills are adapted for extracting dissolved oxygen from water in their explanation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes brainstorming, 35 minutes writing, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Write a short paragraph deducing the habitat of a newly discovered organism with gills, justifying why it must live in water using evidence about oxygen.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw their explanation with labels if writing is a barrier.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student justifies why a specific respiratory structure is suited for water or air.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 45 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Read a description of an unknown animal with gills. Deduce its habitat (aquatic) and justify why it cannot survive on land using evidence about oxygen concentration.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to touch the backbone model to feel the structure.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can define a vertebrate as an animal with a backbone.
materials: Plastic skeleton models or printed cardboard cutouts
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explanation, 15 minutes model exploration, 5 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure models do not have sharp edges.
activities.task: Introduce the concept of vertebrates having a backbone and invertebrates lacking one using models.

activities.differentiation: Provide cards with a small bone icon on the back for self-checking.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least 16 out of 20 animal cards.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 35 minutes sorting, 15 minutes review.
activities.task: Sort 20 animal cards into two groups: vertebrates and invertebrates.

activities.differentiation: Use larger pasta tubes and thicker string for students with fine motor challenges.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully strings the pasta to create a flexible backbone model.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 35 minutes building, 10 minutes cleanup.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not eat the raw pasta.
activities.task: Build a simple model of a backbone using pasta and string to understand internal support.

activities.differentiation: Read the animal names aloud for students who need reading support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts 8 out of 10 animals into vertebrate or invertebrate categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 35 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Sort the following animals into vertebrates and invertebrates: dog, spider, snail, fish.

activities.differentiation: Allow extra time for students to process the images on the flashcards.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student quickly and accurately sorts 10 flashcards.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 20 minutes game play, 5 minutes review.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not throw the flashcards.
activities.task: Play a quick flashcard game sorting animals into vertebrates and invertebrates.

activities.differentiation: Provide images next to the animal names in the lists.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the odd one out in 4 out of 5 lists.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes review.
activities.task: Identify the odd one out in lists of animals based on the presence of a backbone.

activities.differentiation: Provide a simplified reference sheet with one picture and one keyword per group.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can name one key trait for mollusks, arthropods, and worms.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes explanation, 20 minutes guided identification, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure posters are securely fastened to the wall.
activities.task: Introduce major invertebrate groups (mollusks, arthropods, worms) focusing on key morphological traits.

activities.differentiation: Pair students to discuss their categorization choices before finalizing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least 8 out of 10 specimens.
materials: Plastic invertebrate models or high-quality printed image cards
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes setup, 45 minutes examination and sorting, 15 minutes review.
activities.safety: Ensure models do not have sharp edges or small swallowable parts.
activities.task: Examine models or images of invertebrates and categorize them into their major groups.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the key morphological traits in the descriptions.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly assigns 4 out of 5 descriptions to the correct invertebrate group.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Read descriptions of invertebrates and assign them to the correct group on a worksheet.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank of the invertebrate groups.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the invertebrate group for 4 out of 5 descriptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 45 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Read the description: 'Soft body, sometimes has a protective shell.' Identify the invertebrate group.

activities.differentiation: Provide physical samples of faux fur, feathers, and scales for tactile learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can state the skin covering for mammals and birds.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes explanation, 20 minutes interactive discussion, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure students remain seated during the presentation.
activities.task: Introduce mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish based on skin covering and reproduction.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Create a chart categorizing 15 local Salvadoran animals (e.g., Torogoz, Garrobo, Masacuata) into the five vertebrate classes using picture cards.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference sheet with the characteristics of each class.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly places at least 12 out of 15 animals in the correct class.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes setup, 45 minutes charting, 15 minutes gallery walk.
activities.task: Sort fifteen supplied animal picture cards into the five vertebrate groups using the visible or explicitly provided distinguishing traits.

activities.differentiation: Provide visual aids alongside the verbal clues.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the class based on a set of 3 clues.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 35 minutes game play, 10 minutes debrief.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not run during the game.
activities.task: Play a 'Guess Who' game using vertebrate characteristics to identify the correct animal class.

activities.differentiation: Read the descriptions aloud for students who need reading support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 animals based on their skin covering.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 45 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Categorize an animal that has hair and does not lay eggs into its vertebrate group.

activities.differentiation: Provide a personal copy of the key for students to trace with their fingers.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can point to the correct next step on the key when asked.
materials: Large dichotomous key on the board
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes step-by-step walkthrough, 20 minutes guided practice, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure clear pathways when students come to the board.
activities.task: Walk through a simple 3-step dichotomous key on the board to identify a common animal.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Use a provided dichotomous key to identify 5 local Salvadoran animals (Torogoz, Garrobo, Masacuata, Tacuazín, Sapo) from pictures.

activities.differentiation: Pair students to work through the key together.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully identifies at least 4 out of 5 animals using the key.
materials: Dichotomous key worksheets (with steps for local fauna)
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes identification activity, 15 minutes review.
activities.task: Use a supplied dichotomous key to identify five labelled animal cards. Trace each choice in the key; do not guess from a familiar name.

activities.differentiation: Provide magnifying glasses for students to see traits more clearly.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies 3 out of 4 plastic insects using the key.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 40 minutes identification, 10 minutes cleanup.
activities.safety: Ensure plastic insects do not have sharp edges.
activities.task: Use a dichotomous key to identify different types of plastic insects based on observable traits.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the path options in different colors to help visual tracking.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully identifies 3 animals using a provided 3-step dichotomous key.
materials: Assessment worksheet with key and pictures
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 50 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Use the provided dichotomous key to identify the animal shown in the picture (a frog).

activities.differentiation: Allow students to verbally explain their path through the key.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies both animals following the key's path.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 30 minutes identification, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Quickly identify 2 animals using a familiar dichotomous key from a previous lesson.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template for recording the steps.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately records the step numbers chosen to reach the final identification.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 25 minutes pair work, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Work in pairs to trace the path of an animal on a dichotomous key and write down the steps taken.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer showing the traits of mammals vs fish.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can state one anatomical reason why a whale is a mammal.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes modeling, 20 minutes guided discussion, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure students remain seated during the presentation.
activities.task: Model how to justify classification using anatomical evidence, explaining why a whale is a mammal.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames for structuring the justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student provides at least two anatomical reasons for each animal's classification.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes reading fact sheets, 50 minutes writing, 20 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Write justifications for classifying 3 tricky local animals (cusuco/armadillo, manatee, local bat) based on anatomy.

activities.differentiation: Provide a list of snake and worm anatomical traits for reference during the discussion.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student contributes at least one anatomical fact (e.g., backbone, scales) to the discussion.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 35 minutes group discussion, 15 minutes class share-out.
activities.safety: Ensure group discussions remain at a respectful volume.
activities.task: Discuss in small groups why a snake is classified as a reptile and not a worm, using anatomical evidence.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to dictate their justification to the teacher.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student provides at least two anatomical reasons for classifying the animal as a mammal.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 50 minutes independent work.
activities.task: A dolphin lives in the ocean, but it has hair, breathes air, and gives birth. Justify why it is a mammal.

activities.differentiation: Provide diagrams with high-contrast colors for students with visual impairments.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly points to and names the nucleus as the defining feature of a eukaryotic cell.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for introduction, 15 minutes for guided tracing, 15 minutes for group discussion and checking.
activities.task: Present large diagrams of a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell. Guide students to identify the nucleus in the eukaryotic cell and note its absence in the prokaryotic cell. Students trace the nucleus with a marker on their own copies.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference card showing a clear example of each cell type.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least 8 out of 10 cards into the proper categories.
materials: Sets of 10 cell model cards per pair
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup and instructions, 25 minutes sorting, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students work in pairs to sort 10 cards showing various abstract cell models into two piles: prokaryotic and eukaryotic, based on the presence of a nucleus.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student produces two distinct drawings, one with a labeled nucleus and one without, accompanied by an accurate explanatory sentence.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes drawing and writing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students draw their own models of a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell, ensuring they clearly label the nucleus in the eukaryotic drawing and write a sentence explaining the difference.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the area where a nucleus would typically be to focus attention.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the cell as prokaryotic and justifies the decision by stating the nucleus is missing.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes analysis, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Students analyze a 'mystery cell' diagram that has many complex structures but no nucleus. They must decide if it is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and write a justification based on evidence.

activities.differentiation: Read instructions aloud for students who need reading support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student labels the cell with a nucleus as eukaryotic and circles the nucleus, and labels the cell without a nucleus as prokaryotic.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Provide students with two diagrams of cells, one with a distinct nucleus and one without. Ask them to label each as prokaryotic or eukaryotic and circle the feature that helped them decide.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to hold up a card with the word instead of a hand signal if preferred.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student consistently uses the correct hand signal for the displayed cell type.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes review of rules, 20 minutes gameplay.
activities.task: Rapid-fire flashcard game where the teacher holds up a cell image and students use hand signals (thumbs up for eukaryotic, thumbs down for prokaryotic) to classify it.

activities.differentiation: Provide a partially drawn cell outline.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student draws a cell from memory and circles the nucleus.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instruction, 25 minutes drawing.
activities.task: Students complete a quick exit ticket where they must draw a eukaryotic cell from memory and circle its defining feature.

activities.differentiation: Use icons on the chart (e.g., a crossed-out cell) to support visual learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally list at least two reasons why a virus is not considered a standard living organism.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes guided Q&A, 10 minutes summarizing.
activities.task: Explain the characteristics of viruses using a comparison chart on the board. Emphasize that viruses lack cells, lack metabolism, and need a host to reproduce, which makes them different from living organisms.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of traits for students who need a modified workload.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly colors 'needs a host' and 'causes infections' red, and 'has cells' green.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 25 minutes coloring, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students receive a worksheet with various traits (has cells, needs a host, breathes, causes infections). They must color the boxes that apply to viruses red and the boxes that apply to living cells green.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-made shapes for students with fine motor difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student demonstrates and explains that the virus model requires the cell model to simulate reproduction.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes modeling, 20 minutes demonstrating, 10 minutes cleanup.
activities.safety: Ensure students wash hands after using clay. Do not eat clay.
activities.task: Students use clay to model a virus and a cell. They must demonstrate how the virus cannot do anything on its own until it attaches to the cell model (the host).

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank for the Venn diagram.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student places 'has cells' and 'reproduces alone' in the bacterium section, and 'needs a host' in the virus section.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes diagramming, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students complete a Venn diagram comparing a virus and a bacterium, applying their knowledge of which traits belong to each (e.g., presence of cells, ability to reproduce independently).

activities.differentiation: Read the checklist items aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student checks 'needs a host to reproduce' and 'causes infections', leaving 'has cells' and 'has a metabolism' unchecked.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Give students a checklist of traits (has cells, needs a host to reproduce, has a metabolism, causes infections). Ask them to check only the traits that apply to viruses.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to come closer to observe the emulsion process.
activities.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup and initial demo, 10 minutes adding soap and observing, 10 minutes discussion linking to pathogens.
activities.safety: Ensure the jar is sealed tightly before shaking to prevent spills. Clean up any spills immediately to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Demonstrate the action of soap using a jar with water and oil. Shake it to show they separate. Add liquid soap and shake again to show them mixing. Compare the two mixtures and state that this is an oil model, not a pathogen-killing test. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

activities.differentiation: Provide templates with the first step already drawn.
activities.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes drawing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students draw a three-step comic strip showing what happens to an 'oily pathogen' when washed with only water versus when washed with water and soap. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so one can perform the physical action while the other records observations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 25 minutes experimenting, 10 minutes cleanup and recording.
activities.safety: Ensure floors remain dry. Students must wash hands after the activity.
activities.task: Students conduct a safe experiment by placing a drop of oil on a plastic plate, rinsing it with just water, and then scrubbing it with a soapy sponge to observe the difference. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

activities.differentiation: Provide a cloze paragraph (fill-in-the-blanks) for the explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes sequencing, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students sequence a set of 4 cards showing the process of soap molecules attaching to oil and water, and write a short paragraph explaining why washing hands without soap is ineffective against viruses. Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

activities.differentiation: Read the options aloud for students who need reading support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Describes the observed oil dispersion and states that the model cannot demonstrate universal pathogen killing.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Provide a matching worksheet where students match the substance (Water alone, Water with Soap) to its effect on an oily pathogen (Slides off, Breaks the oily layer apart). Conclude only about the observed oil mixture; do not infer that all pathogens are killed.

activities.differentiation: Use clear visual aids showing 'dirty' water turning 'clean' conceptually.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can state that bleach destroys microorganisms in water and name one household method.
materials: Empty, clean bleach bottle (for visual reference only)
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes survey and discussion, 20 minutes explaining disinfectants, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.safety: Do not use actual bleach in the classroom. Use an empty, thoroughly washed bottle for visual reference only.
activities.task: Survey students about common household water purification methods used in their homes. Discuss the dangers of microorganisms in stagnant water and explain how specific chemicals, like household bleach (lejia), act as disinfectants to destroy these microorganisms.

activities.differentiation: Highlight key terms in the scenarios.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the bleach scenario as correct and explains that sugar/salt do not act as disinfectants.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes reading, 20 minutes writing explanations, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students read three short scenarios about families trying to clean water. They must identify which family used the correct method (bleach) and explain why the other methods (sugar, salt) failed to destroy microorganisms.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn poster layouts.
activities.mastery_criterion: Poster includes the concept that settling dirt does not remove invisible microorganisms, but bleach destroys them.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes poster creation, 10 minutes gallery walk.
activities.task: Students are given a hypothetical problem: a community water tank is contaminated. They must design a poster explaining to the community why adding bleach (in correct proportions) is necessary, rather than just letting the dirt settle.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer to structure the paragraph.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student justifies that microorganisms are invisible and require purification methods like bleach to be destroyed.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes discussion of the claim, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students evaluate a false claim: 'Clear water is always safe to drink.' They write a paragraph justifying why this is false, referencing invisible microorganisms and the need for purification.

activities.differentiation: Read the scenario and options aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student selects bleach (lejia) and justifies that it acts as a disinfectant that destroys or stops the growth of microorganisms.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 35 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Present a scenario where a family needs to clean stagnant water. Provide options: add sugar, add bleach (lejia), or just let it sit in the sun. Ask the student to choose the best option and write one sentence justifying why.

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual anchor chart with symbols for water (moisture) and a thermometer (temperature).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can list moisture and warm temperatures as optimal conditions for microbial growth.
materials: Photos of fresh and moldy bread
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes analyzing photos, 10 minutes summarizing.
activities.safety: Do not bring actual moldy food into the classroom to avoid spore inhalation. Use photos only.
activities.task: Introduce the optimal conditions for microbial growth: moisture, warm temperatures, and oxygen. Use photos of fresh bread versus moldy bread to explain how these conditions accelerate decomposition.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank with terms like 'moisture', 'warm', 'dry'.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the damp, warm environment as the fastest for rotting due to moisture and temperature.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes analysis and labeling, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students analyze a set of photos showing food stored in different places (a damp basement, a sunny dry windowsill, a refrigerator). They must label which environment will cause the food to rot fastest and why.

activities.differentiation: Use pictures of the climates alongside the text.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student matches the humid jungle to the fastest decomposition, justifying it with the presence of moisture and warmth.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes reading and matching, 20 minutes writing justifications, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students are given descriptions of three climates (dry desert, humid jungle, cold tundra). They must match the climate to the expected speed of food decomposition and justify their choice.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames for the prediction and justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student predicts the maize in the damp shed will spoil first because microbes need moisture to grow.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading scenario, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes discussion.
activities.task: Students evaluate a scenario where harvested maize is stored in a damp shed versus a dry silo. They predict which batch will spoil first and justify using evidence about microbial needs.

activities.differentiation: Read the options aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student circles 'wet and warm'.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Give students a list of environments (dry and cold, wet and warm, dry and hot). Ask them to circle the environment where a piece of bread will grow mold the fastest.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of cards in the set.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches 'wet' and 'warm' to 'fast rot'.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 15 minutes gameplay, 5 minutes review.
activities.task: Students play a quick matching game where they match condition cards (e.g., 'wet', 'dry', 'warm', 'cold') to outcome cards ('fast rot', 'slow rot').

activities.differentiation: Allow verbal responses.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student writes down moisture (water/wetness) and warmth (temperature).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes observation, 20 minutes writing, 5 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Provide a single image of a rotting fruit. Ask students to write down the two environmental conditions that most likely caused it to rot quickly.

activities.differentiation: Use a physical sponge to demonstrate water being squeezed out as an analogy for dehydration.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that salt removes water from food, preventing microbial growth.
materials: Diagram showing water leaving a food item when salted
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes analogy demonstration, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.task: Explain dehydration as a preservation method. Describe how adding salt to food draws out the water, and since microorganisms need water to survive, the food is preserved.

activities.differentiation: Provide a recording sheet with guided observation questions.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student records that the salt becomes wet, demonstrating that it pulls moisture out of the 'food'.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes setup, 20 minutes observation and recording, 10 minutes cleanup.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not ingest the salt. Wash hands after the activity.
activities.task: Students use wet sponges to represent fresh food. They cover one sponge in a thick layer of salt and leave another plain. They observe and record how the salt draws moisture out of the sponge over the session.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank including 'moisture', 'microorganisms', 'survive', 'salt'.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains that the salt removed the moisture, making it impossible for decomposing microorganisms to survive.
materials: Photos of fresh and salted meat
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes observation, 25 minutes writing, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students compare photos of fresh meat and heavily salted dried meat. They write a paragraph explaining why the salted meat can be stored at room temperature without rotting.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the correction.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student corrects the statement by explaining that salt preserves food by removing water (dehydration), not by freezing.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes discussion of the misconception, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students evaluate a misconception: 'Salt preserves food by freezing it.' They must write a correction explaining the true mechanism of salt preservation.

activities.differentiation: Read the prompt aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student predicts the salted fish will last longer because the salt removes the water, and microorganisms need water to survive.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 35 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Show a picture of fresh fish and a picture of fish covered in thick salt. Ask the student to predict which will last longer without rotting and explain why using the word 'water' or 'moisture'.

activities.differentiation: Use a physical thermometer to point to the 'slow growth' zone.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can state that cold temperatures slow down microbial growth rather than killing the microbes.
materials: Diagram of a thermometer showing slow vs fast growth zones
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes diagram analysis, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.task: Explain how refrigeration works to preserve food. Emphasize that cold temperatures do not kill microorganisms, but rather slow down their growth and reproduction.

activities.differentiation: Limit the number of cards to sort.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts the foods and justifies that refrigeration slows down the rotting process for perishable items.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes sorting and justifying, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students sort picture cards of various foods into two categories: 'Needs Refrigeration' and 'Can Stay on Table'. They must verbally justify one choice from each category based on microbial growth speed.

activities.differentiation: Provide a letter template with fill-in-the-blanks.
activities.mastery_criterion: The letter explains that warm temperatures allow bacteria to reproduce quickly, while the fridge slows them down.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes brainstorming, 25 minutes writing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students write a short letter to a friend explaining why they shouldn't leave milk out on the counter all day, specifically mentioning what happens to the bacteria in warm versus cold temperatures.

activities.differentiation: Read statements aloud and discuss as a small group before writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the 'kills all bacteria' statement as false and rewrites it to state that the fridge slows down bacteria.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes evaluating and rewriting, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students evaluate a set of True/False statements about refrigeration (e.g., 'The fridge kills all bacteria'). They must rewrite the false statements to make them true.

activities.differentiation: Allow verbal responses for students with writing difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student states it prevents spoiling and clarifies that cold slows down microbial proliferation, not kills them.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Ask the student: 'Why do we put milk in the refrigerator instead of leaving it on the table? Does the cold kill the bacteria or just slow them down?'

activities.differentiation: Use a visual metaphor of 'good bacteria building a fortress' to explain the toxic environment concept.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that good bacteria make acid to keep bad bacteria away.
materials: Diagram of good bacteria producing acid shields
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes diagram analysis, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.task: Introduce the concept of 'good' bacteria. Explain how in foods like cheese or yogurt, beneficial microorganisms produce acid that creates a toxic environment for 'bad' (pathogenic) bacteria, preserving the food.

activities.differentiation: Number the backs of the cards for self-checking.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sequences the cards and identifies the step where good bacteria create a protective environment.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes sequencing, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students sequence a set of cards showing the cheese-making process, focusing on the step where good bacteria are added to produce acid and protect the milk from spoiling by bad bacteria.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn characters for students to color and add dialogue to.
activities.mastery_criterion: The comic and caption accurately depict good bacteria producing a substance (acid) that is toxic to pathogens.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes brainstorming, 25 minutes drawing and writing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students write a short comic strip where a 'good bacteria' defends a piece of cheese from a 'bad bacteria' by producing acid. They must include a caption explaining the science.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer comparing the two items.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains that yogurt contains beneficial microbes that create an environment toxic to spoilage microbes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes observation, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students compare a glass of fresh milk and a cup of yogurt. They write a paragraph explaining why the yogurt lasts longer in the fridge than the fresh milk, referencing the role of beneficial microorganisms.

activities.differentiation: Read the short text aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student mentions that good bacteria produce substances (acid) that stop bad bacteria (pathogens).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading, 25 minutes independent writing.
activities.task: Provide a short text about cheese making. Ask the student to write one sentence explaining how the 'good' bacteria in cheese protect it from 'bad' bacteria.

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual chart with icons for metabolism and reproduction.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can list metabolism and independent reproduction as key traits of living organisms.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes guided discussion, 10 minutes summarizing.
activities.task: Introduce the characteristics of living organisms, focusing on metabolism and independent reproduction. Use a chart to compare living organisms with non-living things.

activities.differentiation: Use 3D models or tactile diagrams for students who benefit from hands-on learning.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can identify and describe the protective covers of pathogens.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes analyzing diagrams, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.task: Explain the structure of pathogens, specifically focusing on their protective covers like cell walls and capsules. Show diagrams of different pathogens highlighting these layers.

activities.differentiation: Provide a simple comparison chart on the board.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can state one characteristic of fungi and one of protozoa.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 10 minutes analyzing photos, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.safety: Use photos of mold, do not bring actual moldy food to avoid spore inhalation.
activities.task: Introduce fungi and protozoa. Explain that fungi grow from spores on food, and protozoa live in water and hunt bacteria. Show pictures of mold on bread and a paramecium.

activities.differentiation: Highlight key words like 'spores', 'food', 'water', and 'hunt' in the descriptions.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly classifies the spore-growing organism as fungi and the water-hunting organism as protozoa.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes classification, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students read short descriptions of mystery microorganisms and classify them as either fungi or protozoa based on their habitat and feeding behavior.

context_tasks.local-crops: Discuss local Salvadoran preservation methods. Show examples or pictures of 'encurtido' (pickled vegetables) and 'pescado seco' (dried fish). Explain how salt, vinegar, and sun-drying keep food from spoiling.

activities.differentiation: Connect the concepts to foods students might eat at home.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can name encurtido and dried fish as local preservation methods.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction, 10 minutes sharing personal experiences, 10 minutes summarizing.
activities.task: Compare supplied pictures and process records for dried, salted and acidified food examples. Identify the preservation step in each record. These are pictures only; do not prepare, taste or judge the safety of stored food.

activities.differentiation: Provide pictures alongside the text on the matching chart.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches encurtido to acid/vinegar and dried fish to dehydration.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes matching, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students create a matching chart connecting the local food (Encurtido, Pescado seco) to the scientific principle that preserves it (Acid/Vinegar environment, Dehydration/Removal of water).

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual anchor chart with icons representing each of the six simple machines.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally state the defining feature of at least three simple machines when prompted.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for direct instruction, 15 minutes for guided observation of the physical items, 5 minutes for closing summary.
activities.safety: Ensure the screw and wedge do not have dangerously sharp points.
activities.task: Introduce the six simple machines by displaying physical examples (a ruler for a lever, a spool for a wheel and axle, a doorstop for a wedge, a ramp for an inclined plane, a screw, and a basic pulley). Explain the defining characteristic of each group.

activities.differentiation: Include the name of the object on the picture card to assist with vocabulary recognition.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least 20 out of 24 cards into the proper simple machine categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 20 minutes sorting activity, 5 minutes peer review.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety; ensure clear pathways during group work.
activities.task: Students work in pairs to sort 24 picture cards of everyday objects (e.g., knife, doorknob, seesaw, slide) into six labeled piles corresponding to the simple machine groups.

activities.differentiation: Provide a checklist with hints (e.g., 'Look near the door for a wheel and axle').
activities.mastery_criterion: Student lists at least four valid examples of simple machines found in the classroom.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes active searching, 5 minutes sharing findings.
activities.safety: Instruct students not to climb on furniture or touch electrical outlets during the search.
activities.task: Conduct a classroom scavenger hunt where students must find and list at least one real-world example of each of the six simple machines within the room (e.g., door hinges, pencil sharpener).

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-folded booklets with sentence starters for the labels.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student produces a mini-book with six distinct, correctly labeled simple machine drawings.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes folding and setup, 20 minutes drawing and labeling.
activities.safety: Use safety scissors if cutting is required for the book folding.
activities.task: Students create a 'Simple Machines Mini-Book' by folding paper and drawing one example of each of the six simple machines, labeling them correctly.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank of the six simple machine types.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least 4 out of 5 provided everyday tools into their corresponding simple machine type.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes distribution and instructions, 15 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Provide students with images of a knife, a ramp, a doorknob, a seesaw, and a screw. Ask them to write the name of the simple machine group each belongs to.

activities.differentiation: Use color-coded stickers on the ruler to represent fulcrum (red), effort (green), and load (blue).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can point to the fulcrum, effort, and load on the physical ruler model for a 1st class lever.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes guided student replication, 10 minutes discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure coins are not put in mouths to prevent choking hazards.
activities.task: Demonstrate the three classes of levers using a ruler, an eraser (fulcrum), and coins (load/effort). Show how moving the components changes the class (1st, 2nd, 3rd).

activities.differentiation: Provide templates with pre-marked holes for the brass fasteners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student constructs three models with the fulcrum, effort, and load in the correct relative positions for each class.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes building models, 5 minutes cleanup.
activities.safety: Instruct students on the safe handling of brass fasteners to avoid skin pricks.
activities.task: Students build paper models of the three lever classes using cardboard strips and brass fasteners, labeling the parts on each model.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference sheet showing the abstract layout of 1st, 2nd, and 3rd class levers.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the three components and identifies the lever class for at least two of the three tools.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes review of classes, 20 minutes independent analysis, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Analyze diagrams of a wheelbarrow, scissors, and tweezers. Students draw arrows to indicate the fulcrum, effort, and load, and state the lever class for each.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so they can discuss the mechanical action before deciding on the class.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least three tools into their proper lever class based on component location.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup and safety briefing, 20 minutes testing and sorting, 10 minutes class discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure all tools are blunt and clean. Supervise handling to prevent pinching fingers.
activities.task: Students are given a mixed bag of safe, everyday tools (e.g., tongs, bottle opener, pliers). They must test them, locate the fulcrum, effort, and load, and sort them by lever class.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use their color-coded reference cards during the assessment.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the three components and identifies it as a second-class lever.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Show a diagram of a wheelbarrow. Ask the student to label the fulcrum, effort, and load, and state which class of lever it is.

activities.differentiation: Provide a diagram of the human skeleton highlighting major joints.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can point to their elbow and identify it as the fulcrum when performing a bicep curl motion.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes guided movement and explanation, 15 minutes mapping concepts to the body.
activities.safety: Ensure students have enough personal space to move without hitting others. Do not force any stretches.
activities.task: Guide students through physical movements (nodding head, standing on tiptoes, bending arm). Explain how bones act as lever arms and joints as fulcrums.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn stick figures for students who struggle with drawing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly circles the knee, elbow/shoulder, and neck joints as fulcrums in the respective drawings.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 15 minutes drawing and labeling, 5 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students draw stick figures performing three actions (kicking a ball, lifting a box, looking up). They must circle the joint acting as the fulcrum in each action.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer with boxes pointing to the arm parts to fill in.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately maps the three lever components to the arm curl movement.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 15 minutes partner observation and mapping, 10 minutes role swap and review.
activities.safety: Use light books to prevent muscle strain.
activities.task: In pairs, one student holds a book in their hand and curls their arm. The partner observes and maps the effort (bicep), fulcrum (elbow), and load (book).

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank (fulcrum, effort, load, joint, muscle, food).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the three components on the jaw diagram.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes introduction to jaw mechanics, 15 minutes labeling, 5 minutes review.
activities.task: Students analyze a diagram of a human jaw chewing food. They must label the temporomandibular joint as the fulcrum, the jaw muscles as effort, and the food as the load.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to describe the components verbally if drawing is a barrier.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately maps the toes as the fulcrum, the ankle/body weight as the load, and the calf muscle pulling up as the effort.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes physical action, 15 minutes drawing and labeling.
activities.safety: Ensure floor is clear of slipping hazards when standing on tiptoes.
activities.task: Ask the student to stand on their tiptoes and then draw a simple diagram of their foot, labeling the fulcrum, effort, and load.

activities.differentiation: Provide a structured observation sheet to record 'Hard to push' or 'Easy to push' for different fulcrum positions.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student states that moving the fulcrum closer to the load makes it easier to lift.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 25 minutes experimentation, 10 minutes synthesizing the law of the lever.
activities.safety: Ensure rulers are sturdy and will not snap under pressure. Keep fingers clear of the pinch point under the book.
activities.task: Conduct an experiment using a sturdy ruler on a pencil fulcrum. Students try lifting a heavy book by pressing the other end, moving the fulcrum closer to and further from the book to feel the difference in required effort.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames for the justification (e.g., 'I placed the fulcrum here because...').
activities.mastery_criterion: Student draws the fulcrum close to the crate and writes that increasing the distance from effort to fulcrum reduces the required force.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes drawing, 20 minutes writing justification, 10 minutes sharing designs.
activities.task: Students design a lever system on paper to lift a heavy crate. They must draw the optimal fulcrum placement and write a short paragraph justifying their choice based on the distance between effort and fulcrum.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the distance between the effort and fulcrum in different colors on the illustrations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student selects Setup A and justifies it by noting the longer distance between the effort and the fulcrum.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes analyzing illustrations, 25 minutes writing predictions and justifications, 10 minutes class review.
activities.task: Students compare two illustrations of lever setups (Setup A has fulcrum near load, Setup B has fulcrum near effort). They predict which requires less effort and write a justification using evidence from the law of the lever.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-labeled axes on the graph paper.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly plots the data points and writes a conclusion stating that as distance from effort to fulcrum increases, effort required decreases.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reviewing data, 20 minutes graphing, 15 minutes writing conclusions.
activities.task: Students are given a hypothetical data table showing effort required at different fulcrum distances. They graph the data and write a conclusion about the relationship between distance and effort.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw their answer in addition to writing the justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student decides to place the fulcrum near the load and justifies it by mentioning the increased distance between fulcrum and effort.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes reading scenario, 25 minutes independent writing.
activities.task: Present a scenario where a heavy box needs to be lifted with a plank. Ask the student to decide where to place the rock (fulcrum) to make it easiest to lift, and justify their choice using the law of the lever.

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual reminder of the ruler experiment.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student marks the end of the crowbar furthest from the crate and explains it maximizes distance from the fulcrum.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes distribution, 10 minutes task completion, 5 minutes review.
activities.task: Quick review scenario: Show a picture of a person using a crowbar to open a crate. Ask students to mark an 'X' where the person should hold the crowbar to use the least effort, and write one sentence explaining why.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank for the justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student draws the fulcrum immediately next to the 50kg weight and writes that this reduces the required effort.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 10 minutes drawing and writing, 5 minutes peer check.
activities.task: Flash diagram task: Students are given a blank lever template and must quickly draw the setup (load, fulcrum, effort) that makes lifting a 50kg weight the easiest, justifying the fulcrum placement.

activities.differentiation: Use a large, clear diagram of a can opener on the board to supplement the physical object.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can point to and name at least two simple machines within the manual can opener.
materials: manual can openers (clean, no sharp edges exposed unnecessarily)
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes introduction to complex machines, 20 minutes guided examination, 10 minutes summarizing findings.
activities.safety: Ensure can openers are clean and students do not touch the sharp cutting wheel.
activities.task: Examine a manual can opener as a class. Guide students to identify the different simple machines that make it up (levers for the handles, wedge for the cutter, wheel and axle for the turner).

activities.differentiation: Provide a checklist of simple machines to look for on the bicycle.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies and locates at least three different simple machines on the bicycle diagram.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes independent analysis, 10 minutes class review.
activities.task: Students analyze a detailed diagram of a bicycle, locating and naming the simple machines present (e.g., wheel and axle, levers for brakes, screws).

activities.differentiation: Work in pairs to allow for collaborative identification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student lists at least two valid simple machines for their assigned complex machine.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 25 minutes analysis and listing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Invention breakdown: Provide pictures of large complex machines (e.g., a construction crane, a mechanical clock). Students list the simple machine parts they can identify visually.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with a starting mechanism (e.g., a lever) to build upon.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student's drawing clearly incorporates and correctly labels three distinct simple machines working together.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes brainstorming, 20 minutes drawing and labeling, 10 minutes gallery walk.
activities.task: Students design a hypothetical complex machine on paper (e.g., a machine to feed a pet) that must incorporate at least three different simple machines, labeling each one.

activities.differentiation: Allow verbal responses for students with writing difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student identifies at least two different simple machines and accurately locates them on the bicycle.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Show a picture of a bicycle. Ask the student to name two simple machines found in it and point out where they are.

activities.differentiation: Use clear, concrete examples and avoid overly abstract philosophical edge cases during introduction.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally distinguish between a tangible object and an intangible process or knowledge.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes direct instruction with examples, 15 minutes guided Q&A.
activities.task: Introduce the concepts of hard (tangible) and soft (intangible) technology by comparing a physical book (hard) to the story/rules inside it (soft), and a smartphone (hard) to its software (soft).

activities.differentiation: Provide icons next to the words for visual learners (e.g., a picture of a hammer).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least 16 out of 20 items.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent sorting, 5 minutes review.
activities.task: Students categorize a list of 20 items (e.g., hammer, recipe, computer, software, chair, business plan) into 'Hard Technology' and 'Soft Technology' columns.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-cut images for students who struggle with fine motor skills.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student's collage accurately reflects the distinction between tangible products and intangible knowledge/processes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 20 minutes creating collage, 5 minutes cleanup.
activities.task: Students create a T-chart collage using magazine cutouts or drawings, placing examples of hard technology on one side and soft technology (represented by symbols like math equations or musical notes) on the other.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames for debate (e.g., 'I think it is hard technology because I can touch the...').
activities.mastery_criterion: Student articulates that the physical object is hard technology, but the information it holds is soft technology.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes introducing edge cases, 15 minutes structured debate, 5 minutes conclusion.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety. Ensure respectful debate guidelines are followed.
activities.task: Class debate on edge cases: Present items like 'a printed recipe book' or 'a USB drive containing software'. Students must argue whether the focus is on the hard or soft technology aspect.

activities.differentiation: Read the items aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts all 4 items into their respective categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 15 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Given a list (a smartphone, a business plan, a wooden chair, a software algorithm), sort them into 'Hard Technology' and 'Soft Technology'.

activities.differentiation: Draw a flowchart on the board as the physical demonstration occurs.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally trace the energy transformation in the flashlight from chemical to light.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes guided flowchart drawing, 10 minutes discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure batteries are not leaking and are handled properly. Do not shine the flashlight directly into eyes.
activities.task: Demonstrate energy transformations using a battery-powered fan and a flashlight. Trace the energy from chemical (battery) to electrical, to mechanical (fan) or light/heat (flashlight).

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank of energy forms (electrical, mechanical, heat, light, sound).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately identifies electrical energy as the input and the correct output energy (heat, light/sound, mechanical) for all three appliances.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes poster creation, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students create an 'energy chain' poster for three common household appliances (e.g., toaster, television, washing machine), identifying the input and output energy forms.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of pairs to 5 for students who need a modified workload.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches at least 8 out of 10 appliance cards to their energy transformation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 25 minutes playing the matching game, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Matching game: Students match cards showing appliances to cards describing their specific energy transformation (e.g., Blender -> Electrical to Mechanical).

activities.differentiation: Provide a fill-in-the-blank flowchart for the sequence.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the sequence: mechanical (cranking) -> electrical -> sound/light.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes observation, 20 minutes flowchart creation, 10 minutes class discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure hand-crank devices are used gently to avoid pinching fingers.
activities.task: Students examine a hand-crank radio or flashlight (or a video of one if unavailable) and trace the energy transformations from human mechanical energy to the final output.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw and label the transformation instead of writing a full sentence.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student states that electrical energy is transformed into mechanical (kinetic) energy.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: Describe the energy transformation that occurs when you turn on an electric fan.

activities.differentiation: Provide calculators for students who struggle with basic multiplication.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can replicate the calculation 100W x 2h = 200Wh on their whiteboard.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction and modeling, 15 minutes guided practice on whiteboards, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Direct instruction on the formula: Power (Watts) x Time (hours) = Energy Consumption (Watt-hours). Walk through an example using a 100W bulb left on for 2 hours.

activities.differentiation: Keep the numbers round (e.g., 50W, 100W, 2 hours) to focus on the process rather than complex arithmetic.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly calculates the Watt-hours for at least 4 out of 5 appliances.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes review of formula, 25 minutes independent calculation, 10 minutes peer grading.
activities.task: Students calculate the daily Watt-hours for a list of 5 appliances, given their power ratings in Watts and daily usage in hours.

activities.differentiation: Provide a step-by-step guide (Step 1: find daily Wh. Step 2: multiply by 7).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly multiplies daily consumption by 7 to find the weekly total.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes modeling a multi-step problem, 25 minutes independent work, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Word problems: Students solve multi-step problems, such as finding the total weekly energy consumption of a television used 3 hours a day.

activities.differentiation: Break the task into smaller group roles (one calculates total watts, one calculates total hours).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly calculates total wattage (300W) and multiplies by hours (6) to get 1800Wh.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes scenario setup, 20 minutes group calculation, 15 minutes class discussion on results.
activities.task: Students estimate the energy consumption for a hypothetical school day by calculating the Wh of 10 classroom lights (30W each) left on for 6 hours.

activities.differentiation: Provide the formula at the top of the page.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student provides the correct numerical answer (400) and unit (Wh).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work.
activities.task: A television uses 100 W of power. If it is turned on for 4 hours, what is the total energy consumption in Watt-hours?

activities.differentiation: Use a visual analogy, like a leaky faucet, to explain phantom load.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can explain what phantom load is and why unplugging devices saves energy.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes direct instruction on phantom load, 15 minutes scenario analysis, 10 minutes Q&A.
activities.task: Discuss 'phantom load' (energy consumed by devices plugged in but turned off). Analyze a scenario of a house left with everything plugged in while the family is on vacation.

activities.differentiation: Provide a letter template with sentence starters for the proposal and justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student proposes a valid action and justifies it by mentioning energy consumed while off.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes brainstorming habits, 20 minutes writing the letter, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students write a short letter to a family member proposing one specific energy-saving habit (e.g., unplugging the TV at night) and justifying it using the concept of phantom load.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so one can spot the device and the other can provide the justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student identifies a plugged-in device and verbally justifies unplugging it to stop phantom load.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes role-play setup and safety rules, 20 minutes auditing, 10 minutes reporting findings.
activities.safety: Instruct students NOT to actually unplug any classroom devices, only to point them out.
activities.task: Role-play: Students act as 'energy auditors' inspecting the classroom. They identify devices plugged in but not in use, recommend unplugging them, and explain why to the class.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-printed facts about energy waste that students can glue onto their posters.
activities.mastery_criterion: Poster includes a clear action and a scientifically accurate justification regarding energy waste.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes poster creation, 10 minutes gallery walk.
activities.task: Students create an energy-saving campaign poster for the school, featuring a rule (e.g., 'Unplug chargers!') and a scientific justification based on energy consumption.

activities.differentiation: Highlight key phrases in the scenario text (e.g., 'plugged in all day', 'at work').
activities.mastery_criterion: Student proposes unplugging the devices and justifies it by mentioning phantom load or unnecessary energy consumption while off.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes reading scenario, 25 minutes independent writing.
activities.task: Read a scenario where a family leaves their microwave and TV plugged in all day while at work. Propose one action they should take to lower their energy bill and explain why it works.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference chart with visual icons for macronutrients and micronutrients.
activities.mastery_criterion: Classifies the nutrient terms using the supplied record and allows several nutrient groups in one food.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for introduction, 25 minutes for modeling the sorting process, and 20 minutes for guided group sorting.
activities.safety: Ensure printed materials have no sharp edges.
activities.task: Introduce macronutrients and micronutrients. Display printed images of 15 common foods and model how to sort them into categories based on their primary nutrient type and whether they are of animal or vegetal origin. Use multi-nutrient food records: a food may contain several nutrient types. Never classify the whole food as a single nutrient.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of food cards to 10 for students needing more time.
activities.mastery_criterion: Classifies the nutrient terms using the supplied record and allows several nutrient groups in one food.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 45 minutes for sorting and gluing, 20 minutes for peer review.
activities.task: Students work in pairs to create a large poster categorizing 20 different food cards into a matrix of macronutrient/micronutrient and animal/vegetal origin. Use multi-nutrient food records: a food may contain several nutrient types. Never classify the whole food as a single nutrient.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses for students with writing difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Classifies the nutrient terms using the supplied record and allows several nutrient groups in one food.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes for independent work, 10 minutes for collection and review.
activities.task: Students complete a written table where they must classify a provided list of 10 foods (e.g., rice, chicken, orange) by their primary nutrient type and origin. Use multi-nutrient food records: a food may contain several nutrient types. Never classify the whole food as a single nutrient.

activities.differentiation: Provide tables with larger print and highlight the kcal column.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct kcal value on the table for a given food item.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explaining the table, 20 minutes modeling the calculation, 20 minutes guided practice.
activities.task: Explain how to read a nutritional table. Model calculating the total kilocalories of a sample meal by finding each item on the table, writing down its kcal value, and summing them up on the board.

activities.differentiation: Provide menus with fewer items for students who need simplified addition tasks.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate mathematical sums matching the table values for all three menus.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes review, 45 minutes calculating, 15 minutes sharing results.
activities.task: Students receive three hypothetical daily menus and a nutritional reference table. They must calculate the total kilocalories for each menu, showing all addition steps.

activities.differentiation: Provide grid paper to help align numbers during addition.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct mathematical sum matching the specific values in the provided table.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent calculation, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students use a provided nutritional table to calculate the total kilocalories in a specific meal consisting of 1 tortilla, 3 tablespoons of beans, and 1 cup of atol.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so one finds the value and the other adds.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate the total kcal for at least three flashcard meals.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 30 minutes activity, 5 minutes cleanup.
activities.task: Flashcard activity where students draw a card with a meal, look up the items on their reference table, and quickly calculate the total kcal on a mini-whiteboard.

activities.differentiation: Allow the use of calculators for verification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Peer verification confirms the correct sum of kilocalories based on the table.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes creating the meal, 15 minutes calculating, 15 minutes peer verification.
activities.task: Students create a 5-item hypothetical meal, calculate its total kcal using the table, and then swap with a peer to verify the calculation.

activities.differentiation: Use simple, round numbers for initial modeling (e.g., 500 kcal intake, activity burns 500 kcal/hour).
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct comparison and difference; explicitly avoids an individual food or exercise prescription.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes concept introduction, 20 minutes modeling, 20 minutes guided discussion.
activities.safety: No exercise challenge, calorie target or student food/body data are collected.
activities.task: Use teacher-provided fictional energy-use records for two activities over equal time intervals. Compare the estimates, calculate a difference and explain why the records do not prescribe exercise or food choices for individual children.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the written justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct comparison and difference; explicitly avoids an individual food or exercise prescription.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instructions, 45 minutes independent work, 15 minutes sharing justifications.
activities.safety: No exercise challenge, calorie target or student food/body data are collected.
activities.task: Use teacher-provided fictional energy-use records for two activities over equal time intervals. Compare the estimates, calculate a difference and explain why the records do not prescribe exercise or food choices for individual children.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral justification for students who struggle with writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct comparison and difference; explicitly avoids an individual food or exercise prescription.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.safety: No exercise challenge, calorie target or student food/body data are collected.
activities.task: Use teacher-provided fictional energy-use records for two activities over equal time intervals. Compare the estimates, calculate a difference and explain why the records do not prescribe exercise or food choices for individual children.

activities.differentiation: Use enlarged diagrams and allow pointing plus oral explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies the zero/unit error and states a matching correction.
materials: Ruler and unoccupied scale or printed images
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explanation, 20 minutes demonstration, 20 minutes Q&A.
activities.safety: No student height, mass, BMI or health data are measured or shared.
activities.task: Inspect fictional diagrams of a model measured with a ruler and a scale. Find a missing unit or non-zero starting point, describe its effect on the record, and correct the recording procedure.

activities.differentiation: Use enlarged diagrams and allow pointing plus oral explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies the zero/unit error and states a matching correction.
materials: Ruler and unoccupied scale or printed images
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes setup, 45 minutes group practice, 15 minutes review of recorded units.
activities.safety: No student height, mass, BMI or health data are measured or shared.
activities.task: Inspect fictional diagrams of a model measured with a ruler and a scale. Find a missing unit or non-zero starting point, describe its effect on the record, and correct the recording procedure.

activities.differentiation: Use enlarged diagrams and allow pointing plus oral explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies the zero/unit error and states a matching correction.
materials: Ruler and unoccupied scale or printed images
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes individual demonstrations (rotating), 10 minutes wrap-up.
activities.safety: No student height, mass, BMI or health data are measured or shared.
activities.task: Inspect fictional diagrams of a model measured with a ruler and a scale. Find a missing unit or non-zero starting point, describe its effect on the record, and correct the recording procedure.

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual sequence chart.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally list the three main steps of cultivation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes presentation, 20 minutes discussion, 20 minutes summarizing.
activities.task: Outline the basic steps of plant cultivation on the board: soil preparation, sowing/transplanting, and care (watering, pest control). Discuss each step using images of a farm.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn panels that students only need to color and label.
activities.mastery_criterion: Comic strip includes distinct panels for soil preparation, sowing, and care.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes planning, 45 minutes drawing, 15 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students create a 3-panel comic strip illustrating a farmer performing the essential steps to cultivate a plant successfully.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses.
activities.mastery_criterion: Includes at least three distinct, accurate steps of cultivation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent writing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students write a short list describing three essential steps a farmer or urban gardener must take to cultivate a plant successfully.
