activities.differentiation: Use physical props to represent each stage.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the correct order of the mapped stages.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explanation, 20 minutes mapping activity, 20 minutes review.
activities.task: Define a supply chain. Map the supply chain of a tomato on the board, from growing/harvesting, to transportation, to selling at a market, to purchasing at home.

activities.differentiation: Number the first and last cards to provide a framework.
activities.mastery_criterion: Logical sequence of at least four distinct supply chain stages glued in order.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instructions, 45 minutes sequencing and gluing, 15 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Students receive a set of mixed cards showing the steps of a supply chain for coffee. They must sequence the cards correctly and glue them onto a flowchart template.

activities.differentiation: Provide a flowchart template with empty boxes.
activities.mastery_criterion: Flowchart includes growing/harvesting, transportation, selling, and purchasing/preparing in a logical sequence.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes drawing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students draw a flowchart showing the steps a tomato takes from being grown on a farm to being eaten at home, labeling each step.

activities.differentiation: Use a visual diagram showing the extra steps for the imported fruit.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state one reason why an imported product has a longer supply chain.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes presentation, 20 minutes comparative discussion, 20 minutes summarizing.
activities.task: Compare the supply chain of a local mango with an imported apple. Discuss how distance adds links to the chain, requiring more transportation, fuel, and time.

activities.differentiation: Provide a fill-in-the-blank paragraph template.
activities.mastery_criterion: Paragraph explicitly references the number of links or distance as the cause for increased resources/time.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes analyzing diagrams, 45 minutes writing, 15 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students analyze two provided supply chain diagrams (one local, one imported) and write a paragraph contrasting their resource use and time.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral explanations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Explanation explicitly references the number of links or distance in the supply chain as the cause.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent writing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students write an explanation of why an apple imported from another country might cost more and take longer to arrive than a mango grown in their town, using the concept of supply chain links.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-labeled axes for the demonstration.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the x-axis, y-axis, and title on the modeled graph.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explanation, 20 minutes modeling, 20 minutes guided practice.
activities.task: Model how to draw a bar chart using a simple data table of food origins. Demonstrate labeling the x-axis and y-axis, choosing a scale, and drawing the bars to the correct height.

activities.differentiation: Provide grid paper with the scale already marked on the y-axis.
activities.mastery_criterion: Chart includes title, labeled axes, correct scale, and accurate bar heights.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instructions, 45 minutes drawing, 15 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Students are given a data table showing hypothetical survey results of favorite local vs. imported fruits. They must construct a complete bar chart on grid paper.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with axes drawn but not labeled.
activities.mastery_criterion: Chart includes title, labeled axes, correct scale, and accurate bar heights.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent drawing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Using a provided data table showing how many students ate local vs. imported fruits, students draw a bar chart with labeled axes and a title.

activities.differentiation: Use clear, simple vocabulary (e.g., 'germs' instead of 'pathogens').
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can explain what the colored water represents and why it is dangerous.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explanation, 20 minutes demonstration, 20 minutes discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure colored water is non-toxic and clean up spills immediately to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Explain the concept of cross-contamination. Use a simulated demonstration with a sponge (representing raw meat) soaked in colored water and a clean piece of plastic (representing bread) to show how germs transfer if the same knife/surface is used.

activities.differentiation: Read the scenarios aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct identification of safe/unsafe practices with justifications referencing germ transfer.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes instructions, 45 minutes independent analysis, 15 minutes class review.
activities.task: Students read 3 short scenarios about food preparation in a kitchen. They must identify which scenarios are safe or unsafe regarding cross-contamination and write a justification for each.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies the transfer of germs/contamination from raw to cooked food as the reason.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent writing, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students write a response to the prompt: 'Why is it important to use a different knife for cutting raw chicken and slicing cooked bread? Justify your answer.'

activities.differentiation: Provide visual cue cards with symbols (a plant for biotic, a rock for abiotic) for students who need visual support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally state the difference between biotic and abiotic components.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for introduction and definition, 15 minutes for modeling the sorting process, 5 minutes for closing questions.
activities.safety: Ensure soil is clean potting soil to avoid pathogens. Wash hands after handling.
activities.task: Introduce the concepts of biotic and abiotic components. Show a tray of mixed items (rocks, soil, water, leaves, twigs, plastic insects) and model how to classify them into two distinct groups on the board.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw items instead of writing words.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly list 5 biotic and 5 abiotic items from their immediate environment.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes prep and instructions, 30 minutes observation walk, 20 minutes sharing and categorizing in class.
activities.safety: Establish clear boundaries for the schoolyard walk. Do not touch unknown plants or animals.
activities.task: Students go on a guided walk around the schoolyard to observe the environment. They carry a clipboard and draw or write 5 biotic and 5 abiotic items they find, then return to class to share.

activities.differentiation: Pre-cut images for students with fine motor difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 cut-out items onto the T-chart.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 35 minutes cutting and sorting, 15 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Provide students with nature magazines. They must cut out 10 pictures of environmental items and glue them onto a T-chart labeled Biotic and Abiotic.

activities.differentiation: Read the list of items aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 environmental items into biotic and abiotic categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students are given a written list of 10 items found in a local park and must classify each as biotic or abiotic by checking the correct box.

activities.differentiation: Use color-coded cards (green for producers, red for consumers, brown for decomposers).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the producer, consumer, and decomposer in the modeled chain.
materials: large picture cards of grass, grasshopper, frog, fungi
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes concept introduction, 20 minutes modeling the chain and arrows, 10 minutes guided questions.
activities.task: Explain producers, consumers, and decomposers. Use large picture cards on the board to model building a simple food chain, explicitly drawing arrows to show the direction of energy flow.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with empty boxes and pre-drawn arrows for students who struggle with spatial organization.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students build valid food chains with correct directional arrows indicating energy flow.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 35 minutes building and recording chains, 15 minutes sharing with another pair.
activities.task: Students work in pairs with sets of organism cards. They must arrange the cards into at least three different valid food chains and draw the energy flow arrows on a recording sheet.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn organism stickers to attach to the cups.
activities.mastery_criterion: The mobile accurately represents a food chain sequence.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes planning, 35 minutes construction, 10 minutes cleanup and display.
activities.task: Students create a 3D food chain mobile using paper cups, string, and drawings of organisms. They must hang them in order of energy flow, from producer at the top to decomposer at the bottom.

activities.differentiation: Limit the number of distractor cards provided to the student.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students build a valid food chain with at least three trophic levels and correct directional arrows.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 30 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Using provided cards of local organisms, students independently arrange them into a food chain and draw arrows showing energy flow on their assessment paper.

activities.differentiation: Provide a printed copy of the text for students to highlight along with the teacher.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can state the difference between an animal's habitat and its niche.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes definitions and analogies, 15 minutes guided reading and highlighting.
activities.task: Define habitat (address) and niche (job). Read a short text about a local bird aloud, pausing to highlight its habitat in one color and its niche in another color on the projector.

activities.differentiation: Highlight key sentences in the profile cards to help students locate information.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly separate habitat and niche information for at least 3 out of 4 animals.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent or pair work, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students receive a set of animal profile cards. They must read each profile and fill out a graphic organizer separating the habitat details from the niche details for each animal.

activities.differentiation: Provide a structured template for the job application.
activities.mastery_criterion: The poster clearly distinguishes the physical location from the ecological role.
materials: reference books or printed fact sheets
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes research and planning, 35 minutes poster creation, 10 minutes gallery walk.
activities.task: Students choose a local animal and create a 'Job Application' poster for it, clearly stating its 'address' (habitat) and its 'skills/duties' (niche) in the ecosystem.

activities.differentiation: Use larger font and double spacing for the text.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the habitat and the niche from a descriptive paragraph of an animal.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent reading and underlining, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students read a description of an otter and underline its habitat in blue and its niche in red.

activities.differentiation: Provide a guided notes sheet with the terms already written.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can name the five interactions and give a basic definition for each.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes presentation of the five concepts, 15 minutes Q&A and concept checking.
activities.task: Introduce the five ecological interactions (predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism) using a slide presentation with clear, relatable examples for each.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use props or draw their scenario on the board instead of acting.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately portray and identify the ecological interactions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes group planning, 35 minutes performances and guessing, 10 minutes debrief.
activities.safety: Ensure physical acting is safe and does not involve actual hitting or rough play.
activities.task: Students work in small groups to act out short, silent skits representing one of the five interactions. The rest of the class must guess which interaction is being portrayed.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of scenario cards to 5 (one for each type).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 scenario cards.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 35 minutes sorting activity, 15 minutes reviewing answers as a class.
activities.task: Students are given 10 scenario cards describing animal interactions. They must sort them into five labeled envelopes corresponding to the five interaction types.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank of the five interaction terms.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label 4 out of 5 interaction scenarios.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 35 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students read 5 short scenarios of animal interactions on a worksheet and label each with the correct ecological term.

activities.differentiation: Use a visual diagram on the board alongside the physical string model.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally explain that removing one species affects both its predators and its prey.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes setup and building the web, 20 minutes modeling the removal and discussing impacts, 10 minutes summarizing.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not trip on the yarn or wrap it around their necks.
activities.task: Model a food web using students holding strings connecting them as different organisms. Ask what happens if one student (e.g., the grasshopper) drops their strings, and trace the impact on predators and prey.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters (e.g., If the primary consumer disappears, the predator will...).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students provide a logical prediction supported by evidence of energy flow disruption.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes analyzing the diagram, 30 minutes writing predictions, 15 minutes sharing and discussing.
activities.task: Students analyze a diagram of a local food web. They must write a short paragraph predicting what would happen to two specific populations if a disease wiped out the primary consumer.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so they can discuss the logic before making changes on the board.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately track the cascading effects of species removal on their game boards.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes explaining rules, 35 minutes gameplay, 10 minutes reflection.
activities.task: Students play a board game where event cards remove certain species from their ecosystem board. They must calculate and record the resulting population changes based on game rules.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses for students with severe writing difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students provide a logical prediction supported by evidence of energy flow disruption.
materials: assessment worksheets with food chain diagram
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 35 minutes independent writing, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students explain in writing what would happen to the frog and grass populations if all grasshoppers were removed from a provided food chain diagram.

activities.differentiation: Provide a partially completed sketch for students to finish.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly predict the increase in prey population and justify it.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes scenario presentation, 20 minutes sketching and partner discussion, 15 minutes class review.
activities.task: Review activity: Present a new scenario where a predator is overhunted. Students must quickly sketch the resulting changes in the food chain and justify their sketch to a partner.

activities.differentiation: Read the cards aloud and allow extra time to write.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students consistently identify the correct ecological consequence of missing organisms.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 30 minutes flashcard rounds, 10 minutes final review.
activities.task: Flashcard review: Students are shown 'What if?' cards regarding missing organisms and must write down the immediate consequence on a mini-whiteboard, holding it up for teacher check.

activities.differentiation: Use a magnifying glass to help students see the meniscus clearly.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can describe the correct eye-level technique for reading a graduated scale.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes explanation of the tool and units, 15 minutes modeling the reading technique.
activities.safety: Wipe up any spilled water immediately to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Introduce the pluviometer. Show a large physical model or clear diagram of a graduated cylinder. Explain how to read the meniscus at eye level in millimeters.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-marked bottles for students who struggle with ruler alignment.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately read the water level on their homemade millimeter scale.
materials: clear plastic bottles cut in half
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes construction, 30 minutes pouring and reading practice, 10 minutes cleanup.
activities.safety: Teacher should pre-cut the plastic bottles to avoid sharp edges. Wipe spills.
activities.task: Students build a simple pluviometer using a plastic bottle and a ruler. They pour different amounts of water into it and practice reading the measurements in millimeters.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so they can verify readings with a partner.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately record the measurements within a 2mm margin of error.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes station rotation, 10 minutes reviewing answers.
activities.safety: Use plastic cylinders if possible. Wipe spills immediately.
activities.task: Set up 5 stations with graduated cylinders containing different amounts of colored water. Students rotate through the stations and record the measurements in millimeters on a lab sheet.

activities.differentiation: Ensure images are high contrast and large print.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately read the water level on a millimeter scale within a 2mm margin of error.
materials: assessment worksheets with clear images of graduated scales
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students read the water level in three different simulated pluviometers (printed images) and record the measurements in millimeters.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer with the definitions pre-written.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can define internal and external geological phenomena.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes presentation and definitions, 10 minutes guided categorization of examples.
activities.task: Explain the difference between internal geological phenomena (originating inside the Earth) and external phenomena (surface level). Show pictures of earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides, and rockfalls.

activities.differentiation: Include clear visual cues on the cards (e.g., a cross-section of the Earth for internal).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify the majority of the event cards.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 35 minutes sorting, 15 minutes class review.
activities.task: Students work in pairs to sort a deck of 20 event cards (text and image) into two piles: Internal Phenomena and External Phenomena.

activities.differentiation: Provide tracing templates for the drawings.
activities.mastery_criterion: Posters accurately depict and explain the origin of one internal and one external event.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes planning, 40 minutes drawing and writing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students create a split-page poster. On one side, they draw and label an internal phenomenon; on the other, an external phenomenon, writing a brief explanation of where the force originates.

activities.differentiation: Read the list aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify 4 out of 5 geological events.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students sort a written list of events (earthquake, landslide, volcanic eruption, tsunami, rockfall) into internal and external phenomena on a worksheet.

activities.differentiation: Provide a diagram of the chemical reaction for visual learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the gas release as the cause of the simulated eruption pressure.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes setup and safety briefing, 15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes explanation of the gas release.
activities.safety: Students must wear safety goggles. Ensure good ventilation. Do not ingest materials.
activities.task: Demonstrate the baking soda and vinegar volcano. Explicitly explain that the bubbles are carbon dioxide gas being released, simulating volcanic pressure, not actual magma thermodynamics.

activities.differentiation: Assign specific roles (measurer, pourer, observer) to ensure all students participate.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully execute the reaction and observe the gas release.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes safety and instructions, 30 minutes experimentation, 15 minutes cleanup and discussion.
activities.safety: All students must wear safety goggles. Wipe spills immediately. Do not ingest.
activities.task: In small groups, students perform the volcano simulation themselves, varying the amount of baking soda to observe changes in the amount of gas produced.

activities.differentiation: Provide a partially drawn cross-section for students to complete and label.
activities.mastery_criterion: Diagrams accurately represent the simulation components, specifically highlighting the gas release.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes review of the simulation, 40 minutes drawing and labeling, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Students draw a detailed, cross-sectional diagram of the volcano simulation they performed, labeling the liquid mixture, the container, and specifically drawing and labeling the escaping carbon dioxide gas bubbles.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to verbally explain their diagram to the teacher.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully execute the reaction and identify the gas bubbles as the simulated volcanic pressure in their diagram.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 15 minutes micro-simulation, 20 minutes drawing and labeling.
activities.safety: Wear safety goggles. Do not ingest.
activities.task: Students perform a micro-version of the volcano simulation individually and then draw a diagram labeling the liquid mixture and the escaping gas on their assessment sheet.

activities.differentiation: Use local, familiar examples to make the concepts concrete.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can distinguish between threats caused by nature and those caused by human activity.
materials: images of natural and anthropogenic threats
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes definitions, 15 minutes analyzing image examples together.
activities.task: Define natural threats (e.g., heavy rainfall) and anthropogenic threats (e.g., trash blocking drains, deforestation). Show contrasting images of both types.

activities.differentiation: Circle areas of interest in the photographs for students who need focus assistance.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify multiple threats and categorize them accurately.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 35 minutes photo analysis, 15 minutes class discussion.
activities.task: Students analyze a set of photographs taken around a hypothetical town. They must identify and list all the natural and anthropogenic threats they can find in the images.

activities.differentiation: Read the case studies aloud in a small group setting.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately highlight and categorize the threats in the text.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes reading and highlighting, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students read three short case studies of different communities. For each, they must highlight natural threats in yellow and anthropogenic threats in green.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer with specific boxes for 'Natural' and 'Anthropogenic'.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify at least one natural and one anthropogenic threat from a given text.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students read a short story about a town and list one natural threat and one anthropogenic threat mentioned in the text.

activities.differentiation: Provide individual, smaller copies of the map for students to look at closely.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify hazard symbols and explain basic vulnerability based on location.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes introducing maps and symbols, 25 minutes modeling vulnerability evaluation, 15 minutes guided practice.
activities.task: Introduce community risk maps. Explain map symbols for hazards (steep slopes, flood zones) and resources (safe zones). Model how to evaluate which area is more vulnerable by pointing to map features.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-drawn town layout where students only need to add the hazard symbols and houses.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students create a map with clear symbols and logically justify vulnerability based on their placement.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes planning, 30 minutes map creation, 15 minutes writing justifications.
activities.task: Students work in groups to create a simple risk map of a fictional town. They must place houses in different zones and write a justification for which house is most vulnerable to a specific threat.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the specific buildings in question on the maps.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students consistently use map evidence (symbols, topography) to justify their vulnerability assessments.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes analyzing maps and writing answers, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Provide students with three different risk maps. For each map, they must answer a scenario question (e.g., 'If heavy rain falls, is the school or the hospital more vulnerable?') and justify their answer using map evidence.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames for the justification paragraph.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students justify why one location is more vulnerable than another based on specific map features.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions and map review, 45 minutes independent writing, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Students look at a provided community risk map. They must decide which house (A or B) is more vulnerable to a landslide and write a paragraph justifying their choice using map symbols.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to discuss with a partner before writing their answer.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students quickly and accurately assess vulnerability and provide verbal justification.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup and map introduction, 30 minutes rapid-fire questions and justifications, 5 minutes wrap-up.
activities.task: Review activity: Project a new risk map on the board. Ask rapid-fire questions about vulnerability. Students write 'A' or 'B' on mini-whiteboards and hold them up, then randomly select students to justify verbally.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of matches required.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly match scenarios to outcomes and provide logical written justifications.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 25 minutes matching and writing, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Matching game: Students match scenario cards (e.g., 'House near a deforested steep slope') with vulnerability outcome cards (e.g., 'High risk of landslide'). They must write one sentence justifying each match.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-printed labels for students to attach.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label 4 biotic and 4 abiotic components in their diorama.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes planning, 35 minutes building, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students create a diorama of a local ecosystem using a shoebox, explicitly labeling at least 4 biotic and 4 abiotic components.

activities.differentiation: Provide graph paper with pre-drawn axes and scales.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately plot the millimeter measurements on a bar graph.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes data review, 35 minutes graphing, 10 minutes discussion.
activities.task: Students analyze a week's worth of simulated rainfall data collected in their pluviometers, graphing the daily measurements in millimeters.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so they can collaborate on identifying threats.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and log at least two natural and two anthropogenic threats.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes instructions, 35 minutes perimeter walk, 15 minutes debrief.
activities.safety: Establish clear boundaries for the walk and ensure adequate supervision.
activities.task: Students walk around the school perimeter to conduct a threat assessment, logging potential natural and anthropogenic threats on a clipboard.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn circles for students with fine motor difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly labels 5 layers and describes the core's energy production.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins introduction, 30 mins drawing and labeling, 15 mins sharing and reviewing.
activities.safety: Do not look directly at the Sun.
activities.task: Draw and label the Sun's layers on a poster board, then write a description of the core.

activities.differentiation: Read descriptions aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Matches all 5 layers to their correct descriptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins instructions, 25 mins independent work, 10 mins peer review.
activities.task: Complete a matching worksheet connecting the names of the Sun's layers to their descriptions.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral explanation of the core for students who struggle with writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Scores 1 point for each correct label and 1 point for the core description.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins assessment completion.
activities.task: Label a blank cross-section diagram of the Sun and write one sentence about the core.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Use a globe and a flashlight to model day and night, then walk the globe around the light to model seasons, discussing how this creates the wet and dry seasons in El Salvador.

activities.differentiation: Use a larger globe for better visibility.
activities.mastery_criterion: Explains that rotation causes day/night and translation with tilt causes seasons, including local wet/dry seasons.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins modeling rotation, 20 mins modeling translation, 35 mins guided discussion and writing.
activities.safety: Ensure flashlight is not shined in eyes.
activities.task: Use a globe and a flashlight to model day and night, then walk the globe around the light to model seasons, discussing how this creates the wet and dry seasons in the supplied location.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Write a short story from the perspective of a person in El Salvador experiencing the wet season and a person in Japan experiencing a different season, explaining the Earth's position.

activities.differentiation: Provide a story template with fill-in-the-blanks.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurately describes the time difference due to Earth's rotation and the seasonal difference due to translation and tilt.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins brainstorming, 30 mins writing, 15 mins sharing.
activities.task: Write a short story from the perspective of a person in the supplied location experiencing the wet season and a person in Japan experiencing a different season, explaining the Earth's position.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Write a paragraph explaining why it is night in El Salvador when it is day in Japan, and how Earth's translation and tilt cause El Salvador's specific location to experience wet and dry seasons instead of four temperate seasons.

activities.differentiation: Allow bullet points instead of a full paragraph.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies rotation for day/night and explicitly links translation plus axial tilt to the specific changing seasons in El Salvador.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins writing.
activities.task: Write a paragraph explaining why it is night in the supplied location when it is day in Japan, and how Earth's translation and tilt cause the supplied location's specific location to experience wet and dry seasons instead of four temperate seasons.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference image on the board.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly labels rotation on axis and translation around Sun.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins sketching, 20 mins class review.
activities.task: Quickly sketch the Earth's rotation and translation, labeling each movement.

activities.differentiation: Pair students for collaborative answering.
activities.mastery_criterion: Answers all three questions correctly based on Earth's movements.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins flashcard activity, 15 mins discussion.
activities.task: Answer three flashcard questions about what causes day, night, and seasons.

activities.differentiation: Use a larger, slower-spinning top for clearer observation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Defines precession as slow change in orientation and nutation as periodic wobble caused by external gravity.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins demonstration, 20 mins defining terms and discussing gravity, 20 mins group discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure tops are spun on flat, clear surfaces.
activities.task: Demonstrate precession and nutation using a spinning top, then define the terms in notebooks, explicitly discussing how the gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon causes Earth's nutation.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn charts.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurately distinguishes between the two movements in the chart.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins setup, 25 mins chart creation, 10 mins review.
activities.task: Create a two-column chart comparing precession and nutation with drawings and definitions.

activities.differentiation: Read definitions aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly matches both terms to their definitions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins instructions, 25 mins quiz completion.
activities.task: Match the terms precession and nutation to their correct definitions on a quiz.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn comic panels to sequence.
activities.mastery_criterion: Comic strip shows collision, debris ring, and Moon formation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins reading, 30 mins drawing, 10 mins sharing.
activities.task: Read a text about the giant impact hypothesis and create a three-panel comic strip showing the event.

activities.differentiation: Provide a vocabulary bank (craters, rocky, atmosphere).
activities.mastery_criterion: Mentions rocky surface, craters, and lack of atmosphere.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins observing photos, 20 mins writing, 10 mins review.
activities.task: Write a descriptive paragraph about the Moon's surface based on photographs.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses.
activities.mastery_criterion: Mentions rocky surface/no atmosphere and the giant impact hypothesis.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins writing.
activities.task: Write two sentences describing the Moon's surface and one explaining the giant impact hypothesis.

activities.differentiation: Work in pairs to hold the model and draw.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurately draws and names the phases based on the model's shadows.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins setup, 40 mins modeling and drawing, 20 mins discussion.
activities.safety: Do not touch the hot lamp bulb.
activities.task: Use a foam ball on a stick and a stationary light source to model and draw the 8 moon phases.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference chart of phases.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly shades the phases for 4 different alignments.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins instruction, 30 mins independent practice, 15 mins review.
activities.task: Given diagrams of Sun-Earth-Moon alignments, predict and shade in the visible moon phase.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies quarter phase and justifies based on viewing angle.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins completion.
activities.task: Predict the moon phase for a 90-degree alignment diagram and justify the answer.

activities.differentiation: Provide the names of the phases to match with drawings.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly sequences the first half of the lunar cycle.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins drawing, 15 mins class review.
activities.task: Draw the sequence of moon phases from new moon to full moon.

activities.differentiation: Allow use of physical models to find the answer.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies full moon.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins thinking/writing, 20 mins discussion.
activities.task: Identify the moon phase if the Earth is directly between the Sun and the Moon.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-marked distances for students to place the balls.
activities.mastery_criterion: Explains how the distance of the moon affects the size of the umbra and the resulting duration of a solar eclipse.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins modeling shadows, 20 mins measuring umbra changes, 35 mins drawing diagrams and discussing.
activities.safety: Do not shine flashlights in eyes.
activities.task: Use flashlights and different sized balls at varying distances to observe how the shadow cone (umbra/penumbra) changes size, relating it to eclipse duration.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use the physical models from the teach activity to help visualize the scenario.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly deduces that the closer moon creates a larger shadow cone and longer eclipses.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins instructions, 30 mins problem solving, 15 mins review.
activities.task: Work through a scenario of a hypothetical planet with two moons at different distances, answering questions about eclipse frequency and duration based on shadow geometry.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the written justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly annotates the diagram showing the closer moon creates a larger umbra and justifies that this leads to a longer solar eclipse.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins writing and annotating.
activities.task: Given a visual diagram showing two moons at different distances from a planet, annotate the diagram to show their shadow cones (umbras) and write a justification for which moon causes a longer solar eclipse.

activities.differentiation: Provide a list of characteristics to place in the Venn diagram.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies Earth at center for geocentric and Sun at center for heliocentric.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins lecture, 30 mins diagram construction, 10 mins sharing.
activities.task: Construct a Venn diagram comparing geocentric and heliocentric models after a brief lecture.

activities.differentiation: Provide scripts for students who struggle with improvisation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurately states the core belief of the assigned model.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins preparation, 20 mins role-play, 10 mins debrief.
activities.task: Role-play scientists from history defending either the geocentric or heliocentric model by stating what is at the center of their universe.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral explanation of the diagram.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies the center for both models and notes a similarity.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins completion.
activities.task: Create a Venn diagram comparing the geocentric and heliocentric models.

activities.differentiation: Pair students to help with counting steps.
activities.mastery_criterion: Calculates steps and recognizes outer planets are much farther apart.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins calculation in class, 45 mins walking the scale outside, 15 mins reflection.
activities.safety: Ensure the field is clear of tripping hazards.
activities.task: Walk a scale model of the solar system on the school field using 1 step = 0.4 AU.

activities.differentiation: Provide a simplified constant multiplier or a reference chart for multiplication.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly calculates the number of steps for at least three planets and accurately identifies the largest gap between consecutive planets.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins instructions, 30 mins calculations and comparisons, 15 mins review.
activities.task: Calculate the scale distances (in steps) for different planets and compare them to determine which planets are closest together and which are farthest apart in the model.

activities.differentiation: Allow use of a calculator.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly calculates 3 steps.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins calculation.
activities.task: Calculate how many steps are needed to represent a planet 1.2 AU away (1 step = 0.4 AU).

activities.differentiation: Highlight key composition words and density numbers on the data cards.
activities.mastery_criterion: Categorizes all 8 planets correctly based on density and composition data.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins introduction, 30 mins sorting and gluing, 15 mins presentation.
activities.task: Analyze data cards of the 8 planets (including density and composition) to discover the pattern and sort them into rocky and gas giant groups.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference chart showing the density thresholds and corresponding materials.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurately classifies exoplanets using density comparisons (rock-like vs gas-like).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins instruction, 25 mins classifying/writing, 10 mins sharing.
activities.task: Review a table of hypothetical exoplanets with raw data (density, radius) linked to familiar materials (e.g., 'density similar to rock' vs 'density similar to air/water') and classify them as rocky or gas giants, writing a justification for each.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank of classification terms.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly sorts the unknown planets and justifies using the density data.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins completion.
activities.task: Classify four unknown planets as rocky or gas giants based on a provided data table of their densities, and justify the choices.

activities.differentiation: Provide the first letter of each planet.
activities.mastery_criterion: Lists Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins writing, 20 mins review.
activities.task: List the four rocky planets from memory.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral response.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies Jupiter as a gas giant because it lacks a solid surface.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins writing, 20 mins discussion.
activities.task: State whether Jupiter is a rocky planet or a gas giant and why.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-cut foldables.
activities.mastery_criterion: Defines asteroids as rocky, comets as icy, and distinguishes meteoroids, meteors, and meteorites by location.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins instruction, 35 mins creating foldables, 10 mins review.
activities.task: Create a foldable defining asteroids, comets, meteoroids, meteors, and meteorites, emphasizing the location change for the last three.

activities.differentiation: Play in small guided groups.
activities.mastery_criterion: Matches all 5 terms correctly during the game.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins setup, 25 mins playing, 10 mins debrief.
activities.task: Play a matching game pairing all 5 terms (asteroid, comet, meteoroid, meteor, meteorite) with their descriptions and locations.

activities.differentiation: Read descriptions aloud.
activities.mastery_criterion: 1 point for each correct match.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins completion.
activities.task: Match the 5 terms (asteroid, comet, meteoroid, meteor, meteorite) to their descriptions on a quiz.

activities.differentiation: Provide reference images of the Moon and the ISS.
activities.mastery_criterion: Explains natural satellites are celestial bodies and artificial are human-made.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins discussion, 20 mins drawing, 10 mins sharing.
activities.task: Draw a natural satellite and an artificial satellite orbiting Earth, labeling the differences.

activities.differentiation: Provide a specific short text about the Hubble telescope.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies a valid artificial satellite and its human-made purpose.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins instruction, 25 mins research/writing, 10 mins sharing.
activities.safety: Ensure safe internet browsing if using tablets.
activities.task: Research one artificial satellite and write three facts about its purpose.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly defines both types and provides valid examples.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins completion.
activities.task: Explain the difference between a natural and artificial satellite, giving one example of each.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-printed dates and mission names to place on the timeline.
activities.mastery_criterion: Associates Apollo 11 with the Moon landing and Voyager with outer planets.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins reading/lecture, 30 mins timeline creation, 10 mins review.
activities.task: Create a timeline of space exploration highlighting Apollo 11 and the Voyager probes.

activities.differentiation: Provide a news report template with fill-in-the-blanks.
activities.mastery_criterion: Includes the main achievement of the chosen mission in the report.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins choosing topic, 25 mins writing, 10 mins reading reports aloud.
activities.task: Write a mock news report announcing either the Apollo 11 landing or the Voyager launch.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses.
activities.mastery_criterion: Identifies Apollo's lunar landing and Voyager's deep space exploration.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins completion.
activities.task: State the main achievement of the Apollo 11 mission and the Voyager probes.

activities.differentiation: Place a visual marker on the wall for students to align the globe's axis with as they walk.
activities.mastery_criterion: Recognizes that the Earth's axis is tilted at 23 degrees and maintains this orientation throughout its orbit.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins demonstration, 20 mins student practice walking the globe, 10 mins discussion.
activities.task: Use a globe to show the 23-degree tilt and walk it around a central light source, ensuring the tilt constantly points in the same direction.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-drawn orbit path.
activities.mastery_criterion: Draws the axis tilted in the exact same direction at all four orbital positions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins instructions, 20 mins drawing, 5 mins review.
activities.task: Draw the Earth at four different points in its orbit around the Sun, focusing purely on drawing the axis correctly tilted and parallel to itself.

activities.differentiation: Allow use of a protractor.
activities.mastery_criterion: Drawings show the axis tilted and parallel to itself at all four positions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 mins setup, 25 mins drawing.
activities.task: Draw the Earth orbiting the Sun at four different points, ensuring the axis is drawn with a consistent 23-degree tilt pointing in the same direction.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn outlines for students who struggle with drawing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels the mouth, esophagus, stomach, and intestines in order.
materials: Large wall diagram of digestive system
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins for direct instruction, 20 mins for drawing, 15 mins for discussion ensures thorough initial exposure.
activities.safety: Ensure students remain seated while drawing to avoid tripping over chairs.
activities.task: Introduce the digestive system organs using a large wall diagram. Spend 15 minutes tracing the path of food from the mouth, through the esophagus, to the stomach and intestines. Spend 20 minutes having students create their own labeled diagrams in their notebooks. Spend 15 minutes discussing the basic function of each organ (mouth for chewing, esophagus for transit, stomach for mixing, intestines for absorption).

activities.differentiation: Include visual icons on the cards for emerging readers.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly pairs at least 4 out of 5 organs with their functions and places them in order.
materials: Sets of organ and function cards
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins review, 25 mins active matching, 15 mins class review allows for repeated exposure and correction.
activities.safety: Ensure card edges are rounded to prevent paper cuts.
activities.task: Students work in pairs with a set of 10 cards (5 organ names, 5 functions). Spend 10 minutes reviewing the organs. Spend 25 minutes playing a matching game where they must pair the organ with its function and place them in the correct transit order. Spend 15 minutes reviewing the correct sequence as a class.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-cut shapes for students with fine motor difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student's 3D model shows the correct anatomical sequence and includes accurate function descriptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins cutting, 25 mins assembly, 15 mins writing provides a tactile learning experience with adequate time for each step.
activities.task: Students create a 3D paper model of the digestive tract. Spend 10 minutes cutting out organ shapes. Spend 25 minutes gluing them in the correct sequence onto a body outline. Spend 15 minutes writing one sentence next to each organ describing its function.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses for students with writing difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the digestive organs and states one basic function for each.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes is sufficient for a focused, independent written task.
activities.task: Administer a written assessment where students are given a list of digestive organs and must draw arrows to show the path of food, then write one basic function for each organ.

activities.differentiation: Use larger, more visible food items if needed for visual clarity.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally distinguish between physical breakdown and substance transformation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins for mechanical demo, 15 mins for chemical demo setup and observation, 30 mins for deep discussion and conceptualization.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not eat the crackers used in the demonstration. Use safety goggles when handling vinegar.
activities.task: Demonstrate mechanical vs. chemical digestion. Spend 15 minutes crushing a cracker (mechanical). Spend 15 minutes placing a cracker in water and another in vinegar to observe changes (chemical model). Spend 30 minutes discussing how crushing changes size but not substance, while the liquid changes the substance's properties.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer for the written comparison.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies crushing as mechanical and dissolving as chemical digestion in their written comparison.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins per activity phase ensures students have time to observe, process, and document their findings.
activities.safety: Ensure good ventilation when using vinegar. Do not ingest chalk or vinegar.
activities.task: Students perform their own digestion modeling. Spend 20 minutes crushing chalk (mechanical). Spend 20 minutes placing chalk in vinegar (chemical). Spend 20 minutes writing a comparison of the two processes in their notebooks, identifying which represents mechanical and which represents chemical digestion.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the justification paragraph.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student differentiates between physical breakdown (mechanical) and substance transformation (chemical) with correct justification.
materials: Video of paper tearing and burning
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins observation, 30 mins for writing and refining the justification.
activities.safety: Do not perform burning in the classroom; use video only.
activities.task: Students observe a video or live demonstration of paper being torn (mechanical) and paper being burned (chemical - modeled via video only for safety). They must write a paragraph classifying each and relating it to human digestion.

activities.differentiation: Read cards aloud for students who need reading support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least 8 out of 10 scenario cards.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins review and 20 mins sorting provides a focused retrieval practice session.
activities.task: Quick recall activity: Spend 10 minutes reviewing previous notes. Spend 20 minutes sorting 10 scenario cards (e.g., 'chewing an apple', 'saliva breaking down starch') into 'Mechanical' or 'Chemical' digestion piles.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw their definitions instead of writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately recalls and communicates the difference between the two types of digestion.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins per phase ensures structured recall and peer validation.
activities.task: Think-pair-share retrieval: Spend 10 minutes individually writing down the definitions of mechanical and chemical digestion from memory. Spend 10 minutes discussing with a partner. Spend 10 minutes sharing with the class.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-drawn face for students to label.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels oxygen entering and carbon dioxide exiting the nose/mouth.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins instruction, 15 mins modeling, 10 mins student practice is a solid introductory block.
activities.task: Introduce respiratory gases. Spend 15 minutes explaining that humans breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Spend 15 minutes drawing a large face on the board with arrows indicating gas exchange. Spend 10 minutes having students copy the diagram and label the gases.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to work in pairs to complete the comic.
activities.mastery_criterion: Comic strip accurately depicts oxygen going in and carbon dioxide coming out.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins brainstorming and 45 mins drawing allows for creative expression of the concept.
activities.task: Create a 'gas exchange' comic strip. Spend 15 minutes brainstorming the journey of an oxygen molecule entering the body and a carbon dioxide molecule leaving. Spend 45 minutes drawing and coloring a 4-panel comic strip illustrating this process.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank (Oxygen, Carbon Dioxide, Nitrogen) for spelling support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student names oxygen as the required gas and carbon dioxide as the expelled waste gas.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes is ample time for a simple labeling assessment.
activities.task: Students are given a diagram of a human face with two blank arrows (one pointing in, one pointing out). They must label the arrows with the correct gases.

activities.differentiation: Verbally guide students who need help connecting the model parts to human anatomy.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies pulling as inspiration and pushing as expiration.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins demonstration and 40 mins hands-on exploration ensures all students interact with the model.
activities.safety: Ensure the cut edges of the plastic bottle are covered with tape to prevent scratches.
activities.task: Demonstrate lung mechanics using a pre-made bottle-and-balloon model. Spend 20 minutes showing how pulling the bottom membrane inflates the inner balloons (inspiration) and pushing deflates them (expiration). Spend 40 minutes letting students take turns manipulating the model and describing what they feel and see.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-assembled models for students with severe fine motor limitations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully builds a working model and writes that expanding the space pulls air in.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 mins assembly and 30 mins testing/writing provides a full hands-on engineering and observation cycle.
activities.safety: Supervise the use of rubber bands to prevent snapping.
activities.task: Students build their own simple lung models. Spend 30 minutes assembling a model using a plastic cup, a straw, and two balloons. Spend 30 minutes testing the models and writing down how the volume changes affect the air inside.

activities.differentiation: Assign less physically demanding roles (like 'air') to students with mobility issues.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately performs their role in the sequence of inspiration and expiration.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins setup and 40 mins active role-play solidifies the mechanical sequence kinesthetically.
activities.safety: Ensure the area is clear of obstacles to prevent tripping during the role-play.
activities.task: Role-play respiratory mechanics. Spend 20 minutes assigning roles (diaphragm, lungs, air). Spend 40 minutes practicing and performing a physical representation where the 'diaphragm' moves down, the 'lungs' expand, and 'air' rushes in, then reversing the process.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to point to diagrams if they are non-verbal.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student manipulates a model to demonstrate how volume changes cause air to enter or leave the simulated lungs.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 40 minutes allows time to assess each student individually or in small groups.
activities.safety: Ensure the model is sturdy and safe to handle.
activities.task: Students are given a bottle-and-balloon model one by one. They must demonstrate inspiration and expiration, and verbally explain which action represents which respiratory movement.

activities.differentiation: Use clear directional arrows for visual learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can state the direction of blood flow for arteries and veins.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins explanation and 25 mins diagramming provides a clear, paced introduction.
activities.task: Introduce arteries and veins. Spend 20 minutes explaining that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood to the heart. Spend 25 minutes drawing a simplified circulatory loop on the board, using red for arteries and blue for veins (noting this is a pedagogical convention).

activities.differentiation: Provide smaller, desk-sized templates for students who cannot work on the floor.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly places and labels arteries (away from heart) and veins (toward heart).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins review, 35 mins active mapping, 15 mins labeling allows for a comprehensive mapping exercise.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not wrap yarn around fingers or necks.
activities.task: Vessel mapping activity. Spend 15 minutes reviewing the concepts. Spend 35 minutes having students trace a body outline on large paper and draw the heart, adding red yarn for arteries (away) and blue yarn for veins (toward). Spend 15 minutes labeling the yarn.

activities.differentiation: Read the descriptions aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student distinguishes arteries from veins based on whether they carry blood away from or toward the heart.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes is sufficient for reading and classifying three descriptions.
activities.task: Students read three short descriptions of blood vessels (e.g., 'This vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs') and classify each as an artery or a vein.

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual diagram of the kidney alongside the physical filter model.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can explain that kidneys filter waste from the blood.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins explanation and 30 mins demonstration provides a strong analogy for the concept.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not drink the water/sand mixture.
activities.task: Introduce the kidneys as filters. Spend 20 minutes explaining how blood passes through the kidneys, which remove waste to form urine. Spend 30 minutes demonstrating filtration by pouring a mixture of water and sand through a coffee filter, comparing the filter to a kidney.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to dictate their written response.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student writes that the filter catches waste while letting clean liquid pass, just like a kidney.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins setup, 20 mins experiment, 20 mins reflection ensures a complete inquiry cycle.
activities.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Do not ingest the materials.
activities.task: Students perform their own filtration experiment. Spend 20 minutes setting up funnels with different materials (paper towel, cotton). Spend 20 minutes pouring 'dirty' water (water with soil) through them. Spend 20 minutes writing how this models the kidney cleaning the blood.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank (Blood, Filter, Waste, Urine, Kidney).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains that kidneys act as filters to remove waste substances from the blood to produce urine.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes is adequate for drafting and reviewing a short paragraph.
activities.task: Students write a short paragraph explaining what happens to blood when it passes through the kidneys and what liquid is formed as a result.

activities.differentiation: Help students who struggle with counting by tapping the desk for each breath.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student predicts that breathing rate will increase with exercise due to oxygen demand.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins discussion, 20 mins baseline measurement, 15 mins prediction sets up the reasoning task.
activities.safety: Ensure students are seated calmly during the resting measurement.
activities.task: Introduce the link between exercise and respiration. Spend 15 minutes discussing why the body needs oxygen. Spend 20 minutes having students count their breaths for one minute while sitting. Spend 15 minutes discussing what they expect to happen if they run.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-labeled graph axes.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student graphs the data and justifies the increase by stating the body needs more oxygen during exercise.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins active testing and 40 mins graphing/writing allows for careful data processing.
activities.safety: Ensure students have enough space to jog in place without hitting others. Do not force students with asthma to overexert.
activities.task: Test the exercise-respiration link. Spend 20 minutes having students jog in place for two minutes, then immediately count their breaths for one minute. Spend 40 minutes graphing the resting vs. active breath counts and writing a justification for the difference based on oxygen need.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral justification for students who struggle with writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student justifies why breathing rate and air volume exchange increase after physical exertion.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 40 minutes provides time to read the scenario, think, and write a reasoned response.
activities.task: Students are given a scenario comparing a person sitting and a person running. They must predict which person will displace more water in a spirometer model and justify the prediction using the body's need for oxygen.

activities.differentiation: Use a digital pulse oximeter for students who cannot find their pulse manually.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can locate their pulse and record their resting heart rate.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins instruction on finding pulse and 30 mins measurement/discussion ensures accuracy.
activities.safety: Instruct students not to press too hard on their necks.
activities.task: Introduce the link between exercise and circulation. Spend 20 minutes teaching students how to find their pulse on their wrist or neck. Spend 30 minutes having them measure their resting pulse for one minute and recording it, discussing what the pulse represents.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to do arm circles instead of jumping jacks if mobility is limited.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student records a higher active pulse and justifies it by the need to transport substances faster.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins activity/measurement and 40 mins analysis/writing provides a complete reasoning cycle.
activities.safety: Ensure safe spacing for jumping jacks. Monitor students for overexertion.
activities.task: Test the exercise-circulation link. Spend 20 minutes having students do jumping jacks for one minute, then immediately measure their pulse. Spend 40 minutes comparing this to their resting pulse and writing an explanation of why the heart beats faster (to deliver oxygen/nutrients).

activities.differentiation: Provide a cloze paragraph (fill-in-the-blanks) for students needing support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student connects increased physical activity to an increased heart rate to supply nutrients and oxygen.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 40 minutes allows for careful analysis of the data and drafting a reasoned explanation.
activities.task: Students are given a data table showing a person's heart rate at rest and after running. They must write a paragraph explaining why the number of beats per minute changed, referencing oxygen and nutrients.

activities.differentiation: Use physical props (e.g., a toy truck) to model the blood moving between stations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally explain that blood connects the other systems by transporting materials.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins review and 40 mins mapping integrates prior knowledge into a new conceptual framework.
activities.task: Introduce the circulatory system as a transport network. Spend 20 minutes reviewing the functions of the lungs, intestines, and kidneys. Spend 40 minutes drawing a large map on the board showing blood picking up oxygen (lungs) and nutrients (intestines), and dropping off waste (kidneys).

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-printed organ images for students to glue and connect with arrows.
activities.mastery_criterion: Poster accurately shows oxygen/nutrients being picked up and waste being dropped off.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins planning and 45 mins drawing allows for a detailed, accurate synthesis project.
activities.task: Create an integration poster. Spend 15 minutes planning a diagram showing the heart, lungs, intestines, and kidneys. Spend 45 minutes drawing the organs and adding arrows with labels showing what blood picks up and drops off at each location.

activities.differentiation: Pair students up to navigate the stations together.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly navigates the stations, picking up and dropping off the correct tokens.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins setup and 40 mins active simulation solidifies the dynamic nature of the integration.
activities.safety: Ensure clear walking paths between stations to prevent collisions.
activities.task: Role-play the transport system. Spend 20 minutes setting up stations (Lungs, Intestines, Kidneys, Cells) and assigning roles (Blood cells carrying tokens). Spend 40 minutes running the simulation where 'blood' picks up 'oxygen' (blue tokens) and 'nutrients' (green tokens), delivers them to 'cells', and takes 'waste' (red tokens) to 'kidneys'.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with the organs already drawn, requiring only the arrows and sentence.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains how blood acts as the vehicle moving nutrients, oxygen, and waste to their correct locations.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 45 minutes provides ample time for drawing, labeling, and writing the justification.
activities.task: Students draw a simple diagram showing the heart, lungs, intestines, and kidneys, draw arrows showing what blood picks up and drops off, and write a sentence justifying why the circulatory system is like a delivery truck.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use their notes for the first 5 minutes of the sketching phase.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly draws the transport arrows between the organs from memory.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins review and 20 mins sketching is a fast-paced retrieval exercise.
activities.task: Quick mapping recall. Spend 10 minutes reviewing the transport concept. Spend 20 minutes having students quickly sketch the four main organs (heart, lungs, intestines, kidneys) on a whiteboard and draw the transport arrows from memory.

activities.differentiation: Provide a list of key words (oxygen, nutrients, waste, blood) to include in the pitch.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student verbally explains the integration of the systems accurately without notes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins writing and 15 mins speaking provides structured verbal retrieval practice.
activities.task: Verbal explanation recall. Spend 15 minutes having students write a short 'elevator pitch' explaining how the body systems work together. Spend 15 minutes having them present their pitch to a partner without looking at their notes.

activities.differentiation: Use a very stark contrast in water volumes to make the color difference obvious.
activities.mastery_criterion: Rejects the exact-intake inference and names a missing variable or observation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins explanation and 30 mins demonstration clearly models the concept of concentration.
activities.safety: No personal bodily data, samples, health diagnosis or fluid-intake prescriptions.
activities.task: Use a fictional written observation, not a biological sample. Evaluate whether one urine-color observation establishes an exact water intake, identify the missing evidence and explain the limit of the conclusion.

activities.differentiation: Provide a structured scenario template for the writing portion.
activities.mastery_criterion: Rejects the exact-intake inference and names a missing variable or observation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins modeling and 45 mins writing allows for deep reasoning and application to a real-world scenario.
activities.safety: No personal bodily data, samples, health diagnosis or fluid-intake prescriptions.
activities.task: Use a fictional written observation, not a biological sample. Evaluate whether one urine-color observation establishes an exact water intake, identify the missing evidence and explain the limit of the conclusion.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw the cups of water and urine to support their written explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Rejects the exact-intake inference and names a missing variable or observation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 minutes is sufficient for reading, predicting, and justifying the response.
activities.safety: No personal bodily data, samples, health diagnosis or fluid-intake prescriptions.
activities.task: Use a fictional written observation, not a biological sample. Evaluate whether one urine-color observation establishes an exact water intake, identify the missing evidence and explain the limit of the conclusion.

activities.differentiation: Provide a smaller, desk-sized version of the poster for students with visual impairments.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally repeat the names of the 5 major bones and 3 joints when pointed to on the poster.
materials: Large anatomical poster of the human skeleton
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for introduction, 20 minutes for guided identification, and 10 minutes for verbal repetition and checking.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not poke or hit themselves or others when locating bones on their bodies.
activities.task: Introduce the human skeleton using a large anatomical poster. Point out and name the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and major joints (elbows, knees, shoulders). Have students repeat the names and locate the general area on their own bodies over their clothes.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-rolled clay cylinders for students with fine motor difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Clay bones are placed in the correct anatomical positions on the cardboard outline.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup and instruction, 25 minutes modeling and placing, 10 minutes cleanup and review.
activities.safety: Wash hands after using clay. Do not ingest clay.
activities.task: Students use modeling clay to form the shapes of the skull, ribs, spine, femur, and humerus, placing them on a cardboard body outline. They must place small clay balls to represent the joints.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference image of the completed puzzle for guidance.
activities.mastery_criterion: Puzzle is assembled correctly and all required bones and joints are accurately labeled.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes assembling, 20 minutes labeling, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.safety: Ensure clear floor space to prevent tripping.
activities.task: Students work in pairs to assemble a life-size paper skeleton puzzle on the floor, labeling the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and circling the joints with a marker.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank for students who struggle with spelling.
activities.mastery_criterion: Labels placed correctly on the skull, ribs, spine, femur, and humerus. Circles placed on elbows, knees, or shoulders.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instruction, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Given a blank diagram of the human skeleton, label the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and circle three joints.

activities.differentiation: Pre-punch holes in the cardboard for students who lack hand strength.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble the model and can make the cardboard bend by pulling the string.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes explanation, 30 minutes guided construction, 15 minutes demonstration.
activities.safety: Use caution with hole punches and brass fasteners to avoid pinching fingers.
activities.task: Guide students step-by-step to build a mechanical model of an arm using two pieces of cardboard joined by a brass fastener (joint) and a string attached to one piece (muscle). Demonstrate how pulling the string moves the cardboard.

activities.differentiation: Provide a partially assembled model for students to complete.
activities.mastery_criterion: Model demonstrates that the rubber band (muscle) must cross the joint to pull the lower stick (bone).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes design planning, 35 minutes building, 15 minutes testing and adjusting.
activities.safety: Ensure rubber bands are not overstretched to prevent snapping.
activities.task: Students design and build a model of a leg (knee joint) using craft sticks and rubber bands, exploring how the rubber band must be positioned to pull the lower stick upward.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-cut straw pieces.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students explain that pulling the string simulates muscle contraction pulling on bones to bend the fingers.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes cutting and taping straws, 25 minutes threading string, 20 minutes testing and explaining.
activities.safety: Use blunt-tipped scissors. Ensure strings are not wrapped tightly around real fingers.
