activities.task: Students are presented with a short text describing two newly observed stars nearing the end of their lives, one very massive and one similar to our Sun. They must write a short essay predicting their final stages and explaining why their paths diverge.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference diagram for students to check their work. Ask advanced students to write the state of matter (solid/liquid) on each flag.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies and labels the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core in the correct order.
materials: plastic knives or dental floss for cutting
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for material distribution, 30 minutes for building and cutting the model, 20 minutes for labeling and peer checking.
activities.safety: Ensure students use safe cutting tools (floss or dull plastic knives). Wash hands after handling dough.
activities.task: Students build a cross-section model of the Earth using four different colors of modeling dough. They cut the sphere in half to reveal the layers and use toothpicks with paper flags to label the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-filled text boxes with missing words for students who need writing support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly labels all four layers in the correct order from exterior to interior.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for coloring, 30 minutes for researching facts and labeling, 15 minutes for class review.
activities.task: Students are given a large blank diagram of the Earth's cross-section. They must color each layer, draw a line to a text box, and write the name of the layer along with one key fact (e.g., composition or state of matter) sourced from their textbook.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank. The task of spatial identification remains the same.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core in the correct order.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 30 minutes for independent completion, 10 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students complete a diagram labeling quiz where they must write the names of the four main layers of the Earth in the correct boxes pointing to a cross-section image.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the captions. Ask advanced students to include the role of volcanic outgassing in their storyboards.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains that the crust formed from the cooling and solidifying of a magma ocean in their storyboard.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for the mixture preparation and observation, 30 minutes for drawing and writing the storyboard, 10 minutes for sharing.
activities.safety: Do not ingest the mixture. Wash hands after the activity.
activities.task: Students mix cornstarch and water to create a thick paste representing magma. They spread it in a shallow dish and observe as it dries and forms a solid crust on top, drawing a storyboard with three panels showing the wet mixture, the drying process, and the final solid crust, writing a descriptive caption for each.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer to help structure the summary. Challenge advanced students to compare this process to the formation of ice on a lake.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student's summary mentions the cooling of magma or internal processes forming the solid layer.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for reading and highlighting, 30 minutes for drafting the summary, 10 minutes for peer reading.
activities.task: Students read a short text about the terrestrial model of crust formation. They must highlight key terms (magma, cooling, solid, crust) and then write a 5-sentence summary explaining the process in their own words, imagining they are explaining it to a younger sibling.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw a diagram to supplement their written summary if they struggle with writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student explains that the crust formed from the cooling of a magma ocean.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students are given a prompt asking them to explain how the Earth's crust formed according to the terrestrial model. They must write a brief summary without using their notes.

activities.differentiation: Provide a vocabulary list (deflect, solar wind, magnetic field). Ask advanced students to research and mention auroras as evidence of this deflection.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student argues that without the magnetosphere, solar wind would make Earth uninhabitable, connecting the shield concept to habitability.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 25 minutes for the hands-on demonstration and observation, 25 minutes for writing the argument, 10 minutes for class discussion.
activities.safety: Iron filings must remain sealed in plastic bags or clear containers to prevent inhalation or eye irritation. Keep fan away from water.
activities.task: Students place a bar magnet inside a plastic bag and sprinkle iron filings on top to visualize a magnetic field. The teacher uses a fan (solar wind) to blow lightweight particles (confetti) at the bag, showing how a physical barrier deflects them. Students then write an argument explaining why Earth's magnetic field is necessary for life, using the demonstration as an analogy.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the key data points on the Mars sheet. Require advanced students to explain the role of Earth's liquid outer core in generating the field.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student connects the absence of the magnetosphere to the destructive impact of solar wind on habitability, using evidence.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for reading the case study, 30 minutes for writing the comparative paragraph, 10 minutes for peer review.
activities.task: Students analyze a case study of Mars, which lost its magnetosphere. They read data about Mars' current atmosphere and surface radiation levels. They must write a comparative paragraph justifying what would happen to Earth's habitability if its magnetosphere disappeared, using the Mars data as evidence.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer for planning the response before writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student connects the absence of the magnetosphere to the destructive impact of solar wind on habitability.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for writing the response, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students answer a constructed-response question: 'Explain what would happen to Earth's habitability if the magnetosphere suddenly disappeared. Use evidence about solar wind in your answer.'

activities.differentiation: Allow students to focus only on the written explanation if drawing is a barrier.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student illustrates and explains that the loss of the magnetic field allows solar wind to reach the surface, destroying habitability.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes to read the scenario, 20 minutes to draw and write, 5 minutes to share with a partner.
activities.task: Students are given a 'What If?' scenario card stating the Earth's core has completely solidified, stopping the magnetic field. They have 15 minutes to sketch a before-and-after picture of Earth's surface and write a brief caption explaining the change in habitability.

activities.differentiation: Provide a map showing the ISS orbit relative to the magnetosphere for visual context.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student articulates that the magnetosphere blocks solar wind/radiation, and leaving it removes that protection.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for individual thinking and notes, 10 minutes for paired discussion, 10 minutes for writing down the final point.
activities.task: Students participate in a 'Think-Pair-Share' where they must verbally justify to a partner why astronauts traveling to Mars face higher radiation risks than those on the International Space Station (which is within Earth's magnetosphere). They then write down their partner's best point.

activities.differentiation: Provide descriptions with bolded keywords (e.g., 'human habitat', 'surface'). Ask advanced students to identify the specific names of real-world examples (e.g., ISS, Curiosity).
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the purpose of different space exploration vehicles and matches them to their descriptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for examining posters and listing features, 25 minutes for matching descriptions, 15 minutes for class review.
activities.task: Students examine large posters of a space station, a satellite, and a rover. They work in groups to list the visible features of each (e.g., wheels, solar panels, living quarters). They then match functional descriptions provided by the teacher to the correct vehicle based on their feature lists.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-folded brochures with section titles already written. Challenge advanced students to add a fourth section for 'Probes'.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the functions and characteristics of space stations, satellites, and rovers in their brochure.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for folding and setup, 40 minutes for creating the content of the brochure, 10 minutes for a gallery walk.
activities.task: Students create a foldable brochure with three sections: Space Station, Satellite, and Rover. In each section, they must draw a simple icon, write its primary function, and list whether it carries humans, orbits a body, or lands on a surface.

activities.differentiation: Read the scenarios aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches all three vehicles to their functional descriptions in the mission scenarios.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 30 minutes for quiz completion, 10 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students complete a multiple-choice and short-answer quiz where they are given descriptions of missions (e.g., 'We need to monitor weather patterns from orbit without a crew') and must identify which vehicle (space station, satellite, or rover) is required.

activities.differentiation: Provide a checklist of the four components for students to check off as they build. Ask advanced students to explain how their specific instrument gathers data.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student creates a functional model with all required satellite components included and identifiable.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for design briefing, 35 minutes for building the prototype, 15 minutes for presentations.
activities.safety: Ensure safe use of scissors. Avoid sharp edges on cans or plastics if used.
activities.task: Students act as aerospace engineers. They are given a list of required satellite components (container, power source, scientific instruments, communication system). They use craft materials to build a 3D prototype of a satellite, ensuring all four components are present and identifiable, then present their model to the class.

context_tasks.seismic-risk: Students read a brief informational text about El Salvador's volcanic chain (e.g., the Apaneca-Ilamatepec range). They then draw a detailed blueprint of a satellite designed to monitor this volcanic activity. They must label the container, solar panels (power), infrared cameras (instruments), and antenna (communication), and write a sentence for each explaining its specific role in this mission.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with the basic shape of the container already drawn. Challenge advanced students to include a propulsion system for orbit correction.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student creates a diagram with all required satellite components labeled and explained in the context of the mission.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for mission briefing and planning, 30 minutes for drawing and labeling, 15 minutes for writing the explanations.
activities.task: Students read a brief informational text about the supplied location's volcanic chain (e.g., the Apaneca-Ilamatepec range). They then draw a detailed blueprint of a satellite designed to monitor this volcanic activity. They must label the container, solar panels (power), infrared cameras (instruments), and antenna (communication), and write a sentence for each explaining its specific role in this mission.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank of the four components for students who need memory support. The application of drawing and labeling remains.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student diagram includes and correctly labels all four required components, with a valid justification for their specific design choices.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for drawing, labeling, and justifying, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students are given a specific mission context (e.g., monitoring weather patterns over the ocean). They must design a satellite for this mission, drawing a diagram and justifying their choice of scientific instruments, power source, container, and communication system based on the mission's novel context.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn data tables. Challenge advanced students to graph the relationship between initial distance and distance moved.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student accurately records the distances and explains that points further away move a greater distance, modeling expansion.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for setup and safety, 25 minutes for data collection, 20 minutes for analysis and discussion.
activities.safety: Students must wear safety goggles to protect their eyes in case the rubber band snaps.
activities.task: Students use a large rubber band with evenly spaced dots to model expansion. They stretch the band along a ruler, record the new positions of the dots, and calculate the proportional increase in distance to reinforce the concept of universal expansion.

activities.differentiation: Provide templates with the terms already written in order for students who need support. Ask advanced students to include captions explaining the role of gravity.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sequences all six stages of accretion and provides accurate visual representations for each.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 40 minutes for drawing and labeling, 10 minutes for sharing.
activities.task: Students create a six-panel comic strip illustrating the accretion process. They must draw and label each stage (dust, chondrules, meteoroids, asteroids, planetesimals, planets) in the correct chronological order.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-cut circles for students with fine motor difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student correctly orders the four layers from exterior to interior and accurately identifies their states of matter.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for cutting and assembly, 30 minutes for labeling and writing facts, 15 minutes for peer review.
activities.task: Students construct a 2D foldable model of the Earth using concentric paper circles of decreasing sizes. They must label each layer (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core) and write its state of matter (solid or liquid) underneath the flap.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the areas on the flawed blueprint where errors are located. Challenge advanced students to add a propulsion system to their corrected design.
activities.mastery_criterion: Student successfully identifies the missing/incorrect components and produces a corrected diagram with all four required parts labeled.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for analyzing the flawed blueprint, 35 minutes for redrawing and labeling, 10 minutes for class discussion.
activities.task: Students are given a 'flawed' blueprint of a satellite that is missing key components or has them incorrectly labeled. They must identify the errors, redraw the blueprint correctly, and ensure the container, power source, scientific instruments, and communication system are all present and properly labeled.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-stacked cups with highly contrasting colors for students who need clearer visual distinctions.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can correctly state that the bottom layer is the oldest and the top layer is the youngest in a physical model.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for introduction and safety briefing, 25 minutes for building the physical models, 20 minutes for guided observation and discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not ingest sand or gravel. Sweep up any spills immediately to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Introduce the principle of superposition by stacking different colored sand and gravel in clear plastic cups. Explain that the bottom layer was deposited first and is the oldest. Students observe the model and practice identifying the oldest and youngest layers.

activities.differentiation: Offer diagrams with fewer layers (e.g., 3 instead of 5) to focus on the core concept before increasing complexity.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sequence the layers and explicitly mention that lower layers were deposited before upper layers.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes to review the task, 40 minutes for independent analysis and writing, 20 minutes for peer review and correction.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety. Ensure proper lighting for reading diagrams.
activities.task: Students analyze paper diagrams of sedimentary rock layers containing different shapes representing fossils. They must sequence the layers from oldest to youngest and write a short paragraph explaining their reasoning based on the principle of superposition.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-cut paper strips for students with fine motor skill difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: The collage is correctly labeled with the bottom-most layer identified as the oldest and the top-most as the youngest.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 45 minutes for cutting and assembling the collage, 20 minutes for labeling and presenting to the teacher.
activities.safety: Instruct on safe scissor handling. Ensure adequate spacing between students while cutting.
activities.task: Students create a 2D paper collage representing a geological cross-section. They cut out different textured papers to represent rock layers, glue them in a specific sequence, and label the relative age of each layer from oldest to youngest.

activities.differentiation: Allow verbal explanation of the sequence for students who struggle with written assessments.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly sequences all layers in the provided diagram from bottom (oldest) to top (youngest).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for distributing materials and reading instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion of the assessment.
activities.task: Given a diagram of sedimentary rock layers with embedded fossils, sequence the layers from oldest to youngest on the provided assessment sheet.

activities.differentiation: Provide a printed mini-storyboard for students to keep at their desks for closer reference.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally repeat the four stages of fossilization in the correct order.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for the storyboard presentation, 20 minutes for guided group discussion, 20 minutes for a whole-class verbal sequencing exercise.
activities.task: Present a storyboard detailing the four stages of fossilization: death, burial by sediments, compaction into rock, and exposure. Discuss each stage using visual aids and emphasize the chronological order.

activities.differentiation: Include simple icons on the text cards (e.g., a skull for death, a shovel for burial) to support reading comprehension.
activities.mastery_criterion: All description cards are glued in the exact chronological sequence: death, burial, compaction, exposure.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for sorting practice, 40 minutes for finalizing the sequence and gluing, 20 minutes for gallery walk to review peers' timelines.
activities.task: Students receive a set of mixed description cards detailing the fossilization process. They must sort the cards into the correct chronological timeline and glue them onto a timeline poster.

activities.differentiation: Provide templates with pre-drawn backgrounds where students only need to draw the organism and write the captions.
activities.mastery_criterion: The comic strip accurately depicts and describes death, burial, compaction, and exposure in order.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for brainstorming the organism, 40 minutes for drawing and writing captions, 20 minutes for sharing with a partner.
activities.task: Students create a four-panel comic strip illustrating the stages of fossilization for a fictional organism. They must include captions for each panel describing the specific stage.

activities.differentiation: Use larger font sizes and increased line spacing on the assessment sheet.
activities.mastery_criterion: All four stages must be placed in the exact chronological sequence.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Arrange four descriptions of an organism dying, being buried, compacting into rock, and being exposed in the correct chronological order on the assessment sheet.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to physically manipulate the foam blocks themselves to feel the directional movements.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can match the physical movement of the foam blocks to the terms convergent, divergent, and transform.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for teacher demonstration, 25 minutes for students to practice with blocks in small groups, 15 minutes for summarizing on the board.
activities.safety: Ensure foam blocks are clean and free of small tearable pieces to prevent choking hazards.
activities.task: Demonstrate plate movements using foam blocks on a table. Show blocks colliding (convergent), moving apart (divergent), and sliding past each other (transform). Draw corresponding arrows on the board.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference key on the desk showing the arrow patterns next to the boundary names.
activities.mastery_criterion: All boundaries on the map are correctly color-coded according to the directional arrows.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for reviewing the color code, 45 minutes for map analysis and coloring, 15 minutes for teacher verification.
activities.task: Students analyze abstract maps showing tectonic plates with directional arrows. They must color-code the boundaries (e.g., red for convergent, blue for divergent, green for transform) based on the arrows.

activities.differentiation: Use self-correcting puzzle cuts so only the correct pieces physically fit together.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble all three-piece puzzles correctly matching name, arrows, and feature.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for explaining the puzzle mechanics, 45 minutes for group puzzle solving, 20 minutes for recording the matches in notebooks.
activities.task: Students complete a matching puzzle activity where they connect three pieces: the boundary name, a diagram of the arrows, and a simple drawing of the resulting geological feature (e.g., trench, ridge).

activities.differentiation: Provide the three vocabulary words in a word bank at the top of the page.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly classifies all three boundary types based on the directional arrows.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Given three diagrams showing arrows of plate movement (moving apart, colliding, sliding past), classify each as convergent, divergent, or transform.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use hand gestures (colliding hands, sliding hands) before saying the word to reinforce memory.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can instantly recall and state the correct boundary type for the given arrow diagram.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for pairing and distributing cards, 25 minutes for the flashcard game, 10 minutes for class debrief.
activities.task: Students participate in a rapid flashcard game in pairs. One student shows a card with arrows, and the other must quickly name the boundary type. They tally correct answers.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of diagrams to 9 for students who need a more focused task.
activities.mastery_criterion: All 15 diagrams are placed in the correct bins based on their arrows.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for setup, 25 minutes for the sorting activity, 10 minutes for checking the bins as a class.
activities.task: Students are given a mixed stack of 15 small diagrams showing various plate movements. They must sort them into three labeled bins (Convergent, Divergent, Transform) as quickly and accurately as possible.

activities.differentiation: Provide a simple T-chart on the board listing 'Energy' under Magnitude and 'Damage/Effects' under Intensity.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally distinguish that magnitude is about the energy of the event, while intensity is about the observable effects on the surface.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for the drop demonstrations, 25 minutes for explicit instruction and defining terms, 15 minutes for Q&A.
activities.safety: Ensure students stand back during the drop demonstration to avoid sand splashing into eyes.
activities.task: Explain the difference between magnitude (energy released) and intensity (surface damage). Demonstrate by dropping a heavy book and a light book onto a tray of sand from the same height (magnitude difference), then dropping the heavy book onto sand vs a hard desk (intensity/surface effect difference).

activities.differentiation: Pre-underline the key sentences in the text so the student only has to decide which color to use.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly highlights energy descriptions in yellow and damage descriptions in pink, with a logical written justification.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for reading the text, 40 minutes for highlighting and writing justifications, 20 minutes for class discussion.
activities.task: Students read excerpts from historical hazard reports. They use a yellow highlighter for sentences describing energy released (magnitude) and a pink highlighter for sentences describing structural damage (intensity). They write a sentence justifying one of their choices.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters (e.g., 'The seismograph recorded an energy release of...' and 'Citizens reported seeing...')
activities.mastery_criterion: Report A contains only energy-related facts; Report B contains only surface-effect descriptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for brainstorming, 45 minutes for drafting the two reports, 15 minutes for sharing with a partner.
activities.task: Students write two short fictional news reports about the same earthquake. Report A must focus strictly on the magnitude (seismograph readings, energy). Report B must focus strictly on the intensity (how people felt it, damage to buildings).

activities.differentiation: Allow students to circle key words in the reports that helped them make their decision.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies both terms and provides a justification based on energy versus surface effects.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent reading and writing.
activities.task: Read two short reports: one detailing the energy released at the epicenter and another describing the structural damage in a city. Identify which report describes magnitude and which describes intensity, justifying the choice.

activities.differentiation: Use images alongside the words on the magnetic cards (e.g., a seismograph line for seismic activity).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can correctly identify seismic activity and gas emissions as valid monitoring parameters.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for direct instruction, 25 minutes for the interactive board sorting, 15 minutes for summarizing.
activities.task: Introduce the physical and chemical parameters used to monitor volcanoes (seismic activity, gas emissions). Contrast these with unrelated environmental factors (wind speed, lunar phases) using a sorting activity on the board.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the data categories in different colors to help students distinguish between the types of information before filtering.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students successfully filter the log, circling only seismic and gas data while crossing out weather data.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explaining the data log format, 40 minutes for independent filtering, 20 minutes for reviewing the correct answers.
activities.task: Students review a mock data log from an observatory. The log contains mixed data (seismic tremors, gas levels, rainfall, wind direction). Students must cross out the irrelevant data and circle the parameters that indicate volcanic activity.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-calculated budget sheet so the focus remains on selecting the correct sensors rather than the math.
activities.mastery_criterion: The final station design includes only seismometers and gas sensors, rejecting unrelated equipment.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explaining the catalog and budget, 45 minutes for selecting sensors and drawing the layout, 15 minutes for sharing designs.
activities.task: Students design a paper layout for a volcanic monitoring station. They are given a budget of hypothetical points and a catalog of sensors (seismometers, gas sniffers, anemometers, telescopes). They must select only the valid volcanic sensors to 'purchase' and place on their map.

activities.differentiation: Read the list of options aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: Selects only seismic activity and gas emissions without including unrelated environmental factors.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Select the correct volcanic monitoring parameters from a mixed multiple-choice list that includes seismic activity, wind speed, gas emissions, and lunar phases.

activities.differentiation: Provide a printed diagram of the jar model with fill-in-the-blank labels for students to complete during the demonstration.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the three main layers in the jar model and state one physical characteristic of each.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for building the model, 25 minutes for discussing characteristics, 15 minutes for labeling the jar as a class.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not eat the materials to maintain hygiene. Check for food allergies if handling is involved.
activities.task: Build a physical soil profile model in a large clear jar using whole cookies (bedrock), crushed cookies (subsoil), and chocolate cereal (organic topsoil). Discuss the physical characteristics of each horizon as it is added.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the color words in the text description to guide the coloring process.
activities.mastery_criterion: The diagram is colored to match the descriptions (e.g., dark top, rocky bottom) and correctly labeled with horizon names.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for reading the descriptions, 45 minutes for coloring and labeling, 15 minutes for peer comparison.
activities.task: Students receive a blank cross-sectional diagram of soil and a text describing the color, organic matter, and rock content of three horizons. They must color the diagram accordingly and label each horizon.

activities.differentiation: Provide a checklist of characteristics (dark, light, rocky, soft) for students to tick off as they observe the bags.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly matches the dark soil to the surface horizon, sandy to subsoil, and gravel to parent material, with valid justifications.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for observation, 40 minutes for matching and writing justifications, 20 minutes for class discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure bags are securely sealed to prevent inhalation of dust or soil spills.
activities.task: Students examine sealed transparent bags containing different safe soil materials (e.g., dark potting soil, sandy subsoil, gravel). They must match each bag to its likely horizon based on visual characteristics and justify their choice in writing.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank of horizon names.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly matches all provided descriptions to the corresponding layers in the diagram.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Label a diagram of a soil profile with the correct horizons based on provided descriptions of color, organic matter, and rock content.

activities.differentiation: Use a jar with very distinct, contrasting layers to make visual identification easier.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can follow the calculation steps and understand that the sand layer's volume relative to the total volume determines its percentage.
materials: Pre-settled jar of soil and water
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for observing the jar, 25 minutes for step-by-step calculation on the board, 15 minutes for guided practice with hypothetical numbers.
activities.safety: Ensure the glass jar is handled carefully to prevent breakage.
activities.task: Demonstrate soil texture by showing a pre-settled jar of soil and water. Point out the distinct layers of sand, silt, and clay. Measure the total height of the soil and the height of the sand layer with a ruler, and calculate the percentage of sand on the board.

activities.differentiation: Provide a step-by-step calculation template where students only need to plug in their measurements.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurately measures the layers in millimeters and correctly calculates the sand percentage using the formula.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for measuring, 40 minutes for calculations and verifying with group members, 20 minutes for reporting results to the class.
activities.safety: Use plastic jars instead of glass to prevent breakage. Ensure lids are taped shut.
activities.task: Students work in groups with pre-settled plastic jars of different soil samples. They use rulers to measure the total soil height and the sand layer height, then calculate the percentage of sand for their specific jar.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-labeled axes on the graph paper.
activities.mastery_criterion: All five percentages are calculated correctly and accurately represented on the bar graph.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for reviewing the data, 35 minutes for calculations, 30 minutes for graphing.
activities.task: Given a worksheet with hypothetical volume data for five different soil samples, students calculate the sand percentage for each and create a bar graph comparing the sand content of the samples.

activities.differentiation: Include the formula (Sand Volume / Total Volume x 100) at the top of the page.
activities.mastery_criterion: Provides the correct mathematical calculation and final percentage.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent calculation.
activities.task: Given the total volume of a settled soil sample in a jar and the volume of its sand layer, calculate the percentage of sand in the sample.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to closely inspect the root structure of an extra grass patch to make the abstract concept of 'stabilization' concrete.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can observe and state that the grass tray lost less soil because the roots held the soil in place.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for setup and demonstration, 25 minutes for observation and discussion of the runoff, 15 minutes for summarizing the role of roots.
activities.safety: Wipe up any spilled water immediately to prevent slipping hazards.
activities.task: Demonstrate erosion by pouring equal amounts of water over two inclined trays: one with bare soil and one covered with a patch of grass. Collect the runoff in clear cups to show the difference in soil loss. Discuss how roots stabilize the soil.

activities.differentiation: Provide a list of possible ground covers for students to choose from rather than generating them from scratch.
activities.mastery_criterion: The experimental design includes a control (bare soil) and variables, with a logical hypothesis referencing root or cover stabilization.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explaining the components of an experimental design, 45 minutes for drafting the design and hypothesis, 15 minutes for peer review.
activities.task: Students design an experiment on paper to test different types of ground cover (e.g., leaves, twigs, planted seeds) against erosion. They must write a hypothesis predicting which cover will be most effective and justify it based on the concept of soil stabilization.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence frames for the justification paragraph (e.g., 'I predict this hillside will erode more because...').
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies deforested areas as high risk and justifies the prediction by explaining the lack of root stabilization.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for analyzing the photos, 40 minutes for writing predictions and justifications, 20 minutes for class discussion.
activities.task: Students analyze photographs of different hillsides (some forested, some deforested). They must predict which areas are at highest risk for erosion during a heavy rainstorm and write a paragraph justifying their predictions using evidence of vegetation cover.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw a diagram alongside their written justification to help express their reasoning.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly predicts the bare soil will erode more and justifies it by referencing the stabilizing effect of vegetation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Predict which of two inclined soil trays (one bare, one covered with grass) will lose more soil when equal amounts of water are poured over them, and justify the choice using evidence of root stabilization.

activities.differentiation: Discuss the rebar analogy as a class for 5 minutes before beginning the writing task.
activities.mastery_criterion: The writing clearly draws a parallel between roots holding soil together and rebar holding concrete together.
materials: Picture of rebar in concrete (for reference)
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for introducing the analogy, 25 minutes for writing, 10 minutes for sharing.
activities.task: Students complete a quick-write activity comparing the structural role of plant roots in soil to the role of steel rebar in concrete, explaining how both provide internal stabilization.

activities.differentiation: Provide a partially completed map where students only need to fill in the linking verbs.
activities.mastery_criterion: The concept map logically connects the terms, showing that vegetation/roots increase stability and decrease erosion/runoff.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for reviewing the terms, 25 minutes for creating the map, 10 minutes for comparing maps with a partner.
activities.task: Students create a concept map connecting the terms: Vegetation, Roots, Soil Stability, Water Runoff, and Erosion. They must write linking verbs on the arrows between the terms.

activities.differentiation: Use highly contrasting images (e.g., a lush cornfield vs a jagged cliff) to make the initial concept obvious.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally match the flat land to agriculture and the steep land to conservation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for image analysis, 25 minutes for direct instruction on capacity categories, 15 minutes for Q&A.
activities.task: Introduce the concept of land use capacity by showing pictures of flat, fertile plains and steep, rocky hillsides. Discuss why the flat land is suited for intensive agriculture and the steep land for forest conservation based on soil aptitude.

activities.differentiation: Include small visual icons on the profile cards (e.g., a steep angle icon for high slope) to aid reading comprehension.
activities.mastery_criterion: All profile cards are sorted into the correct use category based on their physical descriptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explaining the categories, 40 minutes for sorting the cards in groups, 20 minutes for reviewing the correct placements.
activities.task: Students sort profile cards of different land plots (describing slope, soil depth, and rockiness) into ideal use categories (intensive agriculture, pasture, forest conservation).

activities.differentiation: Provide a simplified map with only three distinct zones to color-code.
activities.mastery_criterion: The map correctly assigns agriculture to flat/fertile areas and forestry to steep/rocky areas.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for reading the map key, 45 minutes for analyzing the zones and coloring, 15 minutes for displaying the maps.
activities.task: Students create a land-use map for a fictional town. They are given a base map with topographical lines and soil descriptions. They must color-code areas for agriculture, forestry, and urban development based on the land's capacity.

activities.differentiation: Use a drawing-lines matching format instead of writing out the category names.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly categorizes all provided land descriptions to their appropriate use capacity.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Match descriptions of land plots (e.g., flat fertile plains vs. steep rocky hillsides) to their ideal potential use categories (e.g., intensive agriculture vs. forest conservation).

activities.differentiation: Provide a smaller, personal timeline for students to follow along.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify at least one mass extinction and the Cambrian explosion on the timeline.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for introduction, 25 minutes for timeline exploration, 15 minutes for Q&A.
activities.task: Introduce the geological time scale, highlighting major mass extinctions and the Cambrian explosion. Use a large timeline on the board to point out these events.

activities.differentiation: Color-code the eras to help students narrow down where events belong.
activities.mastery_criterion: All event cards are placed in the correct geological periods.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for instructions, 45 minutes for sorting and gluing, 15 minutes for review.
activities.task: Students are given a blank geological time scale and a set of event cards (mass extinctions, Cambrian explosion). They must place the events in the correct periods on the timeline.

activities.differentiation: Use a simplified timeline with fewer distractors.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly points out the extinction events and the Cambrian explosion.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.
activities.task: Identify the periods of mass extinctions and the Cambrian explosion on a provided geological time scale.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-measured mass values for students who struggle with using the balance, allowing them to focus on the volume measurement and calculation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate measurement recording and correct calculation of density using the mass/volume formula.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins introduction and setup, 30 mins for hands-on measurement and calculation, 15 mins for discussion and review.
activities.safety: Ensure any spilled water is wiped up immediately to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Students measure the mass of different solid blocks using a balance and calculate their volume by water displacement in a graduated cylinder. They record data in a table, calculate the density for each block, and compare their results to identify materials. The teacher reviews the data tables to ensure correct calculations and units.

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual chart showing the relationship between displaced fluid weight and buoyant force.
activities.mastery_criterion: Written justifications correctly link the object's behavior to the weight of the displaced fluid compared to the object's weight.
materials: Various objects (some that float, some that sink)
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins for data collection, 20 mins for calculations, 20 mins for writing justifications.
activities.safety: Use plastic containers instead of glass to prevent breakage if heavy objects are dropped.
activities.task: Students submerge objects of known density into water and measure the displaced volume. They calculate the weight of the displaced water and compare it to the object's weight to predict and observe floating or sinking. They write a short justification for each object's behavior.

activities.differentiation: Use blocks with highly contrasting side areas to make the differences in indentation very obvious.
activities.mastery_criterion: Conclusions explicitly state that smaller contact areas result in greater pressure for the same force.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins setup, 30 mins experimentation and measurement, 15 mins writing conclusions.
activities.safety: Ensure sand is not thrown or blown into eyes.
activities.task: Students place a rectangular wooden block on a bed of sand in three different orientations (flat, side, upright). They measure the depth of the indentation left in the sand for each orientation. They write a conclusion relating the contact area to the pressure exerted (depth of indentation).

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-drawn outline of the bottle for students to trace the water streams onto.
activities.mastery_criterion: Drawings and descriptions correctly show that water from lower holes shoots further due to higher hydrostatic pressure at greater depth.
materials: Tall plastic bottle with holes at different heights
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins observation, 15 mins drawing, 15 mins writing descriptions.
activities.safety: Teacher prepares the bottle with holes beforehand to avoid students using sharp tools.
activities.task: Students observe a demonstration or simulation of a tall water container with holes at different heights. They draw the trajectory of the water streams and write a description of how the distance the water shoots out relates to the depth of the hole.

activities.differentiation: Provide a fill-in-the-blank template for the explanation to guide students in using the correct terminology.
activities.mastery_criterion: Explanations correctly apply Pascal's principle, noting that pressure is transmitted equally, resulting in a larger force on the larger area.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins assembly and exploration, 20 mins guided questioning, 20 mins writing explanations.
activities.safety: Ensure tubing is securely attached to prevent water spraying under pressure.
activities.task: Students connect two syringes of different sizes with plastic tubing filled with water. They push the small plunger and observe the force required and the movement of the large plunger. They write an explanation of how pressure is transmitted through the fluid to create a larger force.

activities.differentiation: Provide definitions of cohesion and adhesion on the board for quick reference during the activity.
activities.mastery_criterion: T-charts accurately distinguish between surface tension (cohesion) and capillarity (adhesion).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 mins for the two mini-experiments, 30 mins for creating and reviewing the T-charts.
activities.safety: Use food-safe coloring and ensure students do not ingest the materials.
activities.task: Students perform two mini-experiments: dropping water onto a coin until it spills (surface tension) and placing a celery stalk in colored water (capillarity). They create a T-chart comparing the two phenomena, identifying the dominant force (cohesion or adhesion) for each.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-labeled graph axes for students who need support with data visualization.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate calculation of flow rate (volume/time) and correct plotting of data points on the graph.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins data collection, 20 mins calculations, 20 mins graphing.
activities.task: Students use a stopwatch and a graduated cylinder to measure the volume of water collected from a tap at different valve openings over 10 seconds. They calculate the flow rate for each setting and graph flow rate vs. valve opening.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to verbally explain their reasoning to the teacher before writing it down.
activities.mastery_criterion: Justifications correctly state that speed increases in the narrow section to maintain a constant flow rate.
materials: Clear plastic tubing with varying diameters
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes inspect the supplied flow diagram, 15 minutes compare controlled diameter cases, 10 minutes individual explanation, remaining minutes for feedback and checking what was held constant.
activities.safety: Teacher handles the injection of food coloring to avoid messes.
activities.task: Teacher demonstrates water flowing through a clear plastic tube that has a wide section and a narrow section, injecting food coloring to show speed changes. Students observe and write a justification for why the speed changes.

activities.differentiation: Provide a partially completed diagram where students only need to add the labels for 'high' and 'low' pressure.
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the model-consistent pressure comparison and one for limiting it to the stated assumptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins experimentation, 20 mins drawing diagrams, 20 mins writing predictions.
activities.task: A supplied ideal-flow model specifies steady incompressible flow along one horizontal streamline with no pump or dissipative loss. Its legend relates higher speed to lower static pressure. Compare two labelled points and explain why the legend alone is not a universal rule for every real airflow.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank including terms like 'lift', 'pressure', 'speed', and 'propeller'.
activities.mastery_criterion: Distinguishes model from measurement and names pressure or force evidence needed for a quantitative claim.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins examining models, 30 mins writing descriptions.
activities.safety: Paper models only; no real drone or propeller equipment.
activities.task: Inspect a supplied drone-flow sketch. Distinguish the model arrows from actual pressure or force measurements and explain why the drawing alone cannot quantify lift. Propose one relevant measurement.

activities.differentiation: Provide formula sheets and step-by-step calculation guides for the density problems.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct calculations and logical rankings based on the principles of statics.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 40 mins independent work, 20 mins peer review.
activities.task: Students complete a structured problem set calculating densities of various objects, determining which face of a block exerts the most pressure, and ranking containers based on hydrostatic pressure at the bottom. They peer-review their answers using a rubric.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to work in pairs to discuss the scenarios before writing their individual answers.
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the model-consistent pressure comparison and one for limiting it to the stated assumptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 45 mins scenario analysis, 15 mins class discussion.
activities.task: A supplied ideal-flow model specifies steady incompressible flow along one horizontal streamline with no pump or dissipative loss. Its legend relates higher speed to lower static pressure. Compare two labelled points and explain why the legend alone is not a universal rule for every real airflow.

activities.differentiation: Provide a basic template for a boat shape for students who struggle with the initial design phase.
activities.mastery_criterion: Designs maximize displaced volume, and justifications correctly reference Archimedes' principle.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 mins design and calculation, 40 mins testing and modifying, 20 mins final justification.
activities.safety: Ensure spilled water is cleaned up.
activities.task: Students design and build a small boat out of aluminum foil that can hold the maximum number of metal washers without sinking. They must calculate the density of their boat before adding washers and justify their design choices based on buoyancy and displaced fluid.

activities.differentiation: Provide extra time and allow oral responses for the short-essay questions for students with writing difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the model-consistent pressure comparison and one for limiting it to the stated assumptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 60 mins for independent completion of the assessment.
activities.task: A supplied ideal-flow model specifies steady incompressible flow along one horizontal streamline with no pump or dissipative loss. Its legend relates higher speed to lower static pressure. Compare two labelled points and explain why the legend alone is not a universal rule for every real airflow.

activities.differentiation: Use simple numbers (e.g., mass 10, volume 2) to reduce cognitive load on arithmetic and focus on the concept.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct grouping of cards based on accurate mental or scratchpad density calculations.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins explanation, 15 mins sorting activity, 5 mins review.
activities.task: Students are given cards with mass and volume data for various unknown materials. They must quickly calculate the densities and sort the cards into groups of identical materials.

activities.differentiation: Provide calculators to ensure arithmetic errors do not mask conceptual understanding.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate calculation and correct identification of the material from the table.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins calculation and identification, 10 mins sharing results.
activities.task: Students receive a 'mystery object' profile with its mass and volume. They calculate its density and use a provided reference table of material densities to identify what the object is made of.

activities.differentiation: Review the inverse relationship between speed and pressure verbally before starting the timer.
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the model-consistent pressure comparison and one for limiting it to the stated assumptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins drawing and labeling, 10 mins peer correction.
activities.task: A supplied ideal-flow model specifies steady incompressible flow along one horizontal streamline with no pump or dissipative loss. Its legend relates higher speed to lower static pressure. Compare two labelled points and explain why the legend alone is not a universal rule for every real airflow.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the prediction (e.g., 'I predict the paper will... because the fast air creates...').
activities.mastery_criterion: One point for the model-consistent pressure comparison and one for limiting it to the stated assumptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins prediction, 5 mins demonstration, 15 mins discussion.
activities.task: A supplied ideal-flow model specifies steady incompressible flow along one horizontal streamline with no pump or dissipative loss. Its legend relates higher speed to lower static pressure. Compare two labelled points and explain why the legend alone is not a universal rule for every real airflow.

activities.differentiation: Provide a step-by-step formula guide for students who need help structuring their calculations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct calculation of buoyant force and accurate prediction of floating or sinking.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins review, 30 mins independent practice, 15 mins peer review.
activities.task: Students solve a series of word problems calculating the buoyant force on different objects submerged in various fluids, determining if they will float or sink.

activities.differentiation: Use simple ratios for piston areas to reduce mathematical complexity for struggling students.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate application of Pascal's principle to find the correct output force.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins guided practice, 40 mins independent problem solving.
activities.task: Students calculate the force output of various hydraulic press systems given the input force and the areas of the pistons.

activities.differentiation: Provide a conversion chart for units (e.g., liters to milliliters, minutes to seconds).
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct use of the flow rate formula and appropriate units in all answers.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins introduction, 35 mins practice, 10 mins review.
activities.task: Students analyze different scenarios (e.g., filling a pool, water flowing through a pipe) and calculate the flow rate or the time required to move a specific volume of fluid.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw diagrams to support their written explanations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Distinguishes model from measurement and names pressure or force evidence needed for a quantitative claim.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins reading scenarios, 40 mins writing explanations.
activities.safety: Paper models only; no real drone or propeller equipment.
activities.task: Inspect a supplied drone-flow sketch. Distinguish the model arrows from actual pressure or force measurements and explain why the drawing alone cannot quantify lift. Propose one relevant measurement.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-made data table for recording volume and time.
activities.mastery_criterion: Conclusions correctly state that higher hydrostatic pressure results in a faster flow rate.
materials: Large water containers with a hole at the bottom
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins setup and data collection, 20 mins calculations, 20 mins discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure floors are kept dry to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Students investigate how the hydrostatic pressure (depth of water in a container) affects the flow rate of water exiting a hole at the bottom.

activities.differentiation: Provide extended time for students who require it.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly calculating density and hydrostatic pressure in 4 out of 5 problems, and accurately explaining Pascal's principle in a short essay.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 60 mins for independent completion of the test.
activities.task: Students complete a written test covering all concepts of fluid statics, including multiple-choice questions, calculations, and short-answer explanations.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use hand signals (thumbs up/down) instead of speaking.
activities.mastery_criterion: Immediate and correct responses indicating that pressure increases with depth.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins quiz, 15 mins review of incorrect answers.
activities.task: Students participate in a rapid-fire quiz where they must state whether pressure increases, decreases, or stays the same in various underwater scenarios.

activities.differentiation: Provide a partially filled concept map for students who need scaffolding.
activities.mastery_criterion: Concept maps correctly show that pressure is constant throughout the enclosed fluid.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins drawing, 10 mins sharing.
activities.task: Students quickly draw a concept map linking 'force', 'area', 'pressure', and 'enclosed fluid' to demonstrate their understanding of Pascal's principle.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of cards for students who process information more slowly.
activities.mastery_criterion: All cards are matched correctly within the time limit.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins matching activity, 10 mins review.
activities.task: Students match cards showing a volume and a time with the corresponding flow rate card.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-weighed objects for students who struggle with the spring scale.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students conclude that the buoyant force is equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 30 mins data collection, 30 mins analysis and conclusion.
activities.task: Students measure the volume of water displaced by various submerged objects and compare the weight of the displaced water to the apparent loss of weight of the object in water.

activities.differentiation: Provide a step-by-step formula guide.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct calculation of displaced fluid weight and buoyant force in 4 out of 5 problems.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 45 mins independent practice, 15 mins review.
activities.task: Students solve word problems calculating the volume of displaced fluid and the resulting buoyant force for objects of different shapes and sizes.

activities.differentiation: Read scenarios aloud for auditory learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: 100% correct matching of scenarios to Archimedes' principle statements.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins quiz, 15 mins review.
activities.task: Students complete a quick quiz matching scenarios of submerged objects with the correct statement about their displaced fluid and buoyant force.

activities.differentiation: Provide a table of fluid densities.
activities.mastery_criterion: Accurate calculation of hydrostatic pressure using the correct formula and units.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 40 mins problem solving, 20 mins peer review.
activities.task: Students calculate hydrostatic pressure at various depths for different fluids (water, oil, saltwater) using the density and depth variables.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to work in small groups.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correct categorization and justification based on cohesion or adhesion forces.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 40 mins categorization, 20 mins class discussion.
activities.task: Students read descriptions of natural phenomena (e.g., water droplets on leaves, sap rising in trees) and categorize them as examples of surface tension or capillarity, justifying their choice.

activities.differentiation: Provide fewer images for students who need more time.
activities.mastery_criterion: All images sorted correctly within 5 minutes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins sorting, 15 mins review.
activities.task: Students quickly sort images into two piles: 'Surface Tension' and 'Capillarity'.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn particle outlines for students who need support focusing on the motion arrows.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly draw and label diagrams showing longer motion arrows for higher temperatures.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for demonstration, 15 minutes for drawing, 15 minutes for class discussion and rule formulation.
activities.safety: Ensure marbles stay within the tray to prevent slipping hazards on the floor.
activities.task: Introduce the particle model using a physical demonstration with marbles in a tray. Shake the tray slowly to represent low temperature, then vigorously to represent high temperature. Students draw diagrams of both states with motion arrows.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to express their rule verbally before writing it down.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students state that food coloring spreads faster in hot water because the particles have higher kinetic energy and move faster.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 15 minutes observation, 15 minutes writing and sharing rules.
activities.safety: Use hot tap water only (no boiling water) to prevent scalds.
activities.task: Students observe food coloring spreading in hot tap water versus cold water. They record observations and write a rule connecting the speed of spreading to particle kinetic energy.

activities.differentiation: Pair students to discuss their sequencing before gluing the diagrams.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sequence the diagrams based on arrow length and explicitly link arrow length to kinetic energy and temperature.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes cutting, 15 minutes sequencing and discussing, 15 minutes writing explanations.
activities.task: Students analyze a set of four diagrams showing particles with varying arrow lengths. They must sequence the diagrams from coldest to hottest and explain their reasoning.

activities.differentiation: Students with mobility constraints can use hand gestures or drumbeats to represent particle speed.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately adjust their movement speed to match the called-out temperatures and move in random directions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes rule setting, 20 minutes activity, 10 minutes debrief.
activities.safety: Establish clear boundaries and a 'no running/touching' rule to prevent collisions.
activities.task: Students act as particles in a designated safe space. The teacher calls out different temperatures, and students adjust their walking speed to represent the average kinetic energy. Emphasize random directionality during the movement simulation to avoid misconceptions.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank (kinetic energy, temperature, speed, particles) for students who need vocabulary support.
activities.mastery_criterion: 1 point for selecting the correct diagram; 1 point for explicitly linking temperature to particle movement/kinetic energy.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection and review.
activities.task: Given diagrams of particles in two identical containers at different temperatures, select the diagram representing the higher temperature and state the rule connecting temperature to particle speed.

activities.differentiation: Provide partially filled maps for students who need scaffolding.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label all five phase changes on their visual map.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes demonstration and explanation, 15 minutes labeling, 10 minutes review.
activities.safety: Wipe up any spilled water immediately to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Present a visual map of phase changes (melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation). Use a cold glass of water to demonstrate condensation and an ice cube melting to demonstrate melting. Students label the map.

activities.differentiation: Highlight key phrases in the stories (e.g., 'turned into a gas') for reading support.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately classify at least 4 out of 5 scenarios with the correct scientific term.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading, 20 minutes classifying, 10 minutes peer review.
activities.task: Students read a series of short stories describing everyday events (e.g., mirror fogging up, puddle disappearing) and classify the phase change occurring in each.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to dictate their explanation to a peer if writing is a barrier.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the process as condensation and draw water vapor turning into liquid droplets.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 15 minutes observation, 15 minutes drawing and labeling.
activities.safety: Ensure bags are tightly sealed to prevent leaks.
activities.task: Students place a sealed plastic bag with a small amount of warm water near a cold window and observe condensation forming. They draw the process and label the phase change.

activities.differentiation: Read the scenarios aloud for students with reading difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: 1 point per correctly classified scenario using the exact scientific term.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Read three scenarios (dew forming on leaves, dry ice disappearing, a puddle drying up) and classify each with the correct scientific term for the phase change.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use abbreviations (e.g., 'Cond' for condensation) if writing speed is an issue.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the phase change for each scenario presented.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes distribution, 20 minutes quick-fire rounds, 5 minutes collection.
activities.task: Quick-fire whiteboard session: The teacher describes a scenario, and students write the phase change term on their whiteboards and hold it up.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank for the fill-in-the-blanks.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly fill in all blanks with the appropriate phase change terms.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 15 minutes independent work, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students complete a 'fill-in-the-blanks' paragraph describing the water cycle, using the correct phase change terms.

activities.differentiation: Use visual diagrams of air columns to support the book analogy.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally explain that higher altitude means lower pressure and a lower boiling point.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes explanation and analogy, 10 minutes guided discussion, 10 minutes note-taking.
activities.safety: Ensure the stack of books is stable and won't fall on anyone.
activities.task: Explain the concept of atmospheric pressure using the analogy of a stack of books. Discuss how lower pressure at higher altitudes makes it easier for liquid particles to escape as gas, lowering the boiling point.

activities.differentiation: Provide sentence starters for the explanatory paragraph.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students identify the trend that boiling point decreases as altitude increases and attribute it to atmospheric pressure.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes data analysis, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.task: Students compare the boiling points of water at sea level and on a high mountain using a provided data table. They write a paragraph explaining the trend.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so one can pull the plunger while the other observes and records.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students explain that pulling the plunger lowers the pressure, allowing the warm water to 'boil' without adding heat.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup and safety briefing, 15 minutes experimentation, 15 minutes discussion.
activities.safety: Use supplied records only; students do not heat liquids or manipulate pressure equipment.
activities.task: Compare a teacher-supplied pressure-versus-boiling-temperature dataset with the same liquid and measurement conditions. Use the paired records to explain the trend; no pressure vessel, syringe or heating experiment is performed.

context_tasks.seismic-risk: Predict whether water will boil at a higher or lower temperature on top of the San Salvador volcano compared to the port of La Libertad. Justify your answer using the concept of atmospheric pressure.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw a diagram to support their written justification.
activities.mastery_criterion: 1 point for predicting a lower boiling point; 1 point for justifying it with lower atmospheric pressure at higher altitudes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Predict whether water will boil at a higher or lower temperature on top of the a supplied volcanic-location case compared to the port of the supplied location. Justify your answer using the concept of atmospheric pressure.

activities.differentiation: Provide a diagram of the bottle and balloon for students to annotate during the explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that the balloon inflates because the gas particles move faster and spread apart when heated.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes explanation of the particle model, 15 minutes student diagramming.
activities.safety: Use hot tap water, not boiling water, to prevent scalds.
activities.task: Demonstrate thermal expansion by placing a balloon over a bottle and setting the bottle in a bowl of hot tap water. Explain the macroscopic expansion using the microscopic particle model.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with the outline of the thermometer for drawing particles.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students draw particles spreading further apart in the warm state, explaining that increased kinetic energy causes expansion.
materials: Cups of cold and warm water
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes observation, 20 minutes drawing and writing, 10 minutes sharing.
activities.safety: Use alcohol thermometers, not mercury. Handle carefully to prevent breakage.
activities.task: Students place a thermometer in cold water, then in warm water, observing the liquid inside rise. They draw a particle model explaining why the liquid takes up more space when warm.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank (expand, particles, kinetic energy, spread apart).
activities.mastery_criterion: Students explain that the metal lid expands because its particles move faster and spread apart when heated, loosening the grip.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading and discussion, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students analyze a scenario where a tight metal lid on a glass jar is loosened by running it under hot water. They write an explanation using the particle model.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to include a labeled diagram as part of their explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: 1 point for mentioning heat transfer to the gas; 1 point for explaining that particles move faster and spread apart (expansion).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Explain why a balloon placed over the mouth of a bottle inflates when the bottle is placed in hot water, using the particle model.

activities.differentiation: Provide a printed version of the T-chart with missing keywords for students to fill in.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students accurately copy the T-chart and can verbally state one difference between heat and temperature.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes direct instruction and charting, 10 minutes discussion, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Create a T-chart on the board comparing Heat and Temperature. Define heat as energy in transit (Joules) and temperature as average kinetic energy (Celsius). Students copy and discuss.

activities.differentiation: Review the definitions verbally before starting the worksheet.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label at least 80% of the statements.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes review, 20 minutes independent work, 10 minutes peer grading.
activities.task: Students are given a list of statements and must label each as describing 'Heat' or 'Temperature'.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template with the cup and hands already drawn.
activities.mastery_criterion: The poster accurately visually distinguishes between energy transfer (heat) and a measure of kinetic energy (temperature).
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes drawing, 10 minutes gallery walk.
activities.task: Students create a mini-poster illustrating the difference between heat (energy moving from a hot cup to hands) and temperature (the thermometer reading of the cup).

activities.differentiation: Pair students to discuss the sorting before finalizing their piles.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort all cards into the appropriate categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes setup, 20 minutes sorting activity, 10 minutes review.
activities.task: Students play a sorting game with cards containing units (Joules, Celsius, Kelvin) and definitions, sorting them into 'Heat' and 'Temperature' piles.

activities.differentiation: Read the statements aloud for students who need reading support.
activities.mastery_criterion: 1 point for correctly sorting the units; 1 point for correctly sorting the conceptual definitions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.
activities.task: Sort a list of statements and units into two categories: 'Heat' and 'Temperature'.

activities.differentiation: Provide a graphic organizer for students to take notes during the demonstrations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can define and give one example of each of the three heat transfer mechanisms.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes instruction, 20 minutes demonstrations, 10 minutes summary.
activities.safety: Ensure water is warm, not boiling.
activities.task: Introduce conduction, convection, and radiation using visual aids. Demonstrate conduction with a metal spoon in warm water, convection with food coloring in warm water, and radiation by feeling the warmth of a sunny window.

activities.differentiation: Highlight keywords in the scenarios (e.g., 'touching', 'currents', 'space') to guide classification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify at least 8 out of 10 scenarios.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes review, 25 minutes independent work, 10 minutes peer grading.
activities.task: Students are given a worksheet with 10 everyday scenarios and must classify each as conduction, convection, or radiation.

activities.differentiation: Provide a structured planning sheet with prompts for each mechanism.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students explain their design choices using the terms conduction, convection, or radiation.
