activities.mastery_criterion: Students score at least 70% on the assessment, demonstrating solid foundational knowledge before moving to complex cellular processes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins instructions, 70 mins testing, 10 mins collection.
activities.task: Students will complete a mid-unit written assessment covering biomolecules, enzymes, cell types, and levels of organization. The test will include multiple-choice questions, matching sections, and short-answer questions requiring them to apply their knowledge to new examples.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-drawn outline of the nucleotide for students who struggle with fine motor skills, allowing them to focus on labeling and coloring.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly draw and label the three components of a nucleotide with appropriate color-coding.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for teacher explanation and board diagram, 20 minutes for student drawing and color-coding, 10 minutes for peer review and correction.
activities.safety: Ensure students remain seated while using colored pencils to avoid accidental pokes.
activities.task: Introduce the three components of a DNA nucleotide using a large board diagram. Students draw their own nucleotide in their notebooks, color-coding the phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and nitrogenous base, and write a one-sentence definition for each part.

activities.differentiation: Offer a reference card showing the 2D structure to help students translate it into a 3D model.
activities.mastery_criterion: The 3D model accurately reflects the structural connection between the phosphate, sugar, and base.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for material distribution and instructions, 25 minutes for building the model, 10 minutes for partner presentations.
activities.safety: Remind students not to ingest the modeling clay and to wash hands after the activity.
activities.task: Students use modeling clay to build a 3D model of a single nucleotide. They must select three different colors to represent the phosphate, sugar, and base, assemble them in the correct structural arrangement, and present their model to a partner.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use a word bank if they struggle with spelling the scientific terms.
activities.mastery_criterion: All three components are correctly identified on at least two of the three diagrams regardless of orientation.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for independent completion of the worksheet, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety; no specific hazards.
activities.task: Students receive a worksheet with three different blank diagrams of nucleotides in various orientations. They must correctly label the phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and nitrogenous base on all three diagrams.

activities.differentiation: Provide partially filled Venn diagrams for students who need structural support.
activities.mastery_criterion: The Venn diagram correctly places 'nucleus' under eukaryotic, 'nucleoid region' under prokaryotic, and 'contains DNA' in the overlapping section.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for direct instruction and visual comparison, 20 minutes for Venn diagram creation, 5 minutes for review.
activities.task: Present side-by-side diagrams of a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell. Explain the difference between a nucleus and a nucleoid region. Students create a Venn diagram comparing where DNA is stored in both cell types.

activities.differentiation: Include visual icons on the cards (e.g., a simple animal icon or bacteria icon) to assist with organism identification.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 cards into the proper DNA location categories.
materials: Sets of 10 cell description cards per group
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for group setup and instructions, 25 minutes for sorting and discussion, 10 minutes for class-wide verification.
activities.safety: Ensure clear pathways when students move to form groups.
activities.task: Students are given 10 cards with descriptions of different cells (e.g., 'A human skin cell', 'A bacterium found in soil'). They must sort the cards into 'Eukaryotic (Nucleus)' and 'Prokaryotic (Nucleoid)' categories based on prior knowledge of organisms and the new DNA location rules.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral responses for students with severe writing difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: The response explicitly states that plant cell DNA is in the nucleus and bacterial DNA is in the nucleoid region.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes to explain the prompt, 20 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students write a short paragraph answering the prompt: 'If you were a scientist looking for DNA in a plant cell versus a bacterial cell, where exactly would you look in each, and why?'

activities.differentiation: Provide a visual analogy of washing greasy hands with and without soap to help conceptualize membrane breakdown.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students hypothesize that without detergent, the membranes will not break, and DNA will remain trapped inside the cell.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for video and explanation, 20 minutes for guided discussion on lipids and soap, 20 minutes for writing the hypothesis.
activities.safety: No physical chemicals used; standard classroom safety.
activities.task: Demonstrate a virtual or video-based plant DNA extraction. Pause the video before the detergent step. Explain the lipid nature of cell membranes and how soap interacts with lipids. Students write a hypothesis about what would happen if this step were skipped.

activities.differentiation: Pair students so that one can handle the wet materials while the other records observations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Uses the controlled detergent comparison to explain membrane disruption and states that precipitate visibility alone does not establish purity.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for setup and safety briefing, 30 minutes for the extraction and cleanup, 15 minutes for documenting findings.
activities.safety: No student handling of alcohol, extraction reagents or biological samples.
activities.task: Analyze teacher-supplied photographs and paired procedural records of fruit DNA extraction with and without detergent. Identify which step disrupts membranes and evaluate why the visible precipitate alone does not establish pure DNA. Students use the records rather than handling alcohol or extraction chemicals.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the steps in the protocol to help students focus on the sequence and identify what is missing.
activities.mastery_criterion: The review identifies the missing detergent, explains its role in breaking lipid membranes, and predicts that no DNA will be extracted.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes reading the protocol, 25 minutes writing the review, 10 minutes for final review and submission.
activities.task: Students are given a flawed protocol for DNA extraction that omits the detergent step. They must write a critical review of the protocol, identifying the missing step, explaining its purpose based on cell structure, and predicting the outcome of the flawed protocol.

activities.differentiation: Provide templates with the written descriptions already in place, requiring the student only to draw the corresponding visuals.
activities.mastery_criterion: The comic strip shows the four stages in the correct chronological order with accurate visual representations of the chromosomes.
materials: Safe stain (e.g., iodine or food coloring)
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 25 minutes for direct instruction, demonstration, and micrograph analysis, 30 minutes for comic strip creation, 5 minutes for cleanup.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety. Ensure safe handling of glass slides and coverslips.
activities.task: The teacher performs a live demonstration of preparing an onion root tip squash, explaining the process of staining and pressing to see cells. Then, introduce the four main stages of mitosis using large printed micrographs of onion root tip cells on the board. Explain the visual hallmarks of each stage (condensing, aligning, separating, dividing). Students create a four-panel comic strip illustrating these stages in order.

activities.differentiation: Limit the set to 4 clear cards for students who are overwhelmed by the larger set.
activities.mastery_criterion: Pairs successfully create at least two complete, correctly ordered timelines from prophase to telophase.
materials: Sets of 12 micrograph cards per pair
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 40 minutes for sorting and arranging, 10 minutes for teacher verification.
activities.task: Students are given a mixed set of 12 micrographs showing various cells in different stages of mitosis. Working in pairs, they must identify the stage of each cell and arrange them into three complete, sequential timelines of mitosis.

activities.differentiation: Pre-cut the images for students with fine motor difficulties.
activities.mastery_criterion: All four images are pasted in the exact correct sequence, and justifications match the visual evidence.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 10 minutes for cutting, 30 minutes for sequencing, pasting, and writing.
activities.safety: Instruct students on the safe use of scissors.
activities.task: Students receive an assessment sheet with four out-of-order micrographs of mitosis. They must cut them out, paste them in the correct sequence on a new sheet, and write a one-sentence justification for the placement of each image.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to work with a partner if they need collaborative support during retrieval.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students can arrange the four stages in the correct order without hesitation.
materials: Small decks of mitosis image cards
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes setup, 20 minutes for repeated sorting rounds, 5 minutes for packing up.
activities.task: Flashcard speed-sort: Students receive a shuffled deck of mitosis stage images and must arrange them in the correct order as quickly as possible, repeating the process three times to improve their speed.

activities.differentiation: Provide calculators for students who struggle with mental math during the doubling calculations.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate that the chromosome number would double each generation (92, 184, 368) if mitosis produced gametes.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 25 minutes for bead demonstration and explanation, 25 minutes for student calculations, 10 minutes for class discussion.
activities.safety: Ensure beads are not swallowed or left on the floor to prevent slipping.
activities.task: Use a bead model to demonstrate chromosome numbers. Show a cell with 46 beads dividing by mitosis (resulting in 46) versus meiosis (resulting in 23). Walk through a hypothetical scenario on the board showing what happens if two 46-chromosome gametes fuse. Students calculate the resulting chromosome numbers for three generations under this hypothetical scenario.

activities.differentiation: Provide a structured template on the poster paper with designated areas for 'The Problem' and 'The Solution'.
activities.mastery_criterion: The poster clearly contrasts the outcome of fertilization with diploid vs. haploid gametes and justifies meiosis as the mechanism for maintaining species chromosome numbers.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for group planning, 40 minutes for poster creation, 10 minutes for gallery walk.
activities.task: Students work in groups to create a poster explaining 'The Meiosis Solution'. They must visually depict the problem of chromosome doubling and how meiosis solves it by halving the number before fertilization. They must include a written justification.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw a diagram to support their written explanation if they struggle with expressive writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: The response predicts the doubling of chromosomes (to 92) and justifies this by explaining that mitosis does not halve the chromosome number like meiosis does.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for prompt explanation, 35 minutes for writing and diagramming, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students answer a written prompt: 'Predict what would happen to the chromosome number of a human offspring if gametes were produced by mitosis instead of meiosis. Justify your answer using the concepts of fertilization and chromosome sets.'

activities.differentiation: Provide printed copies of the scenarios so students can highlight the key phrases instead of writing them down.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the reproduction type for all three scenarios and cite the presence or absence of two parents/genetic exchange.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for definitions, 30 minutes for the scenario reading and voting activity, 10 minutes for debriefing.
activities.task: Define sexual and asexual reproduction focusing on genetic exchange. Read three distinct scenarios aloud (yeast budding, human fertilization, bacterial fission). For each, students hold up a 'Sexual' or 'Asexual' card and write down the key phrase from the scenario that justifies their choice.

activities.differentiation: Reduce the number of case studies to 8 for students who need more time to process text.
activities.mastery_criterion: At least 13 out of 15 case studies are correctly classified with appropriate evidence underlined.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for instructions, 40 minutes for reading and classifying, 10 minutes for peer review.
activities.task: Students are given a set of 15 short case studies of different organisms reproducing. They must classify each case into a T-chart (Sexual vs. Asexual) and underline the evidence in the text that led to their decision.

activities.differentiation: Provide a sentence starter: 'This is [sexual/asexual] reproduction because...'
activities.mastery_criterion: All three scenarios are correctly classified with a valid explanation referencing genetic exchange or parent number.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for reading and writing, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students read three new, unseen scenarios of organism reproduction. They must write a short paragraph for each, classifying it as sexual or asexual and explaining why based on genetic exchange.

activities.differentiation: Provide pre-drawn outlines of the plants for students to label if drawing is a barrier.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label the seed as sexual and the tuber/graft as asexual in their drawings.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 25 minutes for explanation and observation of physical items, 25 minutes for drawing and labeling, 10 minutes for review.
activities.safety: Ensure students do not eat the raw beans or potatoes. Wash hands after handling.
activities.task: Explain the difference between growing plants from seeds (sexual) and vegetative parts (asexual). Show physical examples or high-quality images of a bean seed, a potato tuber, and a grafted branch. Students draw each method and label it as sexual or asexual.

context_tasks.protected-areas: Using the local-crops context, students analyze agricultural fact sheets about how maize (grown from seed) and potatoes (grown from tubers) are propagated in El Salvador. They must categorize the methods described in the fact sheets into sexual and asexual reproduction.

activities.differentiation: Highlight the specific sentences in the fact sheets that describe the propagation method to guide reading.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize maize propagation as sexual and potato tubers as asexual based on the text.
materials: Printed agricultural fact sheets on maize and potatoes
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for reading the fact sheets, 30 minutes for analysis and categorization, 15 minutes for class discussion.
activities.task: Using the local-crops context, students analyze agricultural fact sheets about how maize (grown from seed) and potatoes (grown from tubers) are propagated in the supplied location. They must categorize the methods described in the fact sheets into sexual and asexual reproduction.

activities.differentiation: Include small illustrations next to each action description to aid comprehension.
activities.mastery_criterion: All five actions are correctly sorted into the sexual (seeds/pits) and asexual (rhizomes, cuttings, bulbs) categories.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for sorting and completing the table, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students are given a list of five plant propagation actions (e.g., planting a sunflower seed, burying a piece of ginger rhizome, planting a mango pit, taking a rose cutting, planting a bulb). They must sort them into a table under 'Sexual' or 'Asexual'.

activities.differentiation: Provide a fill-in-the-blank version of the rule for students who need language support.
activities.mastery_criterion: The written rule accurately states that if gametes meet outside the body (usually in water), it is external; if inside, it is internal.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 25 minutes for direct instruction and diagram analysis, 20 minutes for writing and refining the rule, 15 minutes for sharing rules.
activities.task: Define internal and external fertilization based on where gametes meet. Use a diagram of a fish spawning in water versus a mammal. Students write a rule in their notebooks for determining the type of fertilization based on the environment described.

context_tasks.seismic-risk: Using the protected-areas context, students read fact sheets about three animals found in San Salvador volcano protected areas (e.g., a specific tree frog, a snake, a bird). They must determine if each uses internal or external fertilization based on clues about where the eggs and sperm meet, and write a justification.

activities.differentiation: Bold the sentences in the descriptions that indicate where the gametes are released.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the fertilization type for all three animals and cite the environmental meeting place of gametes as evidence.
materials: Printed fact sheets about the reproductive habits of specific fauna from the San Salvador volcano area
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for reading, 30 minutes for determining and writing justifications, 15 minutes for group sharing.
activities.task: Using the protected-areas context, students read fact sheets about three animals found in a supplied volcanic-location case protected areas (e.g., a specific tree frog, a snake, a bird). They must determine if each uses internal or external fertilization based on clues about where the eggs and sperm meet, and write a justification.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to draw the scenario and label the meeting point of the gametes to support their written answer.
activities.mastery_criterion: The student identifies external fertilization and explains that it is because the sperm and egg meet in the river water, outside the mother's body.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for reading the prompt, 35 minutes for writing the response, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students read a short paragraph about a newly discovered aquatic species that releases thousands of eggs into a river, followed by a male releasing sperm over them. They must state whether this is internal or external fertilization and explain why.

activities.differentiation: Provide a pre-labeled diagram where students only need to write the functions.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly label the shell as protection and the yolk as the nutrient/energy source.
materials: Document camera or gather students around
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 minutes for the demonstration and explanation, 30 minutes for drawing and writing functions, 10 minutes for cleanup and review.
activities.safety: Teacher handles the raw egg. Ensure hands are washed and surfaces sanitized after the demonstration to prevent salmonella exposure.
activities.task: Crack open an unfertilized chicken egg into a petri dish (teacher demonstration). Identify the shell, yolk, and albumen. Explain the function of each for a developing embryo. Students draw the egg and write the survival function next to the shell and yolk.

activities.differentiation: Provide a list of possible synthetic materials (e.g., titanium, battery) to help spark ideas for students who struggle with open-ended design.
activities.mastery_criterion: The design includes a protective outer layer (shell equivalent) and an internal energy source (yolk equivalent), with a logical explanation of their functions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 minutes for explaining the challenge, 35 minutes for designing and writing, 10 minutes for sharing designs.
activities.task: Students are given a design challenge: 'Design a synthetic egg for a robotic embryo.' They must draw their design, explicitly including a structure that acts like a shell and a structure that acts like a yolk, and write a paragraph explaining how their synthetic parts perform the same survival functions as the biological ones.

activities.differentiation: Allow oral assessment for students who have difficulty expressing complex reasoning in writing.
activities.mastery_criterion: The student states that the yolk provides energy to grow, and the shell provides protection.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for writing responses, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Students answer two questions: 1) What is the function of the yolk for a bird embryo? 2) What is the function of the shell? They must state their answers based on the functions of these structures.

activities.differentiation: Provide a cross-section diagram for students to trace if they struggle with 3D visualization.
activities.mastery_criterion: Sketches clearly show the blastula as a simple hollow circle of cells and the gastrula with an inward fold.
materials: Deflated rubber ball or soft foam ball
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 25 minutes for demonstration and explanation, 25 minutes for sketching and labeling, 10 minutes for checking understanding.
activities.task: Explain the transition from a single cell to a blastula (hollow ball) and then a gastrula (folded/layered ball). Demonstrate this using a deflated rubber ball: show it round (blastula), then push one side in (gastrula). Students sketch the two stages and label the key difference (hollow vs. folded).

activities.differentiation: Work in pairs so one student can mold while the other assists with the cutting process.
activities.mastery_criterion: Matches both prepared models to the diagrams, points to the hollow space or fold, and identifies one simplification; model craftsmanship is not scored.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 minutes for material distribution, 40 minutes for modeling and cutting, 10 minutes for teacher inspection.
activities.safety: Models are pre-cut by the teacher; students use no cutting tools.
activities.task: Compare teacher-prepared cross-section clay models of a hollow-ball and folded-layer form with the provided diagrams. Match each model to the diagram and identify one shared feature and one simplification.

activities.differentiation: Provide a word bank (e.g., hollow, fold, layers, cells) to assist with the written explanation.
activities.mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies both supplied models using hollow space and folding; does not treat a model as a literal photograph.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for drawing and writing, 5 minutes for collection.
activities.task: Given two labelled cross-section models and a short key, identify the hollow-ball and folded-layer forms. Point to the structural evidence for each choice and state one limitation of the simplified models.

activities.differentiation: Allow students to use hand gestures (making a hollow ball with hands vs. pushing a fist into a cupped hand) if drawing quickly is stressful.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students consistently draw the correct structure (hollow vs. folded) within the time limit.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for distributing materials, 20 minutes for quick-draw rounds, 5 minutes for cleanup.
activities.safety: Ensure markers are used properly and caps are replaced to avoid drying out or fumes.
activities.task: Whiteboard quick-draw: The teacher calls out either 'Blastula' or 'Gastrula'. Students have 30 seconds to draw the correct cross-section on their mini-whiteboards and hold them up. Repeat for several rounds to build speed and accuracy.

activities.differentiation: Provide a reference poster showing the correct cross-sections for students to check against if they get stuck.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and sort the models based on the presence of a hollow center or an invagination.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for sorting, 5 minutes for review.
activities.safety: Standard classroom safety. Do not ingest clay.
activities.task: Students are given a mixed set of clay models (some blastulas, some gastrulas, some incorrect shapes) prepared by the teacher. They must quickly sort them into 'Blastula', 'Gastrula', and 'Incorrect' piles based on their structural features.

activities.differentiation: Provide a template for the connections.
activities.mastery_criterion: The model accurately represents the three components and their connections.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins planning, 35 mins building, 10 mins sharing.
activities.safety: Ensure no sharp edges on recycled materials.
activities.task: Students use recycled materials (bottle caps, straws, cardboard) to construct a large-scale model of a nucleotide, labeling the phosphate, sugar, and base.

activities.differentiation: Read descriptions aloud for auditory learners.
activities.mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize 90% of the descriptions.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 10 mins setup, 20 mins gameplay.
activities.task: Students play a rapid-fire sorting game on the board, categorizing cell descriptions into 'Nucleus' or 'Nucleoid'.

activities.differentiation: Provide a table template for the calculations.
activities.mastery_criterion: The report correctly calculates the exponential growth of chromosomes and justifies why meiosis is necessary.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 15 mins introduction, 30 mins calculation and writing, 15 mins peer review.
activities.task: Students analyze a hypothetical alien species that reproduces using mitosis for gametes. They must calculate the chromosome number over 5 generations and write a scientific report on why this species would face genetic instability.

activities.differentiation: Provide a list of local plants and their propagation methods.
activities.mastery_criterion: The garden plan correctly identifies the propagation method for each plant and categorizes it accurately.
activities.rationale_for_minutes: 20 mins research/planning, 30 mins drawing, 10 mins presenting.
activities.task: Students design a community garden plan using the local-crops context, selecting specific propagation methods (seeds for maize, tubers for potatoes) and justifying their choices as sexual or asexual.
